Contents of https://docs.github.com/api/article/body?pathname=/en/copilot/reference/custom-agents-configuration:
# Custom agents configuration

Reference for configuring custom agents.

This reference article provides detailed configuration information for custom agents. For general information about creating custom agents, see [Creating custom agents for Copilot cloud agent](/en/copilot/how-tos/use-copilot-agents/cloud-agent/create-custom-agents).

> \[!NOTE]
> Custom agents are in public preview for JetBrains IDEs, Eclipse, and Xcode, and subject to change.

## YAML frontmatter properties

The following table outlines the properties that you can configure for agent profiles in GitHub.com, the Copilot CLI, and supported IDEs (unless otherwise noted). Any environment-specific behavior is noted in the property description. The configuration file's name (minus `.md` or `.agent.md`) is used for deduplication between levels so that the lowest level configuration takes precedence.

<div class="ghd-tool rowheaders">

| Property                   | Type                                                     | Purpose                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| -------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `name`                     | string                                                   | Display name for the custom agent. Optional.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| `description`              | **Required** string                                      | Description of the custom agent's purpose and capabilities                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| `target`                   | string                                                   | Target environment or context for the custom agent (`vscode` or `github-copilot`). If unset, defaults to both environments.                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| `tools`                    | list of strings, string                                  | List of tool names the custom agent can use. Supports both a comma separated string and yaml string array. If unset, defaults to all tools. See [Tools](#tools).                                                                                                                                                        |
| `model`                    | string                                                   | Model to use when this custom agent executes. If unset, inherits the default model.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| `disable-model-invocation` | boolean                                                  | Disables Copilot cloud agent from automatically using this custom agent based on task context. When `true`, the agent must be manually selected. Setting `disable-model-invocation: true` is equivalent to `infer: false`. If both are set, `disable-model-invocation` takes precedence. If unset, defaults to `false`. |
| `user-invocable`           | boolean                                                  | Controls whether this custom agent can be selected by a user. When `false`, the agent cannot be manually selected and can only be accessed programmatically. If unset, defaults to `true`.                                                                                                                              |
| `infer`                    | boolean                                                  | **Retired**. Use `disable-model-invocation` and `user-invocable` instead. Enables Copilot cloud agent to automatically use this custom agent based on task context. When `false`, the agent must be manually selected. If unset, defaults to `true`.                                                                    |
| `mcp-servers`              | object                                                   | Additional MCP servers and tools that should be used by the custom agent. **Not used in VS Code and other IDE custom agents.**                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| `metadata`                 | object consisting of a name and value pair, both strings | Allows annotation of the agent with useful data. **Not used in VS Code and other IDE custom agents.**                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |

</div>

Define the agent's behavior, expertise, and instructions in the Markdown content below the YAML frontmatter. The prompt can be a maximum of 30,000 characters.

> \[!NOTE]
>
> * The `argument-hint` and `handoffs` properties from VS Code and other IDE custom agents are currently not supported for Copilot cloud agent on GitHub.com. They are ignored to ensure compatibility.
> * For more information on custom agent file structure in VS Code, see [Custom agents in VS Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/copilot/customization/custom-agents#_custom-agent-file-structure) in the VS Code documentation.

## Tools

The custom agent `tools` property controls which tools are available to your agent, including those from MCP servers.

Your custom agent will have access to MCP server tools that have been configured in both its agent profile and/or the repository settings. For more information on configuring MCP servers for cloud agent in a repository, see [Extending GitHub Copilot cloud agent with the Model Context Protocol (MCP)](/en/copilot/how-tos/use-copilot-agents/cloud-agent/extend-cloud-agent-with-mcp).

You can configure `tools` using the following approaches:

* **Enable all available tools**: Omit the `tools` property entirely or use `tools: ["*"]` to enable all available tools. This will include all MCP server tools configured in the agent profile and/or repository settings.
* **Enable specific tools**: Provide a list of specific tool names or aliases (for example, `tools: ["read", "edit", "search"]`) to enable only those tools. For available tool aliases, see [Tool aliases](#tool-aliases) below.
  * Note that if your repository has MCP servers configured, you can choose to make only specific tools from those servers available to your custom agent. Tool names from specific MCP servers can be prefixed with the server name followed by a `/`. For example, `some-mcp-server/some-tool`.
  * You can also explicitly enable all tools from a specific MCP server using `some-mcp-server/*`.
  * Tools from VS Code extensions can use the extension name as a proxy, like `azure.some-extension/some-tool`.
* **Disable all tools**: Use an empty list (`tools: []`) to disable all tools for the agent.

All unrecognized tool names are ignored, which allows product-specific tools to be specified in an agent profile without causing problems.

### Tool aliases

The following tool aliases are available for custom agents. All aliases are case insensitive:

| Primary alias | Compatible aliases                           | Cloud agent mapping                                  | Purpose                                                                                                  |
| ------------- | -------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `execute`     | `shell`, `Bash`, `powershell`                | Shell tools: `bash` or `powershell`                  | Execute a command in the appropriate shell for the operating system.                                     |
| `read`        | `Read`, `NotebookRead`                       | `view`                                               | Read file contents.                                                                                      |
| `edit`        | `Edit`, `MultiEdit`, `Write`, `NotebookEdit` | Edit tools: e.g. `str_replace`, `str_replace_editor` | Allow LLM to edit. Exact arguments can vary.                                                             |
| `search`      | `Grep`, `Glob`                               | `search`                                             | Search for files or text in files.                                                                       |
| `agent`       | `custom-agent`, `Task`                       | "Custom agent" tools                                 | Allows a different custom agent to be invoked to accomplish a task.                                      |
| `web`         | `WebSearch`, `WebFetch`                      | Currently not applicable for cloud agent.            | Allows fetching content from URLs and performing a web search                                            |
| `todo`        | `TodoWrite`                                  | Currently not applicable for cloud agent.            | Creates and manages structured task lists. Not supported in cloud agent today, but supported by VS Code. |

### Tool names for "out-of-the-box" MCP servers

The following MCP servers are available out-of-box for Copilot cloud agent and can be referenced using namespacing:

| MCP server name | Available tools                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| --------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `github`        | All read-only tools are available by default, but the token the server receives is scoped to the source repository. `github/*` includes all of them, or you can reference `github/<tool name>` where `<tool name>` is a value from the MCP server documentation.                                                                          |
| `playwright`    | All playwright tools are available by default, but the server is configured to only access localhost. `playwright/*` includes all of them, or you can reference `playwright/<tool name>` where `<tool name>` is a value from the MCP server documentation. By default the token it has access to is scoped to the source code repository. |

## MCP server configuration details

The following sample agent profile shows an agent with an MCP server and a secret configured. Additionally, only one tool from the MCP server has been enabled in the `tools` property in the YAML frontmatter:

```text
---
name: my-custom-agent-with-mcp
description: Custom agent description
tools: ['tool-a', 'tool-b', 'custom-mcp/tool-1']
mcp-servers:
  custom-mcp:
    type: 'local'
    command: 'some-command'
    args: ['--arg1', '--arg2']
    tools: ["*"]
    env:
      ENV_VAR_NAME: ${{ secrets.COPILOT_MCP_ENV_VAR_VALUE }}
---

Prompt with suggestions for behavior and output
```

The `mcp-servers` property in an agent profile is a YAML representation of the JSON configuration format used to configure MCP servers for Copilot cloud agent.

Most sub-properties are the same as the JSON representation. The following sections describe changes from the initial implementation of MCP configuration in Copilot cloud agent that are relevant to custom agents. For more information about the JSON configuration format, see [Extending GitHub Copilot cloud agent with the Model Context Protocol (MCP)](/en/copilot/how-tos/use-copilot-agents/cloud-agent/extend-cloud-agent-with-mcp#writing-a-json-configuration-for-mcp-servers).

### MCP server type

For compatibility, the `stdio` type used by Claude Code and VS Code is mapped to cloud agent's `local` type.

### MCP server environment variables and secrets

> \[!NOTE]
> If your MCP server requires secrets or environment variables, these must be configured in the Copilot environment in each repository where the custom agent will be used. For more information on setting up environment variables, see [Customizing the development environment for GitHub Copilot cloud agent](/en/copilot/how-tos/use-copilot-agents/cloud-agent/customize-the-agent-environment#setting-environment-variables-in-copilots-environment).

Custom agent MCP configuration supports the same environment variable and secret replacement capabilities as existing repository-level MCP configurations. Similar to repository-level configurations, secrets and variables can be sourced from the "copilot" environment in the repository's settings. The syntax for referencing these values has been expanded to support common patterns used in GitHub Actions and Claude Code.

Both the repository-level MCP JSON configuration and the custom agent YAML configuration support the following syntax patterns:

* `$COPILOT_MCP_ENV_VAR_VALUE` - Environment variable and header
* `${COPILOT_MCP_ENV_VAR_VALUE}` - Environment variable and header (Claude Code syntax)
* `${COPILOT_MCP_ENV_VAR_VALUE:-default}` - Environment variable and header with default

The custom agent YAML configuration supports the following additional syntax patterns:

* `${{ secrets.COPILOT_MCP_ENV_VAR_VALUE }}` - Environment variable and header
* `${{ vars.COPILOT_MCP_ENV_VAR_VALUE }}` - Environment variable and header

## Example agent profile configurations

The following examples demonstrate what an agent profile could look like for the common tasks of writing tests or planning the implementation of a project. For additional inspiration, see the [Custom agents](/en/copilot/tutorials/customization-library/custom-agents) examples in the customization library. You can also find more specific examples in the [awesome-copilot](https://github.com/github/awesome-copilot/tree/main/agents) community collection.

### Testing specialist

This example enables all tools by omitting the `tools` property.

```text copy
---
name: test-specialist
description: Focuses on test coverage, quality, and testing best practices without modifying production code
---

You are a testing specialist focused on improving code quality through comprehensive testing. Your responsibilities:

- Analyze existing tests and identify coverage gaps
- Write unit tests, integration tests, and end-to-end tests following best practices
- Review test quality and suggest improvements for maintainability
- Ensure tests are isolated, deterministic, and well-documented
- Focus only on test files and avoid modifying production code unless specifically requested

Always include clear test descriptions and use appropriate testing patterns for the language and framework.
```

### Implementation planner

This example only enables a subset of tools.

```text copy
---
name: implementation-planner
description: Creates detailed implementation plans and technical specifications in markdown format
tools: ["read", "search", "edit"]
---

You are a technical planning specialist focused on creating comprehensive implementation plans. Your responsibilities:

- Analyze requirements and break them down into actionable tasks
- Create detailed technical specifications and architecture documentation
- Generate implementation plans with clear steps, dependencies, and timelines
- Document API designs, data models, and system interactions
- Create markdown files with structured plans that development teams can follow

Always structure your plans with clear headings, task breakdowns, and acceptance criteria. Include considerations for testing, deployment, and potential risks. Focus on creating thorough documentation rather than implementing code.
```

## Processing of custom agents

### Custom agents names

In the case of naming conflicts, the lowest level configuration overrides higher-level configurations. This means that a repository-level agent would take precedence over an organization-level agent, and the organization-level agent would override an enterprise-level agent.

### Versioning

Custom agent versioning is based on Git commit SHAs for the agent profile file. This allows you to create branches or tags with different versions of custom agents as needed. When you assign a custom agent to a task, the custom agent will be instantiated using the latest version of the agent profile for that repository and branch. When the agent creates a pull request, interactions within the pull request use the same version of the custom agent for consistency.

### Tools processing

The `tools` list filters the set of tools that are made available to the agent - whether built-in or sourced from MCP servers. When you configure tools in your agent profile, the behavior depends on what you specify:

* If no tools are specified, all available tools are enabled
* An empty tools list (`tools: []`) disables all tools
* A specific list (`tools: [...]`) enables only those tools

### MCP server configurations

For MCP server configurations, there is a specific processing order that ensures proper override behavior: out-of-the-box MCP configurations (like the GitHub MCP) are processed first, followed by the custom agent MCP configuration, and finally MCP configurations specified through repository settings. This allows each level to override settings from the previous level as appropriate.

189. The United States imports 100\% of its manganese, 100\% of its zirconium
190. mineral concentrates, and 74\% of its chromium~\cite{usgs_mcs_2024}---elements
191. central to high-performance aluminum alloys for advanced manufacturing. A single supply disruption could idle domestic
192. additive-manufacturing production dependent on these materials. FLAIME (Fast
193. Learning AI for Mineral Efficiency) addresses this vulnerability with an
194. AI-autonomous closed-loop platform that discovers and qualifies aluminum alloys
195. meeting structural performance targets while minimizing critical mineral
196. content, directly supporting DOE Critical Materials Strategy Pillars~2
197. (Develop Alternatives) and~3 (Materials and Manufacturing Efficiency).

200. the partial Knowledge Gradient for Function Networks (pKGFN) acquisition
201. function to jointly optimize alloy composition, printability, and mechanical
202. properties across the full powder-to-part pipeline---from CALPHAD evaluation
203. through ultrasonic and gas atomization, laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), and
204. ASTM~E8 sub-size tensile testing. By modeling every manufacturing stage as a node in
205. a cost-aware function-network DAG with an embedded mineral-burden objective,
206. BOFN selects maximally informative experiments at each stage, reducing
207. powder-to-tensile cycle time by an estimated 10$\times$ versus conventional
208. sequential campaigns through the combination of BOFN-guided experiment
209. selection ($\geq$3$\times$ fewer iterations) and closed-loop
210. execution---software-orchestrated with human operators in Phase~I,
211. architected for direct robotic integration in Phase~II.  No existing
212. platform closes this complete composition-discovery and
213. manufacturing-qualification loop: the closest structural-alloy SDL
214. automates printing through testing but not the full
215. powder-to-property pipeline~\cite{conn_2025_apex}.
216. 
217. Phase~I explores \num{22698} element combinations---$\sum_{k=3}^{8}\binom{15}{k}$
218. sub-systems spanning ternary through 9-component alloys---drawn from a
219. 15-element Al-alloy palette via an asynchronous, cost-aware multi-fidelity
220. framework (\texttt{pycalphad}, TC-Python/TCAl10, Thermo-Calc AM~Module)
221. that evaluates CALPHAD thermodynamics, Scheil solidification, and
222. printability in parallel at maximum HPC capacity,
223. then focuses experimental validation on the top 3--5 sub-systems---including
224. the Al--Mn--Cr--Zr and Al--Zr anchors---characterizing $\geq$200 compositions
225. (up to 2~unique compositions/day, 6~days/week) through the full
226. powder-to-tensile pipeline with a discovery yield $\geq$3\%. All
227. experimental data and BOFN models will be shared as a FAIR-compliant
228. digital thread via the Genesis Mission platform and open repositories
229. (Zenodo/Figshare with DOIs). The project enters Phase~I at
230. TRL~2 (concept formulated) and targets TRL~4 (closed-loop validated in
231. laboratory) at the conclusion of the 9-month, \$750K effort.

407. (AMMTO): autonomous discovery platforms, closed-loop AI, accelerated
408. qualification, reducing demand for critical minerals.}
409. 
410. \note{Buy America compliance statement below --- required within the
411. first 2 pages of the Project Narrative (FOA \S IV.C).}
412. 
413. \textbf{Overview.}
414. The U.S.\ depends on foreign sources for 100\% of its manganese, 100\%
415. of its zirconium mineral concentrates, and 74\% of its
416. chromium~\cite{usgs_mcs_2024}---elements central to high-performance
417. aluminum alloys for advanced manufacturing.
418. \flaime{} (Fast Learning AI for Mineral Efficiency) is an
419. AI-autonomous closed-loop platform that discovers aluminum alloys meeting
420. structural performance targets while minimizing critical mineral content.
421. By integrating AI-guided optimization with a complete
422. powder-to-print-to-test manufacturing pipeline---the first to unify
423. computational evaluation, powder atomization, laser powder bed fusion
424. (LPBF), and mechanical testing in one loop---\flaime{} targets
425. $\geq$3$\times$ acceleration over conventional alloy development
426. approaches.%
427. \footnote{Buy America Act compliance: this project does not involve
428. construction, alteration, maintenance, or repair of public
429. infrastructure (FOA \S III.F).}
430. 
431. \textbf{Critical minerals challenge.}
432. A single supply disruption in manganese or chromium could idle U.S.\
433. additive manufacturing production dependent on these elements.
434. Manganese is 100\% import-reliant; chromium and zirconium appear on the
435. USGS Critical Minerals List with high supply-concentration risk~\cite{bauer_2023_1998242}.
436. Beryllium is equally vulnerable:
437. ${\sim}$347{,}000~kg~Be/yr enters alloy production, 84\% from one mine,
438. sustaining a \$250--400M/yr Cu-Be market with $<$1\% recycling~\cite{unknown_2025_3001694}.
439. The DOE Critical Materials Strategy calls for action
440. across Pillar~2 (Develop Alternatives), Pillar~3 (Materials and
441. Manufacturing Efficiency), and Pillar~5 (Enabling Activities)~\cite{bauer_2023_1998242}.
442. AMMTO's CMI Hub at Ames National Laboratory has
443. invested $>$\$80M in follow-on R\&D and advanced Al-Ce alloys to TRL~9~\cite{lograsso_2024_2338076},
444. establishing direct precedent for this work.
445. 
446. Despite this momentum, no existing platform unifies
447. powder production, LPBF printing, and tensile testing under a single AI
448. decision loop.  The closest structural-alloy SDL (APEX) automates DED
449. printing through mechanical characterization but remains
450. human-monitored with no peer-reviewed end-to-end
451. validation~\cite{conn_2025_apex}; A-Lab demonstrates fully robotic
452. powder synthesis but targets oxides, not structural
453. metals~\cite{szymanski_2023_s4158602}.  A recent two-dimensional
454. autonomy framework confirms this gap: high \emph{software} autonomy
455. (AI-directed experiment selection) and high \emph{hardware} autonomy
456. (robotic execution) have not yet been achieved
457. together for structural AM~\cite{tobias_2025_autonomy}.  The critical
458. unsolved problem is closing the \emph{decision} loop across this
459. pipeline, not physical automation alone.  All confirmed AM aluminum deployments---AlSi10Mg satellite
460. structures, Scalmalloy telecom parts ($>$100 in orbit), and the AL250C
461. engine demonstrator---use LPBF exclusively~\cite{hart_2021_s4157802},
462. validating \flaime{}'s focus on the qualification-relevant manufacturing
463. modality.
464.

482. 
483. CALPHAD evaluation via Thermo-Calc TCAL10/TCMG6 databases with
484. Scheil solidification analysis identifies printable, low-cracking-susceptibility
485. regions in the Al-Mn-Cr-Zr space (Fig.~\ref{fig:calphad}); SEM/EDS
486. characterization of ultrasonically atomized powders confirms that designed
487. compositions are experimentally achievable, with final panels to be inserted
488. in the placeholder slot.
489. 
490. \flaime{} closes this gap using Bayesian Optimization over Function
491. Networks (\bofn{}) augmented by an explicit mineral-burden
492. objective that penalizes compositions proportional to their weighted
493. supply-risk index~\cite{astudillo_2019_icml,astudillo_2021_21121531}. Existing
494. platforms either stop at powder synthesis
495. (A-Lab) or optimize process parameters without
496. closing the composition loop (ORNL Peregrine). Recent advances in cost-aware
497. Bayesian optimization make AI-autonomous powder-to-property optimization
498. tractable for the first time~\cite{chawla_2025_arxiv251116930}.
499. 
500. The PI is an established software-orchestrated SDL leader: architect of
501. the frugal-twin framework~\cite{lo_2024_d3dd0022}, lead author of the structural-materials
502. section of a comprehensive SDL review~\cite{tom_2024_acschemr}, and builder of SDL
503. infrastructure---hardware control, device communication, database
504. management, and full pipeline integration---across multiple Acceleration
505. Consortium laboratories over nearly three years.  This hands-on
506. operational experience directly informs \flaime{}'s human-in-the-loop
507. architecture.  The \flaime{} platform generalizes beyond aluminum to
508. other Genesis Mission priorities~(\S\ref{sec:objectives}).
509.

539.         pre-registered random baseline, with bootstrap confidence intervals
540.         across $\geq$20 seeds.
541. \end{enumerate}
542. 
543. \noindent Collectively, these objectives demonstrate that a
544. software-orchestrated, AI-autonomous closed-loop platform can
545. simultaneously accelerate alloy discovery \emph{and} reduce critical
546. mineral dependence---the dual mandate of Topic~3B. Phase~I focuses exclusively on Al alloys processed by LPBF,
547. with Cu-Cr-Zr as a stretch demonstration.
548. The broad 15-element palette (Al + Mn, Cr, Zr, Mg, Si, Cu, Ti, Fe, Ni, Ce,
549. Sc, Li, Er, Zn, Sn) spans 0\% to 100\% USGS import reliance, ensuring the
550. mineral-burden objective produces genuine supply-risk tradeoffs rather than
551. trivially satisfied constraints.
552. 
553. \flaime{} advances from TRL~2 (BOFN DAG + CALPHAD pipeline designed)
554. to TRL~4 at Phase~I exit (closed-loop validated on real Al alloys)
555. to TRL~6 in Phase~II (system in relevant environment with
556. industry-scale powders).
557. 
558. The Be-Cu replacement market represents \$250--400M/yr; \flaime{}'s
559. industry pathway proceeds from powder production (Valimet) through
560. qualification to commercial feedstock supply (Fehrmann
561. Materials~GmbH). The platform will be released open-source; a Month-6
562. internal review will assess selective IP protection for top
563. compositions to best serve commercialization.
564. 
565. Phase~II will extend \flaime{} to AMMTO priority alloys (e.g., 316H for
566. nuclear structural applications), leveraging transfer learning from
567. Phase~I surrogates, and transition mechanical testing to
568. full-size ASTM~E8 specimens on larger-format LPBF systems
569. (${\geq}250$\,mm build plates), enabling direct qualification-grade
570. property data and resolving the known sub-size elongation sensitivity
571. documented for AM metals~\cite{wang_2020_17452759,karnati_2022_mpc20210136}.
572. Phase~I's software-orchestrated architecture provides a
573. hardware-agnostic control layer in which each human handoff is a defined
574. API endpoint; Phase~II replaces human actuators with robotic modules
575. (automated powder dispensing, specimen transfer, SEM prep, and mechanical
576. testing) drawn from the emerging ecosystem of self-driving materials
577. laboratories---a transition requiring dedicated automation engineers and
578. \$6--15M investment appropriate to Phase~II scope.
579. Technology transfer is further enabled by
580. integration of BOFN/pKGFN tutorials into the Honegumi platform and
581. Meta's BoTorch ecosystem.

625. \textbf{Activity~1: AI-Guided Computational Exploration}
626. (\emph{PI, BYU; \$TBD}).
627. %
628. The \flaime{} optimizer is a \bofn{} directed acyclic graph whose nodes
629. mirror the physical pipeline: CALPHAD evaluation (Thermo-Calc
630. TCAl10/TCMG6 via TC-Python), powder properties, LPBF process window, and
631. mechanical response.  The pKGFN acquisition function selects the most
632. cost-informative next experiment at each iteration, routing cheap CALPHAD
633. queries (${\sim}\$1$/eval) before committing to expensive builds
634. (${\sim}\$500$/composition).  A mineral-burden node encodes a
635. composition-weighted supply-risk index
636. $\mathrm{MBS}(\mathbf{x})=\sum_i w_i\,x_i$ (weights from USGS
637. import-reliance data), enabling multi-objective optimization of strength
638. \emph{and} critical mineral reduction simultaneously.
639. An asynchronous, cost-aware multi-fidelity framework deploys three
640. CALPHAD fidelity levels---\texttt{pycalphad} (\$0/eval),
[Thermo-Calc licensing/pricing detail removed]
642. AM~Module (${\sim}$\$100--500/eval)---in parallel at maximum HPC
643. capacity (fairshare-limited, not algorithm-sequenced).  All fidelity
644. outputs flow continuously as input features to the unified GP surrogate:
645. Node~0 CALPHAD outputs (phase fractions, solidification range, CSI)
646. inform every downstream model node.  The pKGFN acquisition function
647. computes value-of-information per dollar, naturally prioritizing cheap
648. evaluations first while deciding which expensive assessments to request
649. next given all data already collected.  Preliminary results confirm
650. pKGFN convergence on a manufacturing benchmark (Fig.~\ref{fig:pipeline}) and active
651. CALPHAD evaluation on BYU HPC.
652. 
653. \begin{figure}[ht]
654.   \centering
655.   \includegraphics[width=0.85\textwidth]{../benchmarks/figures/pkgfn_convergence.png}
656.   \caption{pKGFN convergence on a manufacturing benchmark, demonstrating cost-aware advantage over standard Bayesian optimization baselines.}
657.   \label{fig:pipeline}
658. \end{figure}
659. 
660. \textbf{Two-Level Hierarchical Search.}
661. The search proceeds in two levels.
662. \emph{Level~1 (Element Combination Selection):}
663. \bofn{} explores all $\sum_{k=3}^{8}\binom{15}{k}=\num{22698}$
664. sub-systems---from ternary (e.g., Al--Fe--Si) through 9-component
665. alloys---spanning ${\sim}$\num{119000000} unique compositions at
666. 1\,at.\% resolution (Al\,$\geq$\,85\,at.\%), via an asynchronous
667. multi-fidelity evaluation, a novel NChooseK element-selection problem
668. solved via Bayesian optimization.
669. All three CALPHAD fidelity levels run concurrently at maximum HPC
670. parallelism; since the binding constraint is fairshare rate (not cost),
671. asynchronous BO treats pending HPC jobs as fantasy samples, updating the
672. surrogate as each completes---no synchronous batch waits.
673. %
674. \emph{Fidelity~1} (\texttt{pycalphad}, \$0): Sobol/LHS coarse sampling
675. (${\sim}50$ compositions per sub-system, $\sim$\num{1130000} total)
676. computes equilibrium phase fractions, Scheil solidification curves,
677. crack-susceptibility index (CSI), and mineral-burden scores for all
678. \num{22698} sub-systems.
679. At ${\sim}10$~calcs/sec/core on 64~cores, Fidelity~1 completes in under
680. one hour on a single BYU HPC node.
681. %
[Thermo-Calc licensing/pricing detail removed]
683. targeted sub-systems receive Scheil solidification with
684. back-diffusion (MOBAL8 solver), TC-PRISMA precipitation kinetics
685. (e.g., L$_{1\text{2}}$-Al$_3$Zr nucleation and coarsening), and fully
686. assessed multicomponent thermodynamics---capabilities that require
687. commercially assessed ternary interaction parameters unavailable in
688. free databases.
689. %
690. \emph{Fidelity~3} (Thermo-Calc AM~Module): selected compositions
691. receive steady-state printability maps (lack-of-fusion / stable /
692. keyhole regimes), melt-pool geometry, $G$/$R$ conditions overlaid on the
693. columnar-to-equiaxed transition (CET), and Scheil curves with the
694. solute-trapping extension at LPBF cooling rates
695. ($10^{4}$--$10^{6}$~K/s)---identifying unprintable candidates before any
696. powder is atomized.
697. %
698. All CALPHAD outputs flow as features to downstream GP nodes: Fidelity~1
699. phase fractions and CSI inform the Fidelity~2 and~3 models, and all
700. fidelity data feeds the unified surrogate continuously.  For large
701. composition spaces (6+ components, 15K--54K compositions), SVDKL deep
702. kernel GPs handle phase-boundary non-stationarity via learned features
703. while preserving the GP posterior interface needed by BOFN;
704. for small spaces (${\leq}5$ components, ${\leq}3{,}876$ compositions),
705. exact GPs suffice.  The cost-aware pKGFN acquisition function decides
706. which expensive evaluations to request next based on all available data.
707. %
708. \emph{Level~2 (Composition Optimization):}
709. pKGFN optimizes compositions within the top 3--5 sub-systems through
710. the full experimental pipeline.  Al--Mn--Cr--Zr and Al--Zr serve as
711. guaranteed ``anchor'' systems that receive experimental validation
712. regardless of Level~1 rankings, ensuring continuity with prior
713. results while enabling the AI to discover sub-systems a human
714. designer might not consider.
715. 
716. \textbf{Activity~2: Experimental Validation Pipeline}
717. (\emph{PI + partners; \$TBD}).
718. %
719. Powder feedstocks are produced via ultrasonic atomization (AMAZEMET
720. rePOWDER, BYU) for rapid composition iteration and gas atomization
721. (Valimet subaward) for production-scale lots.  SEM/EDS of atomized
722. powders already confirms ${\leq}2$\,wt\% deviation from targets
723. (Fig.~\ref{fig:calphad}).  LPBF printing is performed at the University of Utah (Taylor
724. Sparks lab; 3D~Powder Tech backup).  A minimum-viable-specimen (MVS)
725. progression manages throughput: single tracks $\to$
726. $5{\times}5{\times}5$\,mm density cubes (${\geq}99$\% relative density
727. gate) $\to$ ASTM~E8 sub-size tensile bars (Fig.~\ref{fig:composite}).

787. Low atomization yield $\to$ Valimet gas-atomization fallback.  Modest

832. \guidance{6-MONTH DOE REVIEW POINT (FOA p.61): ``go/no go evaluation at
833. 6 months.''  Structure the milestone table around this checkpoint --- the
834. month 5--7 Go/No-Go gates are the primary decision point for DOE
835. program managers.  The final 9-month milestones confirm completion but
836. the 6-month review determines continuation.}

838. % --- 5. Data Sources and Models (~0.5 page) --------------------------------
839. \section{Data Sources and Models}\pagebudget{0.5}
840. \label{sec:data}
841. 
842. \guidance{FOA: ``Describe which existing or new data sources will be
843. used.  Address your team's access to the data.  If applicable, indicate
844. which AI models or frameworks will be used.  Do NOT include computing
845. resource descriptions here --- that goes in Appendix 2 (Facilities).''}
846. 
847. \textbf{Data sources.}
848. CALPHAD thermodynamic data are drawn from Thermo-Calc's TCAL10 (aluminum) and
849. TCMG6 (magnesium) databases via the TC-Python API under BYU's HPC license
850. (Thermo-Calc collaboration letter, Appendix~7).
851. DFT-computed formation energies from the Materials Project augment CALPHAD
852. features as surrogate-model inputs; experimental benchmarks follow the MMPDS
853. handbook.
854. All \flaime{}-generated data will be published on Zenodo/Figshare with
855. persistent DOIs; the PI's MPTS-52 dataset, heavily reused by the
856. crystal-structure generative-AI community, evidences this open-data commitment.
857. 
858. \textbf{AI models.}
859. Bayesian Optimization over Function Networks (\bofn{}) with the partial
860. Knowledge Gradient (pKGFN) acquisition function drives cost-aware experiment
861. selection atop GPyTorch/BoTorch Gaussian-process surrogates.
862. \bofn{}/pKGFN code will be released as open-source Python packages with
863. Honegumi tutorials and integrated into BoTorch's tutorial ecosystem (Meta
864. letter of support, Appendix~7).
865. 
866. \textbf{Genesis Mission integration.}
867. \flaime{} is designed for integration with the American Science Cloud (AmSC)
868. and will host its digital thread, alloy database, and \bofn{}/pKGFN models on
869. the platform as it becomes available, participating in GM coordination
870. activities.  All datasets are simultaneously deposited on Zenodo/Figshare with
871. persistent DOIs, ensuring immediate FAIR-compliant open access to the broader
872. materials science community.  \bofn{}/pKGFN will be released as a domain-specific
873. ``plug-and-play'' capability per the GM framework.
874. Bidirectionally, \flaime{} will leverage other GM teams' validated
875. data---shared characterization databases and benchmark property
876. sets---to accelerate CALPHAD surrogate training.
877. 
878. % --- 6. Decision Gate Metrics (~0.5 page) -----------------------------------
879. \section{Decision Gate Metrics}\pagebudget{0.5}
880. \label{sec:gates}
881. 
882. \guidance{FOA: ``Provide specific metrics that can be used for the
883. evaluation of Phase I go/no go decision.  DOE encourages the development
884. of metrics to identify AI advantage.  One such metric could include
885. scaling behavior which shows increasing performance as additional data,
886. computing, and/or other resources are applied.  Quantitative statements
887. enabling transformative science and engineering through AI are
888. preferred.''}
889. 
890. \instruct{Key metrics to define: (1) AI advantage metric (e.g.,
891. compositions screened per unit time vs.\ conventional), (2) scaling
892. behavior (does performance improve with more data/compute?), (3)
893. qualification-relevant metric (how much of the traditional qualification
894. process is compressed?).  All metrics must be quantitative.}
895. 
896. \guidance{SCALABILITY (Review Criterion 2, FOA p.84): ``Does the
897. application address potential scalability issues?''  Include at least
898. one metric demonstrating scaling behavior --- e.g., compositions
899. screened per week as dataset grows, or model accuracy as function of
900. training data volume.  AMMTO values paths from lab-scale to
901. production-scale.}
902. 
903. \guidance{AI ADVANTAGE --- define precisely what ``AI advantage'' means
904. for this project: (1)~10x faster screening (5 days/composition vs.\
905. 8--32 weeks conventional), (2)~autonomous experimental campaigns that
906. reduce human labor per composition, (3)~compressed qualification
907. timelines via digital thread.  The FOA uses ``AI advantage'' as a
908. central evaluation concept; your Decision Gate Metrics must quantify it.}
909. 
910. Three quantitative metrics define Phase~I go/no-go evaluation.
911. %
912. \textbf{(1)~AI Acceleration Factor.}
913. $\mathrm{AF}(y) = n_{\mathrm{baseline}} / n_{\mathrm{BOFN}}$ measures the
914. iteration reduction \bofn{} achieves relative to each of four pre-registered
915. baselines---random search~(B1), expert DOE~(B2), standard BO~(B3), and a
916. \bofn{} ablation without the mineral-burden objective~(B4)---with $\geq$20
917. replicate seeds, bootstrap confidence intervals, and win-rate reporting.
918. Phase~I target: AF\,$\geq$\,3$\times$ vs.\ random (conservative; the
919. cross-study SDL median is $\sim$6$\times$~\cite{sabanzagil_2025_s4358802}).
920. %
921. \textbf{(2)~Discovery Yield.}
922. Fraction of BOFN-proposed compositions satisfying all family-specific
923. mechanical thresholds (e.g., Al-Mn-Cr-Zr: YS\,$\geq$\,250\,MPa,
924. EL\,$\geq$\,5\%; verified per ASTM E8 sub-size) \emph{and} supply-risk reduction
925. versus the Scalmalloy incumbent.  The 15-element palette creates genuine
926. supply-risk variance---constituent elements span 0\% (Fe) to 100\% (Sc)
927. USGS import reliance---ensuring mineral-burden scores reflect real
928. supply-chain tradeoffs rather than trivially low baselines.
929. Phase~I target: $\geq$\,3\%.
930. %
931. \textbf{(3)~Mineral-Burden Reduction.}
932. Weighted critical-mineral content (wt\,\%) of the best-performing \flaime{}
933. alloy versus the Scalmalloy incumbent (Al-Mg-Sc-Zr).
934. Phase~I target: $\geq$\,30\% reduction.
935. 
936. \textbf{Scaling behavior.}
937. BOFN surrogate accuracy (cross-validated MAE) and acquisition efficiency
938. improve monotonically as CALPHAD-screened and experimentally validated
939. compositions accumulate, demonstrating increasing performance with additional
940. data.
941.

948. the preparation of this application. GitHub Copilot (Claude Opus 4.6, high-effort reasoning) was used for
949. code development (BOFN/pKGFN benchmark implementation) and document drafting.
950. All AI-generated content was reviewed, validated, and revised by the PI
951. before inclusion.

108. ## Hierarchical Search Space Architecture (from Edison Search Space Reframing Assessment)
109. 
110. > **Source:** `edison-trajectories/edison-search-space-reframing.md` (Edison graded current framing B → proposed reframing A-)
111. > **Addresses:** PR #26 "trivial satisfaction" risk — broad palette creates genuine MBS variance
112. 
113. ### 15-Element Al-Alloy Palette
114. 
115. | Tier                              | Elements               | Rationale                                                                    |
116. | --------------------------------- | ---------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
117. | **Core** (high TCAl10 coverage)   | Mn, Cr, Zr, Mg, Si, Cu | Established Al alloying elements; strong binary/ternary assessment in TCAl10 |
118. | **Expanded** (moderate coverage)  | Ti, Fe, Ni, Ce, Sc     | Important for AM alloys; partially assessed ternaries                        |
119. | **Exploratory** (sparse coverage) | Li, Er, Zn, Sn         | Emerging/niche elements; some binary-only extrapolation                      |
120. 
121. **Supply-risk variance:** Fe = 0% USGS import reliance → Sc = 100% import reliance. This full span ensures the mineral-burden score (MBS) produces genuine supply-chain tradeoffs — directly addressing the PR #26 concern that restricting to inherently low-critical-mineral elements makes the KPI trivially satisfied.
122. 
123. ### Two-Level Search Architecture
124. 
125. **Level 1 — Element Combination Selection (computational, under 1 hour on HPC):**
126. - Evaluate all C(15,k) for k=3..8 = **22,698 sub-systems** spanning ternary through 9-component alloys:
127.   - C(15,3) = 455 ternary (e.g., Al-Fe-Si)
128.   - C(15,4) = 1,365 quaternary (e.g., Al-Mn-Cr-Zr)
129.   - C(15,5) = 3,003 quinary
130.   - C(15,6) = 5,005 senary
131.   - C(15,7) = 6,435 septenary
132.   - C(15,8) = 6,435 octonary
133. - Level 1 uses an **asynchronous, cost-aware multi-fidelity framework**:
134. 
135.   **Fidelity 1 (pycalphad, $0):** Sobol/LHS coarse sampling (~50 compositions per sub-system, ~1.13M total evaluations) computes equilibrium phase fractions, Scheil solidification curves, crack-susceptibility index (CSI), and mineral-burden scores for all 22,698 sub-systems. At ~10 calcs/sec/core on 64 cores, completes in under one hour on a single BYU HPC node.
136. 
[Thermo-Calc licensing/pricing detail removed]
138. 
139.   **Fidelity 3 (Thermo-Calc AM Module):** Selected compositions receive steady-state printability maps (lack-of-fusion/stable/keyhole regimes), melt-pool geometry, G/R conditions overlaid on the columnar-to-equiaxed transition (CET), and Scheil curves with solute-trapping extension at LPBF cooling rates (10⁴–10⁶ K/s). Identifies unprintable candidates before any powder is atomized.
140. 
141. - All fidelity levels run at maximum HPC parallelism (fairshare-limited, not algorithm-sequenced); async BO treats pending jobs as fantasy samples, updating the surrogate as each completes
142. - CALPHAD outputs (phase fractions, solidification range, CSI) flow as features to all downstream GP nodes — not discarded after evaluation
143. - GP scaling: exact GP for ≤5 components (≤3,876 compositions), SVDKL deep kernel GP for 6–7 components (15K–54K), SVDKL+RF for 8 components (170K+)
144. - Cost-aware pKGFN decides which expensive evaluations to request next based on all available data
145. - **Novel contribution:** NChooseK element-combination selection via Bayesian optimization with mineral-burden objective — no published precedent
146. - **Published precedents for scale:** Vazquez 2023 (500K TC-Python evals), Wang 2025 (150K→2B via ML surrogate), Sundar 2025 (CALPHAD BO)
147. 
148. **Level 2 — Composition Optimization (experimental, 9-month campaign):**
149. - pKGFN optimizes compositions within top 3–5 sub-systems through the full powder-to-tensile pipeline
150. - Al-Mn-Cr-Zr and Al-Zr are guaranteed "anchor" systems — receive experimental validation regardless of Level 1 rankings
151. - Composition dimensionality per sub-system: 4-component = 816 compositions (exact GP tractable), 6-component = 155K (SVDKL needed)
152. - Experimental budget: ≥200 compositions through MVS pipeline
153. 
154. ### TCAl10 Coverage Note
155. 
156. Al-Mn-Cr-Zr has 0/4 constituent ternaries assessed in TCAl10 — all predictions rely on binary extrapolation. This is acceptable for dilute Al-rich compositions but should be acknowledged as a limitation. The 15-element palette achieves 53.3% assessed ternary coverage overall, which is strong for quaternary prediction.

186. - **Draft content (R4-revised, ~85 words — opens with the problem, not the acronym):**
187.   > The U.S. depends on foreign sources for 100% of its manganese and the majority of its chromium and zirconium — elements central to high-performance aluminum alloys for advanced manufacturing. FLAIME (Fast Learning AI for Mineral Efficiency) is an autonomous closed-loop platform that discovers aluminum alloys meeting structural performance targets while minimizing critical mineral content. By integrating AI-guided optimization with a complete powder-to-print-to-test manufacturing pipeline — the first to unify computational evaluation, powder atomization, laser powder bed fusion, and mechanical testing in one loop — FLAIME targets ≥3× acceleration over conventional approaches.

314. - [ ] **Unique claim**: "No existing SDL integrates powder → LPBF → tensile in closed loop"

316. - [ ] **Platform-first framing**: Lead with the national problem and autonomous platform need, not the alloy system
317. - [ ] **Critical minerals framing**: Al-Mn-Cr-Zr as critical-mineral-lean alternatives (Mn, Cr, Zr are on USGS 2022 Critical Minerals List; Mn is 100% import-reliant)

319. ### D.3 PI Credibility (Addressing Early-Career Profile)

325. - [ ] **11 letters total**: 3 collaboration (Valimet, AMAZEMET, Thermo-Calc) + 8 support

335. ### D.5 Presentation Quality (Critical — 5-page limit)
336. 
337. - [ ] **Every sentence earns its space**: No filler, no repetition
338. - [ ] **Figures/tables**: Count against 5-page limit; budget ~4 figures at ~1.4 pages total (per Edison R5 guidance)
339. - [ ] **~500 words per page** at 11pt Times — plan word counts per section
340. - [ ] **Word-count targets (R13 rebalance)**: §1 ~300w, §2 ~250w, §3 ~400w, §4 ~200w + table, §5 ~160w, §6 ~180w, buffer ~80w (total ~1,570w body text, leaving space for 4 figures + 1 table)
341. - [ ] **No Table of Contents**: Wastes space in 5-page document
342. - [ ] **All references in Appendix 1** (free pages — don't waste narrative space on bibliographic details)
343. - [ ] **Computing resources in Appendix 2** (FOA explicitly says "do not include in narrative")
344. - [ ] **Overview paragraph opens the narrative**: Lead with the national problem, not jargon (Edison R4: "The U.S. depends on foreign sources for 100% of its manganese…")

346. ### D.6 Narrative Guardrails (Avoid Reviewer Red Flags)
347. 
348. - [ ] Al alloy performance claims limited to **≤ 300°C applications** — do not claim hot-section or turbine blade replacement
349. - [ ] No superalloy replacement claims — Al alloys serve different applications than IN718/316H

352. - [ ] **Critical Mineral Demand Reduction Index (CMDRI)** quantified vs. Scalmalloy (primary) and AlSi10Mg (secondary) comparators
353. - [ ] **Honest reporting framework**: Time-ledger decomposition separating automation × AI × throughput acceleration components

370. ## E. FAQ-Derived Clarifications (Quick Reference)
371. 
372. *Key clarifications from the official FAQ (v2, 2026-03-23) that supplement or clarify the RFA. Reference these when questions arise during drafting.*
373. 
374. | Topic                          | FAQ Clarification                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
375. | ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
376. | **Phase I goals**              | "Provide a quantitative assessment of whether the proposed approach to demonstrating AI advantage…is on a trajectory to yield a transformative scientific capability or transformative approach to an energy application" |
377. | **Go/No-Go timing**            | At 6 months; may request up to 3-month extension to complete planned tasks                                                                                                                                                |
378. | **Phase II from Phase I**      | "Only a small fraction of Phase I teams will be selected"; Phase II teams may include multiple Phase I teams, add/remove members                                                                                          |
379. | **Budget period**              | Single period: July 1, 2026 → March 31, 2027                                                                                                                                                                              |
380. | **Phase II funding**           | ~$6M–$15M over 3 years ($2M–$5M/year)                                                                                                                                                                                     |
381. | **PI terminology**             | RFA has only one "PI" (the lead PI); all others are "senior/key persons" — co-PI is informal                                                                                                                              |
382. | **Career stage**               | No career-stage limitations on PI eligibility                                                                                                                                                                             |
383. | **First-time DOE PI**          | Explicitly eligible per FAQ: "anyone who meets the requirements of a lead PI may apply"                                                                                                                                   |
384. | **Consortium membership**      | NOT required for eligibility; receipt of award does NOT grant membership                                                                                                                                                  |
385. | **Foreign partners**           | May be team members but NOT lead; must demonstrate unique capabilities not available domestically                                                                                                                         |
386. | **Cost share**                 | Not required for universities/non-profits on basic/applied R&D; for-profits: ≥20% (R&D) or ≥50% (demo) from non-federal sources                                                                                           |
387. | **DMSP**                       | Not required at Phase I application; required during award negotiation                                                                                                                                                    |
388. | **AI tool use**                | Must disclose; "fair-use concept" applies; machine-generated narratives may constitute research misconduct                                                                                                                |
389. | **Collaborator template**      | Single Excel file, 2 tabs, all personnel consolidated — do NOT convert to PDF                                                                                                                                             |
390. | **Late submissions**           | RFA remains open; DOE reserves right to decline late applications without review                                                                                                                                          |
391. | **Multiple focus areas**       | Phase I limited to single focus area; Phase II can have secondary focus areas                                                                                                                                             |
392. | **Collaborative vs. subaward** | Collaborative applications "strongly encouraged"; two mechanisms available                                                                                                                                                |
393. | **Letter of commitment**       | Required from ALL partner institutions including lead; signed by authorized official                                                                                                                                      |

396. 
397. ## F. Award Mechanism Notes
398. 
399. *Key details about the Other Transaction (OT) Authority mechanism used by Genesis Mission.*
400. 
401. - Awards issued under DOE's **Other Transaction Authority** (2 CFR 930), NOT standard grants
402. - Two OT formats: **(1) milestone-based** (does NOT need to comply with 2 CFR 200 cost principles) or **(2) cost-reimbursement** (similar to standard research grants under 2 CFR 200)
403. - Non-negotiable **"Fast-track OT"** agreements for rapid award and early start date (Webinar slide 15)
404. - Cost principles determined **post-selection** under 2 CFR 930.210 (RFA §III.E)
405. - Under milestone-based OT: greater flexibility for equipment purchases, payments tied to milestone completion
406. - Under cost-reimbursement OT: capital equipment (≥$5,000 per 2 CFR §200.1) may require prior written approval
407. - **No cost-plus awards** (FAQ); fee not applicable for non-profits
408. - **Computing resources**: "will not be allocated at the time of funding awards" — DOE uses a subsequent process; DOE "foresees that computing resources may be available from…National Laboratories and/or private-sector Genesis Mission partners" (Webinar slide 17)
409. 
410. ### Post-Award Planning Items (not required at submission)
411. 
412. - NEPA environmental questionnaire — required after award (~$1K–$1.5K, budgeted in budget-breakdown-phase1.md)
413. - Data Management and Sharing Plan (DMSP) — required during award negotiation
414. - IP/Data Rights provisions — will be specified in the OT agreement post-selection
```

# Edison Scientific LITERATURE_HIGH Output — Al vs Cu Material Strategy for Topic 3B

**Task ID:** `13fc6d7e-e22e-4b3f-89d4-e8459c2ed1f9`
**Mode:** LITERATURE_HIGH | **Date:** 2026-04-10 | **Size:** ~28K chars
**Part of:** Topic 3B Deep-Dive Series (10 queries, ~331K chars total)

> *Raw Edison Scientific output below. The query prompt appears first, followed by the model's structured response.*

---

Question: 
RESEARCH QUESTION: For a DOE Genesis Mission proposal targeting Topic 3B (Critical Minerals), what should be the relationship between Al alloys and Cu alloys in the proposal — and what does the optimal material strategy look like?

Context: There is confusion about whether the proposal should:
(a) Focus entirely on Al alloys and frame them as critical-mineral-lean
(b) Shift primarily to Cu-Cr-Zr as a Be-Cu replacement
(c) Use Al as Phase I demonstration with Cu-Cr-Zr as Phase I stretch / Phase II target
(d) Pursue both Al and Cu alloys in parallel

The platform (FLAIME) uses induction-heated ultrasonic atomization (max ~1300°C). Al alloys melt at ~570-660°C. Cu-Cr-Zr melts at ~1075°C. Both are within range.

Investigate:
1. For Topic 3B, which material demonstrates stronger "critical mineral demand reduction": Al alloys or Cu-Cr-Zr?
2. Can a single proposal credibly cover BOTH Al and Cu alloy families?
3. What is the argument for Al alloys as the "anchor" vs. Cu alloys as the "anchor"?
4. Risk assessment: is Cu-Cr-Zr atomization via ultrasonic atomization demonstrated in literature? 
5. Scoping: for a 9-month $500-750K Phase I, is it feasible to do both Al and Cu-Cr-Zr?
6. How would reviewers perceive a "two alloy family" proposal vs. a focused single-family proposal?
7. Phase I/Phase II strategy: best division of materials between phases?
8. What SPECIFIC Al alloy compositions should be targeted for maximum critical minerals story?
9. What SPECIFIC Cu-Cr-Zr compositions are most relevant for Be-Cu replacement?
10. Precedent: have successful DOE proposals covered multiple alloy families in a single autonomous platform?

Cite all sources.


## Recommended relationship between Al and Cu alloy efforts (Topic 3B)
A Topic 3B (Critical Minerals) proposal should treat **Al alloys as the Phase I anchor (primary demonstration)** and **Cu–Cr–Zr as a Phase I stretch objective / Phase II primary target**, rather than trying to run two fully parallel alloy-development programs in Phase I. This structure maximizes credibility under tight Phase I constraints while still capturing the high-value Be–Cu substitution story in a risk-managed way. The key is to frame the effort as a **single transferable autonomous manufacturing/process platform** (induction-heated ultrasonic atomization + closed-loop optimization) driven by staged “challenge problems,” where different alloy families are successive demonstrations of the same platform capability rather than separate projects. (edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 10-12, edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 5-7, decost2022towardsautomateddesign pages 1-4, stach2021autonomousexperimentationsystems pages 6-8)

| Approach | Critical-mineral demand reduction | Technical fit to ultrasonic atomization at <=1300C | Literature maturity / risk | Phase I feasibility (9 months) | Reviewer perception | Recommended role in proposal |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Al alloys (Mg-free Al-Zr; Al-Si) | Stronger Topic 3B story if framed as avoiding Mg and REE/Sc additions: Mg is near-critical in DOE’s assessment, and REEs are commonly critical; Al itself is noncritical short-term. Dilute Al-Zr compositions such as Al-0.25 wt% Zr are documented, and Al-Si is a low-risk Al family (bauer20232023criticalmaterials pages 16-18, bauer20232023criticalmaterials pages 133-136, hayes2018criticalmineralsa pages 1-2, czerwinski2024aluminumalloysfor pages 42-43, kahveci2019measurementandprediction pages 1-2) | Excellent fit. Induction-based ultrasonic atomization on rePowder operates up to ~1300C and has directly produced Al-10Cu powder at 1100C under argon/vacuum; Al alloy ultrasonic atomization is well represented in the literature (ukabhai2025investigationofalcu pages 1-3) | Lowest technical risk of the options; Al ultrasonic atomization is established, with known process windows and manageable issues such as minor particle fusion / cooling effects (ukabhai2025investigationofalcu pages 1-3) | High. Best suited for end-to-end Phase I demonstration of atomization + closed-loop optimization + metrology on the platform (edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 10-12, edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 5-7) | Likely favorable as a focused, credible Phase I anchor with a clear critical-mineral-lean message (edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 10-12, edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 5-7) | Primary Phase I anchor |
| Cu-Cr-Zr (C18150-type) | Mixed story. Strong substitution case for replacing Be-Cu with a Be-free alloy, but copper itself is not a short-term DOE critical material and rises mainly to near-critical/greater energy importance in longer-term views; thus the demand-reduction story is weaker than Mg-lean Al unless framed specifically as Be-Cu substitution and safer supply/use (bauer20232023criticalmaterials pages 133-136, reich2025criticalminerals pages 5-6, reich2025criticalminerals pages 1-2, morozova2018microstructureandproperties pages 1-2) | Plausible fit within platform temperature envelope: copper-alloy ultrasonic atomization has been shown on rePowder-type systems, and the induction module reaches ~1300C; however no direct CuCrZr ultrasonic atomization citation was found (ciftcli2025alloydevelopmentfrom pages 1-3, ukabhai2025investigationofalcu pages 1-3) | Moderate risk. Cu-containing / copper-alloy UA is feasible, but direct CuCrZr UA precedent was not located; higher-melting alloys raise concerns around oxidation, contamination, evaporation, amplitude limits, and melt accumulation (ciftcli2025alloydevelopmentfrom pages 1-3, sojoodi2025integrationofcircular pages 18-19, presz2024ultrasonicatomizationas pages 11-12, ukabhai2025investigationofalcu pages 1-3) | Medium if limited to feasibility / powder-window demonstration; low for full optimization and qualification in Phase I (edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 10-12, edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 5-7) | Reviewers may view it as interesting and relevant for Be-Cu replacement, but riskier than Al if made the sole near-term anchor without direct UA precedent (morozova2018microstructureandproperties pages 1-2, edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 10-12) | Phase I stretch goal; stronger Phase II target |
| Two-family phased strategy | Best combined story: use Al to show direct critical-mineral-lean reduction now, and CuCrZr to show future Be-Cu substitution on the same autonomous platform (bauer20232023criticalmaterials pages 16-18, bauer20232023criticalmaterials pages 133-136, morozova2018microstructureandproperties pages 1-2) | Credible if presented as one platform with shared process physics / workflows and staged challenge problems rather than two equal campaigns (edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 10-12, edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 12-14, edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 5-7) | Balanced risk: leverages low-risk Al for platform proof while containing CuCrZr risk to a bounded stretch demonstration (edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 10-12, edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 5-7) | Best fit for 9 months if scoped as Al end-to-end + CuCrZr feasibility only; not advisable as two parallel full alloy-development efforts (edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 10-12, edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 5-7) | Most likely positive if framed as a phased, challenge-driven platform demonstration; negative if framed as two unfocused parallel alloy programs (edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 10-12, edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 5-7, decost2022towardsautomateddesign pages 1-4, stach2021autonomousexperimentationsystems pages 6-8) | Recommended overall structure: Al anchor in Phase I, CuCrZr stretch in Phase I / main expansion in Phase II |


*Table: This table compares Al-alloy and Cu-Cr-Zr options for a DOE Topic 3B proposal across critical-mineral impact, technical risk, and Phase I fit. It is useful for deciding which alloy family should anchor the proposal and how to scope a credible phased strategy.*

## 1. Which material demonstrates stronger “critical mineral demand reduction”: Al alloys or Cu–Cr–Zr?
**Al alloys generally support the stronger “critical mineral demand reduction” framing**—provided you deliberately target **Mg-lean/Mg-free and REE/Sc-free** Al compositions. In DOE’s Critical Materials Assessment, **magnesium is near-critical in the short term**, while several rare earth elements are critical; aluminum itself is noncritical in the short term. (bauer20232023criticalmaterials pages 133-136)

Copper’s criticality is more mixed depending on jurisdiction and horizon: DOE’s short-term matrix lists **copper as noncritical** (though increasing in importance later), while other critical-minerals reviews describe copper as central/critical for electrification and show national lists vary. (bauer20232023criticalmaterials pages 133-136, reich2025criticalminerals pages 5-6, czerwinski2022criticalmineralsfor pages 1-2)

Therefore:
- **Al anchor story:** “reduce demand for Mg / avoid REEs while delivering performance,” using Al compositions that avoid near-critical Mg and critical REEs. (bauer20232023criticalmaterials pages 133-136, hayes2018criticalmineralsa pages 1-2)
- **Cu–Cr–Zr story:** “replace Be–Cu with a Be-free high-strength, high-conductivity copper alloy,” which is a substitution and safety/regulatory story more than a copper-demand-reduction story. (morozova2018microstructureandproperties pages 1-2)

## 2. Can a single proposal credibly cover BOTH Al and Cu alloy families?
Yes—**if** you explicitly adopt a **challenge-problem, staged maturation** structure and define crosscutting platform KPIs (powder sphericity/PSD, oxygen pickup, throughput, repeatability, closed-loop convergence), then show that two material classes are **two demonstrations of the same workflow** rather than two independent alloy programs. The challenge-problem approach, staged maturity cycles, and standardized interfaces/workflows are repeatedly emphasized as how to credibly cover heterogeneous technical domains without losing focus. (edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 10-12, edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 5-7, oconnor2025reducedgravityand pages 48-51)

Autonomous experimentation literature also provides precedent that a single autonomous platform can present **multiple distinct case studies** to demonstrate flexibility and generality (e.g., two alloy vignettes on one platform; multiple material classes on MINERVA; broad AE campaigns across materials). (decost2022towardsautomateddesign pages 1-4, hao2025autonomousmaterialssynthesis pages 19-21, stach2021autonomousexperimentationsystems pages 6-8)

## 3. Argument for Al alloys as the “anchor” vs Cu alloys as the “anchor”
### Al as anchor
- **Critical-minerals narrative is cleaner**: avoid Mg (near-critical) and avoid REEs/Sc (often critical across studies). (bauer20232023criticalmaterials pages 133-136, hayes2018criticalmineralsa pages 1-2)
- **Lower technical risk for ultrasonic atomization**: induction-based ultrasonic atomization (rePowder) is directly demonstrated for Al-containing alloys (e.g., Al–10Cu at 1100 °C) with good sphericity and LPBF-suitable PSD, and the induction module is rated to ~1300 °C. (ukabhai2025investigationofalcu pages 1-3)

### Cu–Cr–Zr as anchor
- **Strong application pull** when framed as **Be–Cu replacement**: Cu–Cr–Zr alloys are engineered for high strength + high conductivity; Be–Cu can reach very high strength but much lower conductivity. (morozova2018microstructureandproperties pages 1-2)
- However, **riskier as Phase I anchor** because direct CuCrZr ultrasonic atomization precedent was not located in the retrieved literature, and higher-melting / copper systems increase sensitivity to oxygen pickup and process constraints. (sojoodi2025integrationofcircular pages 18-19, presz2024ultrasonicatomizationas pages 11-12)

Net: make **Al the anchor** and position Cu–Cr–Zr as the “next material-class challenge problem.” (edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 10-12, edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 5-7)

## 4. Risk assessment: is Cu–Cr–Zr ultrasonic atomization demonstrated?
**Direct ultrasonic atomization of CuCrZr specifically was not found** in the retrieved sources; this is a real proposal risk you should acknowledge.

That said, the broader feasibility case is solid:
- The Amazemet rePowder system (induction-heated ultrasonic atomization) can melt up to ~1300 °C and has demonstrated ultrasonic atomization at 1100 °C for Al–10Cu under argon/vacuum, producing spherical powder (d50 15–75 µm). (ukabhai2025investigationofalcu pages 1-3)
- Induction-based ultrasonic atomization of a **copper alloy** on a rePowder-type system is reported (figure evidence, though without CuCrZr composition/temperature details). (ciftcli2025alloydevelopmentfrom pages 1-3)
