A Topic 3B (Critical Minerals) proposal should treat **Al alloys as the Phase I anchor (primary demonstration)** and **Cu–Cr–Zr as a Phase I stretch objective / Phase II primary target**, rather than trying to run two fully parallel alloy-development programs in Phase I. This structure maximizes credibility under tight Phase I constraints while still capturing the high-value Be–Cu substitution story in a risk-managed way. The key is to frame the effort as a **single transferable autonomous manufacturing/process platform** (induction-heated ultrasonic atomization + closed-loop optimization) driven by staged “challenge problems,” where different alloy families are successive demonstrations of the same platform capability rather than separate projects. (edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 10-12, edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 5-7, decost2022towardsautomateddesign pages 1-4, stach2021autonomousexperimentationsystems pages 6-8)

| Approach | Critical-mineral demand reduction | Technical fit to ultrasonic atomization at <=1300C | Literature maturity / risk | Phase I feasibility (9 months) | Reviewer perception | Recommended role in proposal |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Al alloys (Mg-free Al-Zr; Al-Si) | Stronger Topic 3B story if framed as avoiding Mg and REE/Sc additions: Mg is near-critical in DOE’s assessment, and REEs are commonly critical; Al itself is noncritical short-term. Dilute Al-Zr compositions such as Al-0.25 wt% Zr are documented, and Al-Si is a low-risk Al family (bauer20232023criticalmaterials pages 16-18, bauer20232023criticalmaterials pages 133-136, hayes2018criticalmineralsa pages 1-2, czerwinski2024aluminumalloysfor pages 42-43, kahveci2019measurementandprediction pages 1-2) | Excellent fit. Induction-based ultrasonic atomization on rePowder operates up to ~1300C and has directly produced Al-10Cu powder at 1100C under argon/vacuum; Al alloy ultrasonic atomization is well represented in the literature (ukabhai2025investigationofalcu pages 1-3) | Lowest technical risk of the options; Al ultrasonic atomization is established, with known process windows and manageable issues such as minor particle fusion / cooling effects (ukabhai2025investigationofalcu pages 1-3) | High. Best suited for end-to-end Phase I demonstration of atomization + closed-loop optimization + metrology on the platform (edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 10-12, edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 5-7) | Likely favorable as a focused, credible Phase I anchor with a clear critical-mineral-lean message (edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 10-12, edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 5-7) | Primary Phase I anchor |
| Cu-Cr-Zr (C18150-type) | Mixed story. Strong substitution case for replacing Be-Cu with a Be-free alloy, but copper itself is not a short-term DOE critical material and rises mainly to near-critical/greater energy importance in longer-term views; thus the demand-reduction story is weaker than Mg-lean Al unless framed specifically as Be-Cu substitution and safer supply/use (bauer20232023criticalmaterials pages 133-136, reich2025criticalminerals pages 5-6, reich2025criticalminerals pages 1-2, morozova2018microstructureandproperties pages 1-2) | Plausible fit within platform temperature envelope: copper-alloy ultrasonic atomization has been shown on rePowder-type systems, and the induction module reaches ~1300C; however no direct CuCrZr ultrasonic atomization citation was found (ciftcli2025alloydevelopmentfrom pages 1-3, ukabhai2025investigationofalcu pages 1-3) | Moderate risk. Cu-containing / copper-alloy UA is feasible, but direct CuCrZr UA precedent was not located; higher-melting alloys raise concerns around oxidation, contamination, evaporation, amplitude limits, and melt accumulation (ciftcli2025alloydevelopmentfrom pages 1-3, sojoodi2025integrationofcircular pages 18-19, presz2024ultrasonicatomizationas pages 11-12, ukabhai2025investigationofalcu pages 1-3) | Medium if limited to feasibility / powder-window demonstration; low for full optimization and qualification in Phase I (edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 10-12, edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 5-7) | Reviewers may view it as interesting and relevant for Be-Cu replacement, but riskier than Al if made the sole near-term anchor without direct UA precedent (morozova2018microstructureandproperties pages 1-2, edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 10-12) | Phase I stretch goal; stronger Phase II target |
| Two-family phased strategy | Best combined story: use Al to show direct critical-mineral-lean reduction now, and CuCrZr to show future Be-Cu substitution on the same autonomous platform (bauer20232023criticalmaterials pages 16-18, bauer20232023criticalmaterials pages 133-136, morozova2018microstructureandproperties pages 1-2) | Credible if presented as one platform with shared process physics / workflows and staged challenge problems rather than two equal campaigns (edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 10-12, edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 12-14, edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 5-7) | Balanced risk: leverages low-risk Al for platform proof while containing CuCrZr risk to a bounded stretch demonstration (edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 10-12, edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 5-7) | Best fit for 9 months if scoped as Al end-to-end + CuCrZr feasibility only; not advisable as two parallel full alloy-development efforts (edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 10-12, edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 5-7) | Most likely positive if framed as a phased, challenge-driven platform demonstration; negative if framed as two unfocused parallel alloy programs (edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 10-12, edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 5-7, decost2022towardsautomateddesign pages 1-4, stach2021autonomousexperimentationsystems pages 6-8) | Recommended overall structure: Al anchor in Phase I, CuCrZr stretch in Phase I / main expansion in Phase II |


*Table: This table compares Al-alloy and Cu-Cr-Zr options for a DOE Topic 3B proposal across critical-mineral impact, technical risk, and Phase I fit. It is useful for deciding which alloy family should anchor the proposal and how to scope a credible phased strategy.*

## 1. Which material demonstrates stronger “critical mineral demand reduction”: Al alloys or Cu–Cr–Zr?
**Al alloys generally support the stronger “critical mineral demand reduction” framing**—provided you deliberately target **Mg-lean/Mg-free and REE/Sc-free** Al compositions. In DOE’s Critical Materials Assessment, **magnesium is near-critical in the short term**, while several rare earth elements are critical; aluminum itself is noncritical in the short term. (bauer20232023criticalmaterials pages 133-136)

Copper’s criticality is more mixed depending on jurisdiction and horizon: DOE’s short-term matrix lists **copper as noncritical** (though increasing in importance later), while other critical-minerals reviews describe copper as central/critical for electrification and show national lists vary. (bauer20232023criticalmaterials pages 133-136, reich2025criticalminerals pages 5-6, czerwinski2022criticalmineralsfor pages 1-2)

Therefore:
- **Al anchor story:** “reduce demand for Mg / avoid REEs while delivering performance,” using Al compositions that avoid near-critical Mg and critical REEs. (bauer20232023criticalmaterials pages 133-136, hayes2018criticalmineralsa pages 1-2)
- **Cu–Cr–Zr story:** “replace Be–Cu with a Be-free high-strength, high-conductivity copper alloy,” which is a substitution and safety/regulatory story more than a copper-demand-reduction story. (morozova2018microstructureandproperties pages 1-2)

## 2. Can a single proposal credibly cover BOTH Al and Cu alloy families?
Yes—**if** you explicitly adopt a **challenge-problem, staged maturation** structure and define crosscutting platform KPIs (powder sphericity/PSD, oxygen pickup, throughput, repeatability, closed-loop convergence), then show that two material classes are **two demonstrations of the same workflow** rather than two independent alloy programs. The challenge-problem approach, staged maturity cycles, and standardized interfaces/workflows are repeatedly emphasized as how to credibly cover heterogeneous technical domains without losing focus. (edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 10-12, edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 5-7, oconnor2025reducedgravityand pages 48-51)

Autonomous experimentation literature also provides precedent that a single autonomous platform can present **multiple distinct case studies** to demonstrate flexibility and generality (e.g., two alloy vignettes on one platform; multiple material classes on MINERVA; broad AE campaigns across materials). (decost2022towardsautomateddesign pages 1-4, hao2025autonomousmaterialssynthesis pages 19-21, stach2021autonomousexperimentationsystems pages 6-8)

## 3. Argument for Al alloys as the “anchor” vs Cu alloys as the “anchor”
### Al as anchor
- **Critical-minerals narrative is cleaner**: avoid Mg (near-critical) and avoid REEs/Sc (often critical across studies). (bauer20232023criticalmaterials pages 133-136, hayes2018criticalmineralsa pages 1-2)
- **Lower technical risk for ultrasonic atomization**: induction-based ultrasonic atomization (rePowder) is directly demonstrated for Al-containing alloys (e.g., Al–10Cu at 1100 °C) with good sphericity and LPBF-suitable PSD, and the induction module is rated to ~1300 °C. (ukabhai2025investigationofalcu pages 1-3)

### Cu–Cr–Zr as anchor
- **Strong application pull** when framed as **Be–Cu replacement**: Cu–Cr–Zr alloys are engineered for high strength + high conductivity; Be–Cu can reach very high strength but much lower conductivity. (morozova2018microstructureandproperties pages 1-2)
- However, **riskier as Phase I anchor** because direct CuCrZr ultrasonic atomization precedent was not located in the retrieved literature, and higher-melting / copper systems increase sensitivity to oxygen pickup and process constraints. (sojoodi2025integrationofcircular pages 18-19, presz2024ultrasonicatomizationas pages 11-12)

Net: make **Al the anchor** and position Cu–Cr–Zr as the “next material-class challenge problem.” (edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 10-12, edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 5-7)

## 4. Risk assessment: is Cu–Cr–Zr ultrasonic atomization demonstrated?
**Direct ultrasonic atomization of CuCrZr specifically was not found** in the retrieved sources; this is a real proposal risk you should acknowledge.

That said, the broader feasibility case is solid:
- The Amazemet rePowder system (induction-heated ultrasonic atomization) can melt up to ~1300 °C and has demonstrated ultrasonic atomization at 1100 °C for Al–10Cu under argon/vacuum, producing spherical powder (d50 15–75 µm). (ukabhai2025investigationofalcu pages 1-3)
- Induction-based ultrasonic atomization of a **copper alloy** on a rePowder-type system is reported (figure evidence, though without CuCrZr composition/temperature details). (ciftcli2025alloydevelopmentfrom pages 1-3)

Key technical risks for Cu alloys / higher-melting systems to manage in the proposal include: atmosphere sensitivity and oxidation pickup; the fact that ultrasonic/plasma atomization is not a decontamination method (O/C present in feedstock remains); equipment amplitude requirements; and failure modes like melt accumulation that can halt atomization. (sojoodi2025integrationofcircular pages 18-19, presz2024ultrasonicatomizationas pages 11-12)

## 5. Phase I feasibility: can you do both Al and Cu–Cr–Zr in 9 months ($500–750K)?
A **full parallel** optimization of both alloy families in Phase I is likely to read as over-scoped.

A **phased-within-Phase-I** approach is feasible:
- **Al track (primary):** end-to-end closed-loop demonstration (powder production → powder metrology → decision/optimization loop) on a Mg-lean Al composition.
- **CuCrZr track (stretch):** demonstrate melt handling + stable atomization + initial powder-quality window (e.g., oxidation/PSD/sphericity) sufficient to de-risk Phase II.

This matches common guidance for complex platforms: define challenge problems, harden workflows early, then expand validation and automated optimization in later phases. (edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 10-12, edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 5-7)

## 6. Reviewer perception: two alloy families vs focused single-family
Reviewers typically reward focus, but the autonomy literature shows that **multiple case studies are acceptable and sometimes expected** when the platform is the product and the case studies prove generality.

A “two family” proposal is likely to be viewed positively if you:
- explicitly state “**one platform, two staged challenge problems**,”
- use shared KPIs and shared data/controls,
- keep CuCrZr Phase I scope narrowly defined as feasibility/risk-reduction. (edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 10-12, edwards2025inertialfusionenergy pages 5-7, decost2022towardsautomateddesign pages 1-4, stach2021autonomousexperimentationsystems pages 6-8)

It will be viewed negatively if it reads like “two independent alloy-development programs” with two independent experimental matrices.

## Energy-sector downstream applications of AM aluminum alloys (DOE/AMMTO / Genesis Mission Topic 3B framing)

Energy-relevant downstream adoption of additively manufactured (AM) aluminum alloys is strongest in **thermal management and fluid-handling hardware**, where aluminum’s thermal conductivity and low density combine with AM-enabled internal flow features and part consolidation to improve **system efficiency, power density, and maintainability**. The most DOE-resonant, evidence-backed categories in the retrieved corpus are:

1) **Thermal management for electrification and power electronics** (heat exchangers, cold plates, heat sinks, heat pipes). (ghahfarokhi2021opportunitiesandchallenges pages 6-7, chouhan2025manufacturabilityofa20x pages 1-3, kappe2022designconceptsand pages 1-2)
2) **Fluid power efficiency** (hydraulic/pump components where efficiency directly reduces fuel/energy use). (brock2020laserpowderbed pages 1-5, brock2020laserpowderbed pages 54-58)
3) **Geothermal** (DOE stakeholder-identified opportunity areas plus AM heat-exchanger prototypes; aluminum is cited as a service material but AM-aluminum deployment in geothermal is not yet well documented in the accessible geothermal report sections). (polsky2021studyofadditive pages 114-118, polsky2021studyofadditive pages 15-17)
4) **Nuclear-adjacent instrumentation and shielding** via Al-based MMCs (heat sinks and neutron components). (bai2024empiricalinvestigationof pages 1-2)

Within this evidence set, **A20X/A205 (Al–Cu–Mg–Ag–TiB2 family)** appears prominently for thermal management (heat sinks) with strong property claims, but **named OEM product deployments** remain scarce. **Scalmalloy** appears as a lightweight high-strength aluminum alloy enabling advanced heat-pipe wick designs and integration into structures. (chouhan2026heattransferperformance pages 1-2, kappe2022designconceptsand pages 1-2)

199. FLAIME integrates Bayesian Optimization over Function Networks (BOFN) with
200. the partial Knowledge Gradient for Function Networks (pKGFN) acquisition
201. function to jointly optimize alloy composition, printability, and mechanical
202. properties across the full powder-to-part pipeline---from CALPHAD evaluation
203. through ultrasonic and gas atomization, laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), and
204. ASTM~E8 sub-size tensile testing. By modeling every manufacturing stage as a node in
205. a cost-aware function-network DAG with an embedded mineral-burden objective,
206. BOFN selects maximally informative experiments at each stage, reducing
207. powder-to-tensile cycle time by an estimated 10$\times$ versus conventional
208. sequential campaigns through the combination of BOFN-guided experiment
209. selection ($\geq$3$\times$ fewer iterations) and closed-loop
210. execution---software-orchestrated with human operators in Phase~I,
211. architected for direct robotic integration in Phase~II.  No existing
212. platform closes this complete composition-discovery and

## Cu-Cr-Zr Recommendation

Based on Edison trajectories (task `13fc6d7e` — Al vs Cu strategy; task `71c1067b` — energy-sector applications; the BeCu replacement market analysis), and PR #26 discussion:

**Recommendation: Keep Cu-Cr-Zr as stretch demonstration, but strengthen the AMMTO framing.**

Rationale:
1. **Beryllium IS on the DOE critical minerals list** → the substitution story is genuine for Topic 3B
2. **Clean energy thermal management** (heat exchangers, power electronics, EV motors) is precisely AMMTO's domain — Edison task `71c1067b` confirms this is the strongest energy-sector AM Al/Cu application area
3. **But:** No direct CuCrZr ultrasonic atomization precedent exists; promoting it to a primary track would add risk without proportional benefit
4. **The current ~20% effort scope is right** — enough to signal platform generality and AMMTO alignment without overcommitting

Specific proposed changes (pending your approval):
- Keep the "Phase I focuses exclusively on Al alloys…with Cu-Cr-Zr as a stretch demonstration" scope statement
- Add 1–2 sentences in the Phase II vision tying Cu-Cr-Zr to **clean energy thermal management** (Be-Cu replacement for power electronics, EV motor components)
- Optionally add a non-gated stretch milestone for Cu-Cr-Zr powder feasibility
- Add Cu-Cr-Zr performance targets (YS ≥200 MPa, ≥50% IACS) to the milestones as conditional/Phase II pathway targets

**Should I proceed with these Cu-Cr-Zr changes?**

201. The United States imports 100\% of its manganese, 100\% of its zirconium
202. mineral concentrates, and 74\% of its chromium~\cite{usgs_mcs_2024}---elements
203. central to high-performance aluminum alloys for advanced manufacturing. A single supply disruption could idle domestic
204. additive-manufacturing production dependent on these materials. FLAIME (Fast
205. Learning AI for Mineral Efficiency) addresses this vulnerability with an
206. AI-autonomous closed-loop platform that discovers and qualifies aluminum alloys
207. meeting structural performance targets while minimizing critical mineral
208. content, directly supporting DOE Critical Materials Strategy Pillars~2
209. (Develop Alternatives) and~3 (Materials and Manufacturing Efficiency).
210. 
211. FLAIME integrates Bayesian Optimization over Function Networks (BOFN) with
212. the partial Knowledge Gradient for Function Networks (pKGFN) acquisition
213. function to jointly optimize alloy composition, printability, and mechanical
214. properties across the full powder-to-part pipeline---from CALPHAD evaluation
215. through ultrasonic and gas atomization, laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), and
216. ASTM~E8 sub-size tensile testing. By modeling every manufacturing stage as a node in
217. a cost-aware function-network DAG with an embedded mineral-burden objective,
218. BOFN selects maximally informative experiments at each stage, reducing
219. powder-to-tensile cycle time by an estimated 10$\times$ versus conventional
220. sequential campaigns ($\geq$3$\times$ from AI-guided experiment
221. selection $\times$ closed-loop execution speedup)---software-orchestrated with human operators in Phase~I,
222. architected for direct robotic integration in Phase~II.  No existing
223. platform closes this complete composition-discovery and
224. manufacturing-qualification loop: the closest structural-alloy SDL
225. automates printing through testing but not the full
226. powder-to-property pipeline~\cite{conn_2025_apex}.
227. 
228. Phase~I explores \num{22803} element combinations---$\sum_{k=2}^{8}\binom{\elementcount}{k}$
229. sub-systems spanning ternary (e.g., Al--Fe--Si) through 9-component alloys---drawn from a
230. \elementcount-element Al-alloy palette via an asynchronous, cost-aware multi-fidelity
231. framework (\texttt{pycalphad}, TC-Python/TCAl10, Thermo-Calc AM~Module)
232. that evaluates CALPHAD thermodynamics, Scheil solidification, and
233. printability in parallel at maximum HPC capacity,
234. then focuses experimental validation on the top 3--5 sub-systems---including
235. the Al--Mn--Cr--Zr and Al--Zr anchors---characterizing $\geq$200 compositions
236. (up to 2~unique compositions/day, 6~days/week) through the full
237. powder-to-tensile pipeline with a discovery yield $\geq$3\%. All
238. experimental data and BOFN models will be shared as a FAIR-compliant
239. digital thread via the Genesis Mission platform and open repositories
240. (Zenodo/Figshare with DOIs). The project enters Phase~I at
241. TRL~2 (concept formulated) and targets TRL~4 (closed-loop validated in

### ✅ `bash`

**Refactor element palette with auto-count**

$ cd /workspaces/digital-alloy-lab-private && cat > /tmp/rev1_palette.py << 'PYEOF'
"""rev-1: Replace fragile element palette redundancy with auto-calculated LaTeX commands."""

with open('genesis-mission-proposal/flaime-genesis-proposal.tex', 'r') as f:
    content = f.read()

# Current preamble commands (lines 152-160):
# \elementcount{15}
# \kmin{2}
# \kmax{8}
# \subsystemcount{22\,803}
# \subsystemcountraw{22803}
# \elementlist{Mn, Cr, ...}
# \elementlisttex{Mn,\,Cr,...}

# The issue: \subsystemcount, \subsystemcountraw are manually typed and must be
# kept in sync with \elementcount, \kmin, \kmax. Also \elementcount must match
# the actual number of items in \elementlist.
#
# Solution: Use LaTeX3 (expl3) to:
# 1. Count elements from the list automatically
# 2. Compute the binomial sum automatically
# 3. Generate formatted versions automatically
#
# However, LaTeX3 integer computation for C(15,k) sums is complex. A simpler
# approach: use a Python pre-computation comment block that makes the dependency
# explicit, plus a \PackageWarning if the count doesn't match.
#
# Actually, the best practical approach: use etoolbox/listcount to auto-count
# the element list, and add a LaTeX assertion that fires if the count doesn't
# match \elementcount. The binomial sum is harder to compute in pure LaTeX,
# so keep it manual but add a verification comment with the formula.

old_palette_block = r"""% Change \elementcount and \elementlist together; \subsystemcount follows from
%   \sum_{k=\kmin}^{\kmax} \binom{\elementcount}{k}.
\newcommand{\elementcount}{15}           % number of non-Al additions
\newcommand{\kmin}{2}                    % minimum additions per sub-system
\newcommand{\kmax}{8}                    % maximum additions per sub-system
\newcommand{\subsystemcount}{22\,803}    % = sum C(15,k) for k=2..8
\newcommand{\subsystemcountraw}{22803}   % raw integer for \num{}
\newcommand{\elementlist}{Mn, Cr, Zr, Mg, Si, Cu, Ti, Fe, Ni, Ce, Sc, Li, Er, Zn, Sn}
\newcommand{\elementlisttex}{Mn,\,Cr,\,Zr,\,Mg,\,Si,\,Cu,\,Ti,\,Fe,\,Ni,\,Ce,\,Sc,\,Li,\,Er,\,Zn,\,Sn}"""

new_palette_block = r"""% ── Element Palette (single source of truth) ──────────────────────────
% EDIT ONLY the three lines marked ★; everything else auto-derives.
%
% After editing, recompute \subsystemcount with:
%   python3 -c "from math import comb; n=15; print(sum(comb(n,k) for k in range(2,9)))"
%   → 22803   (update the two \subsystemcount commands if n/kmin/kmax change)
%
\newcommand{\elementpalette}{Mn,Cr,Zr,Mg,Si,Cu,Ti,Fe,Ni,Ce,Sc,Li,Er,Zn,Sn} % ★ canonical comma-list
\newcommand{\kmin}{2}                    % ★ minimum additions per sub-system
\newcommand{\kmax}{8}                    % ★ maximum additions per sub-system
%
% --- derived commands (do not edit independently) ---
\usepackage{listofitems}
\readlist\PaletteItems{\elementpalette}
\newcommand{\elementcount}{\PaletteItemstotal}  % auto-counted from list
\newcommand{\subsystemcount}{22\,803}    % = sum C(\elementcount,k) for k=\kmin..\kmax
\newcommand{\subsystemcountraw}{22803}   % raw integer (for \num{})
% Human-readable expansions derived from \elementpalette:
\newcommand{\elementlist}{Mn, Cr, Zr, Mg, Si, Cu, Ti, Fe, Ni, Ce, Sc, Li, Er, Zn, Sn}
\newcommand{\elementlisttex}{Mn,\,Cr,\,Zr,\,Mg,\,Si,\,Cu,\,Ti,\,Fe,\,Ni,\,Ce,\,Sc,\,Li,\,Er,\,Zn,\,Sn}
% Verify: if you change \elementpalette, update \elementlist and \elementlisttex to match,
% then recompute \subsystemcount with the python3 command above."""

content = content.replace(old_palette_block, new_palette_block)

with open('genesis-mission-proposal/flaime-genesis-proposal.tex', 'w') as f:
    f.write(content)

# Verify
with open('genesis-mission-proposal/flaime-genesis-proposal.tex', 'r') as f:
    v = f.read()

assert '\\readlist\\PaletteItems{\\elementpalette}' in v, "listofitems not found"
assert '\\PaletteItemstotal' in v, "auto-count not found"
assert '★ canonical comma-list' in v, "edit marker not found"
print("✓ rev-1: Element palette refactored with auto-count via listofitems")

import subprocess
subprocess.run(['sqlite3', __import__('os').path.expanduser('~/.copilot/todos.db'),
    "UPDATE todos SET status='done' WHERE id='rev-1'"], capture_output=True)

<sub>⏱️ 72m 50s</sub>

### ✅ `bash`

**Fix palette to use etoolbox instead**

$ cd /workspaces/digital-alloy-lab-private && python3 << 'PYEOF'
"""Fix rev-1: Replace listofitems with a simpler pure-LaTeX approach using etoolbox."""

with open('genesis-mission-proposal/flaime-genesis-proposal.tex', 'r') as f:
    content = f.read()

# Check if etoolbox is already loaded
has_etoolbox = '\\usepackage{etoolbox}' in content or 'etoolbox' in content.split('\\begin{document}')[0]
print(f"etoolbox already loaded: {has_etoolbox}")

# Replace the listofitems-based block with a simpler approach
# Use a counter + forcsvlist from etoolbox to auto-count
old_block = r"""% ── Element Palette (single source of truth) ──────────────────────────
% EDIT ONLY the three lines marked ★; everything else auto-derives.
%
% After editing, recompute \subsystemcount with:
%   python3 -c "from math import comb; n=15; print(sum(comb(n,k) for k in range(2,9)))"
%   → 22803   (update the two \subsystemcount commands if n/kmin/kmax change)
%
\newcommand{\elementpalette}{Mn,Cr,Zr,Mg,Si,Cu,Ti,Fe,Ni,Ce,Sc,Li,Er,Zn,Sn} % ★ canonical comma-list
\newcommand{\kmin}{2}                    % ★ minimum additions per sub-system
\newcommand{\kmax}{8}                    % ★ maximum additions per sub-system
%
% --- derived commands (do not edit independently) ---
\usepackage{listofitems}
\readlist\PaletteItems{\elementpalette}
\newcommand{\elementcount}{\PaletteItemstotal}  % auto-counted from list
\newcommand{\subsystemcount}{22\,803}    % = sum C(\elementcount,k) for k=\kmin..\kmax
\newcommand{\subsystemcountraw}{22803}   % raw integer (for \num{})
% Human-readable expansions derived from \elementpalette:
\newcommand{\elementlist}{Mn, Cr, Zr, Mg, Si, Cu, Ti, Fe, Ni, Ce, Sc, Li, Er, Zn, Sn}
\newcommand{\elementlisttex}{Mn,\,Cr,\,Zr,\,Mg,\,Si,\,Cu,\,Ti,\,Fe,\,Ni,\,Ce,\,Sc,\,Li,\,Er,\,Zn,\,Sn}
% Verify: if you change \elementpalette, update \elementlist and \elementlisttex to match,
% then recompute \subsystemcount with the python3 command above."""

new_block = r"""% ── Element Palette (single source of truth) ──────────────────────────
% EDIT ONLY the three lines marked ★; everything else auto-derives.
%
% After editing, recompute derived values with:
%   python3 -c "
%   from math import comb
%   elems = 'Mn,Cr,Zr,Mg,Si,Cu,Ti,Fe,Ni,Ce,Sc,Li,Er,Zn,Sn'.split(',')
%   n = len(elems); kmin = 2; kmax = 8
%   total = sum(comb(n,k) for k in range(kmin, kmax+1))
%   print(f'elementcount={n}, subsystems={total}')
%   # Paste: \elementcount → n, \subsystemcount → total (with \,), \subsystemcountraw → total
%   "
%   Current output: elementcount=15, subsystems=22803
%
\newcommand{\elementpalette}{Mn,Cr,Zr,Mg,Si,Cu,Ti,Fe,Ni,Ce,Sc,Li,Er,Zn,Sn} % ★ canonical comma-list
\newcommand{\kmin}{2}                    % ★ minimum additions per sub-system
\newcommand{\kmax}{8}                    % ★ maximum additions per sub-system
%
% --- derived from \elementpalette (auto-counted at LaTeX compile time) ---
\newcounter{elemctr}
\setcounter{elemctr}{0}
\renewcommand*{\do}[1]{\stepcounter{elemctr}}
\expandafter\docsvlist\expandafter{\elementpalette}
\newcommand{\elementcount}{\theelemctr}  % auto-counted: currently 15
%
% --- derived from \elementcount, \kmin, \kmax (recompute with script above) ---
\newcommand{\subsystemcount}{22\,803}    % = sum C(\elementcount,k) for k=\kmin..\kmax
\newcommand{\subsystemcountraw}{22803}   % raw integer (for \num{})
%
% --- formatted expansions (keep in sync with \elementpalette) ---
\newcommand{\elementlist}{Mn, Cr, Zr, Mg, Si, Cu, Ti, Fe, Ni, Ce, Sc, Li, Er, Zn, Sn}
\newcommand{\elementlisttex}{Mn,\,Cr,\,Zr,\,Mg,\,Si,\,Cu,\,Ti,\,Fe,\,Ni,\,Ce,\,Sc,\,Li,\,Er,\,Zn,\,Sn}"""

if old_block in content:
    content = content.replace(old_block, new_block)
    print("✓ Replaced listofitems block with etoolbox auto-count")
else:
    print("ERROR: Old block not found")
    exit(1)

# Make sure etoolbox is loaded (it's commonly bundled; check if already used)
if not has_etoolbox:
    # Add etoolbox before the palette block
    content = content.replace(
        '% ── Element Palette',
        '\\usepackage{etoolbox}  % for \\docsvlist auto-counting\n% ── Element Palette'
    )
    print("✓ Added etoolbox package")

with open('genesis-mission-proposal/flaime-genesis-proposal.tex', 'w') as f:
    f.write(content)

print("✓ Palette block updated")
PYEOF

Discovery 2 starts at char 2271881
Discovery 2: Experimental Throughput Realism and Process-Model Alignment

### Summary

Mock reviews of the FLAIME proposal surfaced unrealistic throughput and brittle experimental assumptions, prompting a substantive redesign that reduces the target from 200 to 75 compositions over 9 months and anchors it in an explicit, resource‑constrained throughput plan. The revision de‑risks the two dominant bottlenecks—external LPBF access and powder atomization—via a machine‑time MOU, a five‑alloy pre‑validation campaign, and a vendor fallback, while concentrating experiments within a few sub‑systems to increase data density and tighten process‑model alignment.

### Background

High‑throughput alloy discovery for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) increasingly relies on closed‑loop strategies that connect computational screening, powder production, printing, and property validation. While such workflows promise rapid iteration, they are fragile when experimental logistics, facility access, and process physics are not rigorously modeled alongside the algorithmic layer. In aluminum alloys, rapid solidification in LPBF operates far from equilibrium, which challenges equilibrium thermodynamics inputs and requires process‑aware modeling to avoid systematic bias. A competitive program therefore needs both a credible, resource‑matched experimental plan and a modeling stack that reflects nonequilibrium process physics, with data collection concentrated enough to train and validate surrogates reliably.

### Results & Discussion

The experimental feasibility review identified external LPBF access as the single most critical bottleneck: the proposal assumed one‑day turnaround at the University of Utah without a formal machine‑time agreement, whereas realistic scheduling, shipping, build, and cooldown yield 4–12 days per composition (median 7 days), with shared‑facility capacity closer to ~8 builds/month rather than the ~22 builds/month implied by a 200‑composition target [[r3](https://platform.edisonscientific.com/kosmos/152fcd53-6e1d-4e49-ad72-6d48cc060b41/trajectories/2388788e-264f-4781-a9dd-f010c6768c70)]. When all stages are assessed, the realistic pipeline averages 11.5 days/composition versus the proposed 4.8 days, implying that to reach 200 compositions in 9 months would require ~22 parallel tracks and ~110–130 simultaneous tasks—far beyond the stated staffing and coordination plan—and this is compounded by unvalidated ultrasonic atomization yield, potentially consuming 250 atomization‑days for 200 compositions alone [[r3](https://platform.edisonscientific.com/kosmos/152fcd53-6e1d-4e49-ad72-6d48cc060b41/trajectories/2388788e-264f-4781-a9dd-f010c6768c70)]. Additional risks included uncompetitive mechanical property targets relative to incumbent alloys, limited planning for multi‑site physical logistics (sample tracking, chain of custody), and several unstated assumptions (e.g., powder requirements, process parameter development time, replicate acceptance criteria), motivating a scope and risk‑mitigation overhaul [[r3](https://platform.edisonscientific.com/kosmos/152fcd53-6e1d-4e49-ad72-6d48cc060b41/trajectories/2388788e-264f-4781-a9dd-f010c6768c70)].

![An experimental feasibility analysis reveals the discrepancy between proposed and realistic project throughput. The realistic time per composition is 11.5 days, more than doubling the proposed 4.8 days, with atomization and external LPBF access as primary bottlenecks (top left). Consequently, projected cumulative progress (bottom left) and serial throughput (top right) demonstrate the original 200-composition target is unachievable. This assessment of throughput limitations and key experimental risks (bottom right) motivated a substantial revision of the project scope to align with resource constraints.](data:image/png;base64,

The analysis includes (A) a risk radar plot identifying high risk (low scores) in multiple areas, (B) the sparse coverage of the TCAL10 thermodynamic database, (C) the minimal (<1%) experimental coverage of the total composition space, and (D) a severity ranking of non-equilibrium LPBF effects that violate core CALPHAD assumptions. Collectively, these quantified risks underscore the brittleness of the original high-throughput plan and justify the pivot to a focused, lower-scope experimental design to improve process-model alignment. (Source: [[r5](https://platform.edisonscientific.com/kosmos/152fcd53-6e1d-4e49-ad72-6d48cc060b41/trajectories/7d9bdedd-3b35-419b-9207-074d39cce166)])*

To raise data density and strengthen process‑model alignment, the revised narrative concentrates experimental resources within a small number of sub‑systems (3–4 ternary/quaternary families, including Al–Mn–Cr–Zr and Al–Zr anchors), trading breadth for depth so that GP surrogates interpolate within better‑characterized local design spaces rather than extrapolate across thousands of poorly assessed combinations [[r11](https://platform.edisonscientific.com/kosmos/152fcd53-6e1d-4e49-ad72-6d48cc060b41/trajectories/4f2e5860-63f1-4026-aeed-914dbad5a051)]. This design choice directly implements the modeling review’s recommendations to concentrate experiments, couple thermodynamics with process‑aware features (e.g., thermal gradients, cooling rates, melt pool geometry), and propagate uncertainty into acquisition decisions, while the 99% density gate and clarified logistics (barcoded tracking, build scheduling protocols) connect process physics to robust property validation [[r5](https://platform.edisonscientific.com/kosmos/152fcd53-6e1d-4e49-ad72-6d48cc060b41/trajectories/7d9bdedd-3b35-419b-9207-074d39cce166), [r10](https://platform.edisonscientific.com/kosmos/152fcd53-6e1d-4e49-ad72-6d48cc060b41/trajectories/6f7aceb7-701e-4df1-9c62-e34718e6c830), [r11](https://platform.edisonscientific.com/kosmos/152fcd53-6e1d-4e49-ad72-6d48cc060b41/trajectories/4f2e5860-63f1-4026-aeed-914dbad5a051)]. Collectively, the experimental scope reduction, LPBF and atomization de‑risking, and focused sub‑system strategy address the review’s highest‑impact feasibility and scientific integration risks, improving fundability while preserving the program’s core mission of critical‑mineral‑lean alloy discovery aligned with DOE AMMTO objectives [[r3](https://platform.edisonscientific.com/kosmos/152fcd53-6e1d-4e49-ad72-6d48cc060b41/trajectories/2388788e-264f-4781-a9dd-f010c6768c70), [r5](https://platform.edisonscientific.com/kosmos/152fcd53-6e1d-4e49-ad72-6d48cc060b41/trajectories/7d9bdedd-3b35-419b-9207-074d39cce166), [r10](https://platform.edisonscientific.com/kosmos/152fcd53-6e1d-4e49-ad72-6d48cc060b41/trajectories/6f7aceb7-701e-4df1-9c62-e34718e6c830), [r11](https://platform.edisonscientific.com/kosmos/152fcd53-6e1d-4e49-ad72-6d48cc060b41/trajectories/4f2e5860-63f1-4026-aeed-914dbad5a051)].

## Kosmos Recommendation (retrieved)

The Kosmos run ("Genesis Mission Proposal Refinement Through Mock Reviews", 6 iterations) made several aggressive recommendations. **Key findings relevant to your "soften composition count" directive:**

| Current proposal | Kosmos recommendation | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| ≥200 compositions | **~75 compositions** | Serial pipeline = 11.5 days/composition (not 4.8); 200 would need ~22 parallel tracks |
| 2/day throughput | **~0.7/day avg** (8-10/month steady-state after 2-month ramp) | External LPBF = 4-12 days/composition; shared facility ~8 builds/month |
| ≥3× AI acceleration | **≥1.5×** | Kosmos found pKGFN underperformed random (0/10 wins); recommended TSFN instead |
| Screening: ~50 tensile + ~150 density-only | **25 tensile + 50 density-only** | Aligned to 75-composition scope |

**Important caveats:** The Kosmos run (1) replaced pKGFN with TSFN, which conflicts with our current BOFN/pKGFN architecture, and (2) assumed serial execution without pipeline parallelism (atomize N+1 while printing N while testing N-1), which our prior KPI analysis showed enables ~2/day.

**My recommendation:** Soften from "≥200" to a range like "≥100–200" or "targeting ≥150", acknowledging ramp-up. Don't adopt the full 75-composition reduction — our pipeline parallelism and dedicated team justify more than serial estimates. Similarly, keep ≥3× acceleration (our pKGFN benchmarks support it) but add a hedge like "with ≥1.5× as a conservative floor."

"""Compositor v5: 4 modular subfigures → final proposal figure. ≥7pt citations."""
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.image import imread
import os

def compose_figure(subfig_dir='/tmp/fig_workspace',
                   output_path=None, version='v8'):
    paths = {
        'stagegate':   os.path.join(subfig_dir, 'subfig_stagegate.png'),
        'throughput':  os.path.join(subfig_dir, 'subfig_throughput.png'),
        'defects':     os.path.join(subfig_dir, 'subfig_defects.png'),
        'mvs':         os.path.join(subfig_dir, 'subfig_mvs.png'),
    }
    for k, p in paths.items():
        if not os.path.exists(p):
            raise FileNotFoundError(f"Missing subfigure: {p}")

    imgs = {k: imread(p) for k, p in paths.items()}

    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(22, 15))

    # Left: Stage-Gate (full height)
    ax_left = fig.add_axes([0.0, 0.03, 0.52, 0.95])
    ax_left.imshow(imgs['stagegate'])
    ax_left.axis('off')
    ax_left.text(0.02, 0.99, '(a)', transform=ax_left.transAxes,
                 fontsize=16, fontweight='bold', va='top', color='#1A1A2E')

    # Right column
    ax_tr = fig.add_axes([0.53, 0.67, 0.46, 0.31])
    ax_tr.imshow(imgs['throughput'])
    ax_tr.axis('off')
    ax_tr.text(0.02, 0.99, '(b)', transform=ax_tr.transAxes,
               fontsize=16, fontweight='bold', va='top', color='#1A1A2E')

    ax_mr = fig.add_axes([0.53, 0.35, 0.46, 0.30])
    ax_mr.imshow(imgs['defects'])
    ax_mr.axis('off')
    ax_mr.text(0.02, 0.99, '(c)', transform=ax_mr.transAxes,
               fontsize=16, fontweight='bold', va='top', color='#1A1A2E')

    ax_br = fig.add_axes([0.53, 0.03, 0.46, 0.30])
    ax_br.imshow(imgs['mvs'])
    ax_br.axis('off')
    ax_br.text(0.02, 0.99, '(d)', transform=ax_br.transAxes,
               fontsize=16, fontweight='bold', va='top', color='#1A1A2E')

    # FIX 3: Larger citation footer (≥7pt) — two lines for readability
    fig.text(0.5, 0.018,
             '[1] Moylan 2014 NIST JRES 119.017  [2] ISO/ASTM 52902–52941  [3] ASTM E8  '
             '[4] Gheysen 2021  [5] Weaver 2021  [6] Vecchio 2021  '
             '[7] Brenner 2025  [8] Leon 2025  [9] NASA MSFC-3716',
             fontsize=7.5, ha='center', color='#888', style='italic')

    if output_path:
        fig.savefig(output_path, dpi=300, facecolor='white', edgecolor='none',
                    bbox_inches='tight', pad_inches=0.2)
        print(f"Saved composite {version} to {output_path}")
    plt.close(fig)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    compose_figure(output_path='/tmp/fig_workspace/composite.png')

# Genesis Mission Proposal — Gotchas and Weakness Analysis

*Analysis of factors that reduce the likelihood of the FLAIME proposal (DE-FOA-0003612, **Topic 3B — Critical Minerals: AI-Enabled Materials Discovery & Engineering, AMMTO**) being selected. Considers PI profile, institutional factors, preliminary data, team composition, competitive landscape, community standing, and program-specific risks.*

*Updated April 2026 to reflect the Topic 3B pivot. Topic 3B scored 7.5/10 with ~48% expected funding probability after 21 Edison Scientific analyses (~671K chars, 250+ citations) — see `topic-fit-comparative-assessment.md` for the full comparative analysis.*

*Material strategy: Al alloys are PRIMARY Phase I material (~80% effort) — specifically Al-Zr and Al-Mn-Cr-Zr families as critical-mineral-lean alternatives (avoiding Mg, Sc, REEs). Cu-Cr-Zr is COMPLEMENT (~20% stretch) for Be-Cu replacement. AlSi10Mg is baseline for benchmarking only.*

*Informed by repository analysis (grant-targeting-analysis.md, alloy-workflow-review.md, edison-trajectories/) and Edison Scientific literature research (task b66df0b0, LITERATURE query on DOE proposal failure modes for early-career PIs; tasks 039eae23–a5eb0f33, 10-query Topic 3B deep-dive series, ~331K chars; task 9e5ccd24, deep-dive synthesis). Key literature sources: Neumann et al. (2018) GAO report on DOE review processes, Rusco (2012) GAO report on ARPA-E, Mayer et al. (2020) RAND OT case studies, Elwany et al. (2024) DOE Near-Net-Shape Workshop Report, AMMTO (2024) 2023 Peer Review Final Report, Stach et al. (2021) Matter 4:2702 on autonomous experimentation systems, Goldstein & Kearney (2016) on ARPA-E program management, Bauer et al. (2023) DOE Critical Materials Assessment, Lograsso et al. (2024) CMI Cumulative Report.*

## 1. PI Track Record & DOE History

### No Prior DOE Funding
- The PI has no prior DOE awards. DOE review panels formally score "project team qualifications, experience, and capabilities" as one of four explicit merit criteria (Neumann et al. 2018, GAO report on DOE review). Genesis Mission Phase I is milestone-based OT — reviewers will look for evidence the PI can execute on deliverables under DOE's milestone framework.
- GAO reports indicate that ARPA-E program directors collect information about applicants' prior funding from other DOE offices to assess overlap and context (Rusco 2012). Having no prior DOE funding removes this signal entirely, leaving reviewers to rely solely on the proposal narrative.
- **Contrast with competitors:** Arroyave (Texas A&M) has DOE ARPA-E ULTIMATE (DE-AR0001427), ARL HTMDEC (W911NF-22-2-0106), and multiple NSF DMREF awards. Moridi (Cornell) has DOE BES Early Career (DE-SC0022860) plus NSF CAREER. These PIs bring proven DOE execution track records.

### Publication Record
- The repository describes the PI as an "early-career assistant professor" establishing a new lab (VCL). There is no mention of existing publications in AI-accelerated alloy design, autonomous experimentation, LPBF, or materials informatics.
- Edison research confirms that ARPA-E/AMMTO reviewers don't just look for "publications" generically — they assess whether the PI's demonstrated work covers the proposal's critical execution risks (Neumann et al. 2018). A common early-career failure mode is "a mismatch between the PI's demonstrated work and the proposal's critical execution risks (e.g., robotics + alloy processing + qualification)."
- DOE AMMTO reviewers will expect to see publications demonstrating the PI's technical depth in the proposed area. Key competitors have:
  - **Arroyave group:** Khatamsaz et al. (2023) *npj Computational Materials* (97 citations) on Bayesian optimization for alloy design
  - **Moridi:** Wakai et al. (2025) on harnessing metastability in MPEAs during AM
  - **MIT (Taheri-Mousavi, Hart, Olson):** Hybrid ML-CALPHAD-LPBF for high-strength Al alloys
  - **Rao (Virginia Tech):** CAREER on smart AM with sensing and data science
- **Gotcha:** Without a publication trail demonstrating hands-on expertise in the proposed domain, reviewers may question whether the PI can deliver the technical milestones. Even 1–2 arXiv preprints or conference papers showing relevant methodology would help, but if none exist at submission time, this is a significant gap.

### h-index and Citation Metrics
- For DOE programs (especially competitive ones like Genesis Mission), reviewers informally benchmark PIs against the field. If the PI's h-index and citation count are substantially below competitors, this creates a credibility gap — even though the FOA does not formally require a minimum.
- **Mitigation:** Leverage Gus Hart (BYU) as Co-PI or senior collaborator. Hart's co-authorship of Hart et al. (2021) *Nature Reviews Materials* (714 citations) provides immediate credibility in ML for alloys.

---

## 2. Preliminary Data Gap

### No Closed-Loop Demonstration
- The VCL pipeline (AI screening → powder atomization → LPBF → characterization) has **not been demonstrated in closed loop** yet. As of the repository state:
  - Powder samples were shipped to Amazemet (Poland) for ultrasonic atomization PoC — results not yet returned
  - The LPBF printer (Concept Laser M2 Cusing) has been **down for nearly 2 years**

The Genesis Mission
The Genesis Mission is a historic national effort to catalyze
new industries, create high-skill jobs, and usher a new
golden era of American discovery by fully embracing AI and
the ongoing computing revolution.
The Genesis Mission’s American Science and Security
--
Scientific and Engineering Scope
See Section III. Program Description
• Applications from multi-disciplinary, multi-institutional teams are required to
propose projects that address the Genesis Mission National Science and
Technology Challenges to accelerate scientific discovery and R&D workflows
• Teams are encouraged to leverage AI models and frameworks and the
extensive scientific and data resources of the DOE, its National Laboratories,
U.S. Industry, and academia
• Applications submitted under this RFA are expected to address challenges
identified in Topics 1-17 of the National Science and Technology Challenges
and cross-cutting needs of the American Science and Security Platform (Topics
18-21)
• Successful AI models and workflows developed under this effort may be
integrated into the American Science Cloud, Transformational Models
Consortium, and/or other key components of the Genesis Mission platform

Genesis Mission Consortium
• The Genesis Mission Consortium, announced February 6, 2026, is a public-private partnership
supporting the strategic direction of the Genesis Mission, working collaboratively to rapidly
advance progress in science, energy and other emerging technologies, and national security
• Consortium members intend to contribute computing power, AI tokens, technical expertise,
and/or in-kind support to advance Mission goals and build community
• The Consortium will connect leading industry and academic organizations with DOE and the
National Laboratories and their resources, identifying high value partnerships among
members to catalyze data flows and promote novel data applications
• For this RFA, the Consortium is providing an optional partnership initiative to help members
and non-members collaborate on applications. See the Consortium website for additional
information (https://genesismissionconsortium.org/).
• Applicants interested in leveraging the Consortium’s partnership service are encouraged to
do so as soon as possible
• Membership in the consortium is not a pre-requisite for eligibility under this RFA, and receipt
of an award does not grant membership in the Consortium

Award Information
See Section I. Basic Information
• Estimated Funding: Total Funding for FY 2026 is anticipated to be $293.76
million in current and prior fiscal year funds.
• Period of Performance:
◦ Phase I: Nine (9) months
◦ Phase II: Three (3) years

• Maximum/minimum award size:
◦ Phase I: $500,000 to $750,000 per award
◦ Phase II: DOE anticipates Phase II awards will be approximately 3 to 5 times the size of
Phase I awards on a funding per time basis, leading to a total estimated award range of
$2,000,000 to $5,000,000 per year. Total awards are estimated to be $6,000,000 to
$15,000,000 pending out year appropriations. The lower and upper bounds of the awards
are not strict limits and subject to change during award negotiation.

Funding Mechanism
• DOE’s Other Transaction Authorities will provide funding
• A single other transaction agreement is intended to be issued to a lead
member of the applicant team. Interagency agreements will be used when
required. DOE/NNSA National Laboratories will be funded using field work
proposals.
• Non-negotiable Genesis Mission Fast-track OT agreements for rapid award
and early start date will be provided. A milestone-based OT agreement and a
cost reimbursement OT agreement are expected to be posted shortly.
• The RFA uses two different mechanisms to support teams of multiple
institutions: Collaborative Applications and Subawards. Collaborative
Applications are strongly encouraged.

Application Information
• Pre-applications are not required for Phase I awards
• A Letter of Intent for Phase II awards is strongly encouraged but not required
• A Letter of Commitment from all partner institutions must be provided
• Following an initial review for compliance, all applications will be subject to a merit review and
evaluated against the following criteria in descending order of importance:
◦ Scientific and/or Technical Merit and Impact
◦ Technical Approach, Methods, and Feasibility
◦ Team, Resources, and Management
◦ Commercialization Potential for Energy Applications (applied technology development applications only)
◦ Budget and Cost-Effectiveness

• Both Federal and Non-Federal Reviewers may be used.
• Please see Sec. VI. Application Review Information for details on the questions provided to
reviewers, and distinctions for fundamental research and applied technology development
applications

• An amended RFA will be provided soon with details on Phase II LOIs and applications

Frequently Asked Questions about the
Genesis Mission: Transforming Science and Energy with AI
Notice of Request for Application (RFA): DE-FOA-0003612
This FAQ document will be updated as new questions are submitted to
GenesisMissionNOFO@science.doe.gov. Last updated on 3/23/2026.

Getting Help
Q. I have a question that isn’t answered in the RFA or this FAQ document. Whom do I contact?
A. Send your question to GenesisMissionNOFO@science.doe.gov.
Q. How can I get help with PAMS?
A. For help with PAMS, click the “PAMS Help” link on the PAMS website,
https://pamspublic.science.energy.gov/. Help is also available through the question mark (“?”) icon
at the bottom of every page. You may also contact the PAMS Help Desk, which can be reached
Monday through Friday, 9AM – 5:30 PM Eastern Time. Telephone: (855) 818-1846 (toll free) or (301)
903-9610, Email: sc.pamshelpdesk@science.doe.gov.
Q. How can I get help with Grants.gov?
A. Contact 800-518-4726 (toll-free) or support@Grants.gov. Also see Section IX of this RFA for
detailed instructions.

Phase I and II Awards
Q. What is a Phase I project?
A. Phase I projects will design and demonstrate a clear, tangible research workﬂow that
incorporates AI with concrete evaluation of the potential for AI advantage. Projects are from $500K
- $750K for 9 months. At 6 months, there will be a go/no go decision to determine if the project is
eligible to advance to Phase II. Phase I projects may request up to a 3-month extension to the go/no
go review date to complete planned tasks, such as experiments.
Q. What are the goals of a Phase I project?
A. Phase I projects are expected to provide a quantitative assessment of whether the proposed
approach to demonstrating AI advantage in the scientiﬁc and/or technical research workﬂow is on a
trajectory to yield a transformative scientiﬁc capability or transformative approach to an energy
application, thereby justifying consideration for increased investment through a Phase II project.
Q. What is a Phase II project?
A. Phase II projects will be conducted by large teams pursuing promising directions identiﬁed in the
Phase I projects. If a team believes they have already achieved the goals of Phase I projects, they
may apply directly for a Phase II project in FY26. Projects are approximately 3 to 5 times the level of
1

effort of Phase I projects per year for three years. Unlike Phase I projects, Phase II projects that
follow a phase I award in future ﬁscal years may include multiple Phase I teams, remove Phase I
team members, add external researchers, and/or address additional focus areas provided in the
RFA.
Q. How much funding is available?
A. DOE anticipates a total of $293.76 million in prior and current ﬁscal year funds are available to
support awards under this RFA. Future year funding depends on future congressional
appropriations.
Q. What is the anticipated funding for Phase II awards?
A. The RFA says that Phase II awards are “approximately 3 to 5 times the level of effort of Phase I
awards per year for three years”. Based on funding per time, the minimum is approximately
$500,000 * 12 months/9 month = $2 million per year and the maximum is $750,000 * 12 months/9
months = $5 million per year, for a total estimated award size range of $6 million to $15 million.
Q. What is the expected distribution of Phase I vs Phase II projects?
A. It is anticipated that most FY 2026 awards will be Phase I projects.
Q. How many Phase I projects are expected to transition to Phase II projects in FY 2027?
A. Only a small fraction of Phase I teams will be selected for Phase II awards. The larger Phase II
projects may include multiple Phase I teams, removal of Phase I team members, or additional
external researchers.
Q. What happens to Phase I projects that don’t pass the go/no-go decision?
A. Phase I projects not selected for a Phase II award will end.
Q. If a Phase I award passes the go/no-go decision, would a Phase II award be for an additional
three years?
A. Yes, it is anticipated that follow-on Phase II awards would be for an additional three years.
Q. Can institutions apply for both Phase I and Phase II awards using this RFA?
A. Yes. However, the institution may only submit one Phase I OR one Phase II application as the
lead institution per focus area, not both.
Q. What topics and focus areas are included in this RFA?
A. The challenge topics are a subset of the Genesis Mission National Science and Technology
Challenges (Topics 1-17) and cross-cutting needs of the Genesis Mission (Topics 18-21). DOE
program offices have specific focus areas under each of the topics above.
Q. Do you expect to issue another Genesis Mission: Transforming Science and Energy with AI
funding opportunity in FY 2027?
A. Yes. In FY 2027, DOE plans to amend the RFA or to issue an alternative funding opportunity to
update the topics and focus areas to allow a second competition of Phase I small team
applications and Phase II large team applications.

2

Q. What happens if I miss the application or LOI deadlines?
A. The RFA will remain open. Additional applications for Phase I and Phase II applications may be
submitted after the corresponding deadline listed on the cover of the RFA. However, DOE reserves
the right to decline such applications without review. If a Phase II LOI is not submitted by the
deadline, DOE may hold any subsequent Phase II application until FY 2027.
Q. When are Phase I applications due?
A. April 28, 2026, at 11:59 PM ET in Grants.gov.
Q. When are Phase II Letters of Intent (LOI) due?
A. April 28, 2026, at 5:00 PM ET in PAMS.
Q. When are Phase II applications due?
A. May 19, 2026, at 11:59 PM ET in Grants.gov.

Eligibility
Q. What types of institutions are eligible to submit an application as the lead institution?
A. U.S. universities, DOE/NNSA National Laboratories, for-proﬁt institutions, and not-for-proﬁt
institutions are eligible to serve as lead institutions. Non-DOE/NNSA Federally Funded Research
and Development Centers, Other Federal Agencies, and international entities may submit
applications as a member of a team but may not be the lead institution. Note that not-for-proﬁt
institutions described in section 501(c)(4) of the Internal Revenue Code of 985 that engaged in
lobbying activities after December 31, 1995, are not eligible.
Q. Does an eligible individual submitting an application as the PI or in another role need to be
a U.S. citizen or permanent resident.
A. No, DOE does not require that individuals submitting an application as the PI or listed in the
application in another role be a U.S. citizen or permanent resident. However, all personnel working
or proposed to work under an award must have the legal right to perform such work in the
jurisdiction where the work will be performed.
Q. Are there limitations on eligibility based on career stage of the applicant?
A. No, eligible individuals from any career stage may be proposed as a PI as long as they have the
skills, knowledge, and resources necessary to carry out the proposed research.
Q. Are there limitations on the number of applications a PI can submit?
A. Yes. A PI can be the lead-PI on only one Phase I or Phase II application. However, they may be a
senior investigator on an unlimited number of other applications.
Q. Are there limitations on the type of position a lead PI must be in to apply?
A. Yes. PIs must be in a permanent or indeﬁnitely extensible position at the lead institution, whether
part-time or full-time.
Q. If a PI has a joint appointment, can they apply as the lead PI from either institution?
A. PIs on joint appointments can be the PI on an institution’s application if they are paid by the
institution and the work will be done there. However, PIs with joint appointments at DOE/NNSA
3

national labs and another institution can only be the lead PI at the institution that pays for more
than half their salary and beneﬁts.
Q. Are there limitations on the number of applications a senior investigator can participate in
as a member but not the lead PI?
A. No, senior investigators can participate in an unlimited number of Phase I or Phase II
applications.
Q. Can a joint appointee whose salary and beneﬁts are paid by the university (with nine
months reimbursed by the national lab) serve as the lead PI from the university side?
A. No. As the RFA states, "Individuals receiving more than half of their salary and beneﬁts from a
DOE/NNSA National Laboratory may not be named as the PI in an application submitted by an
applicant other than a DOE/NNSA National Laboratory, regardless of any arrangement between the
employing Laboratory and the applicant institution." Since the majority of their salary and beneﬁts
come from the lab, they can only be a lead PI on the lab application.
Q. Can I serve as the lead PI if I have never been funded by DOE before?
A. Yes, anyone who meets the requirements of a lead PI may apply. See section "LIMITATIONS ON
PI" in the RFA for a full list of requirements.
Q. What is the difference between a lead PI, PI, co-PI, or senior/key person?
A. In the RFA, there is only one PI, the lead PI. All other investigators are a senior/key person.
However, outside the RFA it is common to refer to senior/key persons as PIs or co-PIs. For clarity, in
some places the PI is referred to as the lead PI in the RFA and this frequently asked questions
document. Senior/Key Personnel is deﬁned in the section IX.D Reference Material in the RFA.
Q. Are there limitations on the number of applications an institution can submit as the lead?
A. Yes, an institution may only submit one Phase I or Phase II application per focus area.
Q. Are there limitations on the number of applications an institution can submit as a nonlead?
A. No, an institution may be a non-lead institution on an unlimited number of applications.
Q. Are different campuses in a state university system considered separate institutions for
this solicitation?
A. In general, yes. Any institution that has registered with SAM and obtained a different Unique
Entity Identiﬁer (UEI) is considered a separate institution.
Q. What is a focus area?
A. There are 21 topics in the RFA. Under each topic are focus areas. For example, "1. Reenvisioning
Advanced Manufacturing and Industrial Productivity" is a topic and "A. Agentic AI-Driven Chemical
Manufacturing" and "B. AI-Driven Materials Processing" are two different focus areas. The same
institution could submit an application to the 1-A focus area and a different application to the 1-B
focus area.
Q. Can an applicant select more than one focus area?
A. Each applicant must address a topic and focus area speciﬁed in the RFA. Phase I applications
are limited to a single focus area. Phase II applications must identify a primary focus area but can
4

also address secondary focus areas. The primary focus area will be used for determining
limitations on institutional submissions.
Q. Can a seed team funded as a pilot under the DOE’s Transformational AI Models Consortium
apply for a Phase I or Phase II award?
A. Yes.
Q. Can a foreign institution be included as a member of a funded team?
A. Yes, a foreign institution may submit a collaborative application as a member of a team but may
not be the lead institution. Applicants are advised that successful applications that propose nondomestic entities as subrecipients include a detailed demonstration of how the proposed nondomestic subrecipients possess skills, resources, and abilities that do not exist among potential
domestic subrecipients.
Q. What is a domestic organization?
A. As stated in the RFA in Section IV.D. Reference Material, Domestic organization means a public
(including a State or other governmental agency) or private non-proﬁt or for-proﬁt organization that
is located in the United States or its territories, is subject to U.S. laws, and assumes legal and
ﬁnancial accountability for awarded funds and for the performance of the grant-supported
activities.
Q. Are non-proﬁts allowed to propose Cost-Plus-Fixed-Fee or is fee prohibited for this type of
award?
A. “Fee” is not an applicable cost category for non-proﬁts.
Under this RFA, awards will be made using DOE’s “other transaction” authority. Awards will be
structured in one of two formats:
1.
With payments tied to reaching speciﬁc milestones, or
2.
On a cost-reimbursement basis similar to research grants under 2 CFR 200.
There will be no cost-plus awards.

Teaming Requirements
Q. Is the lead institution considered a partner for determining teaming requirements?
A. Yes, the lead institution is considered a partner of the team. For example, for a Phase I

=== DOE/ARPA-E Programs with Backronym Names ===
ARPA-E is famous for its backronym program names:
  ULTIMATE = Ultra-wide bandgap semiconductors: Long-Term Investments ...
  OPEN = Open-source tools for Next-generation Energy R&D
  BETHE = Breakthroughs Enabling THermonuclear-fusion Energy
  GAMOW = Galvanizing Advances in Market-aligned fusion for an Overabundance of Watts
  IONICS = Innovative Optimization of New Ion Conducting Solids
  ROOTS = Rhizosphere Observations Optimizing Terrestrial Sequestration
  SCALEUP = Single-crystal turbine blades ...

Key observations:
1. ARPA-E ALWAYS uses backronyms for PROGRAM names (not individual project titles)
2. Individual PROJECT titles under ARPA-E programs typically spell out the acronym OR don't use one
3. NSF/DOE individual proposal titles sometimes include backronyms but usually expand them
4. The Genesis Mission RFA is NOT an ARPA-E program — it's a DOE-wide cross-office solicitation

For FLAIME specifically:
- FLAIME = Fail-fast Lightweight AI-driven Metallurgy Engine
- Title: 'FLAIME: Bayesian Optimization over Function Networks for ...'
- The acronym is NOT defined in the title itself
- It IS defined in the abstract (line ~204) and narrative §1

RECOMMENDATION:
- Safe approach: Expand in title → 'FLAIME (Fail-fast Lightweight AI-driven Metallurgy Engine): ...'
- Aggressive approach: Keep as-is (reviewers see abstract/narrative first anyway)
- DOE reviewers will read the full application, so undefined title acronym is low risk
- However, the title appears in public-facing databases (OSTI, PAMS) — expansion aids discoverability
- VERDICT: Expand FLAIME in the title for maximum clarity. Cost = ~8 extra words, benefit = zero confusion

edison-trajectories/ai-advantage-statement.md:15:FLAIME defines "AI advantage" as the measurable reduction in experiments, time, and critical mineral burden required to discover and qualify high-performance alloys compared to conventional and non-AI-guided approaches. We quantify this advantage through three interlocking metrics, evaluated against a pre-registered benchmark comprising four baselines (random search, expert DOE, standard Bayesian optimization, and BOFN without the mineral-burden objective) plus BOFN itself as the method under test. First, the **AI Acceleration Factor**, AF(y) = n\_baseline / n\_BOFN, measures iteration efficiency: the number of powder-to-tensile experiments a baseline requires to reach a target property threshold divided by the number BOFN requires. Our Phase I target is AF ≥3× vs. random search and ≥1.5× vs. standard BO, reported with bootstrap confidence intervals and win rates across ≥20 replicate seeds. Second, the **Enhancement Factor**, EF(n) = y\*\_BOFN(n) / y\*\_baseline(n), captures property improvement at fixed experimental budget. Third, a **time-ledger decomposition** (following Kavalsky et al., *Digital Discovery*, 2023) separates total platform acceleration into automation, AI, and throughput components—ensuring honest reporting even if any single component is modest. Critically, FLAIME's AI advantage is inseparable from its manufacturing integration: because BOFN's function-network DAG models every physical stage from atomization through LPBF to tensile testing, its acceleration applies to qualified, printable alloys—not merely predicted compositions. This distinguishes FLAIME from purely computational screening, which cannot close the "processability gap" between predicted and manufactured performance. FLAIME further demonstrates **scaling behavior**: as experimental data accumulates, BOFN's GP surrogate accuracy improves (tracked via nested cross-validation MAE and calibrated prediction intervals), its acquisition function targets higher-performing regions, and the mineral-burden Pareto frontier expands—each showing increasing performance with additional data, directly addressing DOE's scaling criterion.
edison-trajectories/ai-advantage-statement.md:21:FLAIME's AI advantage is the quantifiable acceleration of critical-mineral-lean alloy discovery, manufacturing, and qualification through closed-loop Bayesian optimization—measured on real, ASTM-tested specimens, not simulated compositions. We evaluate this advantage via a pre-registered benchmark comprising four baselines (random search, expert DOE, standard BO, and BOFN without mineral-burden objective) plus BOFN as the method under test, using two primary metrics: the Acceleration Factor AF(y) = n\_baseline / n\_BOFN (Phase I target: ≥3× vs. random, ≥1.5× vs. standard BO) and the Enhancement Factor EF(n) = y\*\_BOFN(n) / y\*\_baseline(n), where y\*(n) denotes the best-so-far observed property value achieved by budget n. Win rates and bootstrap confidence intervals across ≥20 seeds ensure statistical defensibility. A time-ledger decomposition (Kavalsky et al., 2023) further separates AI acceleration from automation and throughput gains, enabling honest attribution of each contributor.
edison-trajectories/calphad_visualization_recommendations.md:51:The FLAIME Pareto front should plot MB = Σᵢ wᵢ·xᵢ (x-axis) versus a CALPHAD-derived strength proxy such as predicted L1₂-Al₃Zr volume fraction or solidus temperature (y-axis). Benchmark alloys containing Sc and REE should be annotated to show they occupy high-MB positions. Quantitative supply risk weights from OECD assessments can anchor the MB scoring: Coulomb et al. (2015) report supply risk values of 4.6 for heavy REE, 3.1 for light REE, 2.4 for Mg, 1.1 for Sc, versus only 0.7 for Mn and 1.1 for Cr (coulomb2015criticalmineralstoday pages 47-51). The USGS methodology defines supply risk as "the confluence of three factors: the likelihood of a foreign supply disruption, the dependency of U.S. manufacturers on foreign supplies, and the ability of U.S. manufacturers to withstand a supply disruption" and identified 23 commodities as highest risk (nassar2020evaluatingthemineral pages 1-2). A companion bar chart of these supply risk weights makes the critical minerals rationale immediately legible to non-specialist reviewers.
edison-trajectories/edison-checklist-review-round6.md:24:1. **FLAIME-specific PI-confirmed parameters** not in Section B.3: Discovery yield ≥3% target, FLAIME = "Fast Learning AI for Mineral Efficiency" acronym definition, specific alloy families (Al-Zr, Al-Mn-Cr-Zr as primary; Cu-Cr-Zr as stretch ~20%), and cross-reference to budget document for exact figures
edison-trajectories/edison-checklist-review-round6.md:130:1. **Add FLAIME-specific cross-check items to B.3:** Add checkboxes for: (a) Discovery yield ≥3% (PI-confirmed), (b) FLAIME = Fast Learning AI for Mineral Efficiency, (c) Alloy families: Al-Zr (~40%), Al-Mn-Cr-Zr (~40%), Cu-Cr-Zr stretch (~20%), (d) Budget target: $750K (PI-confirmed), (e) Personnel: PI + 1 MS + 11 UGs @ $30/hr. These are all PI-confirmed parameters that should be checkable in one place.
edison-trajectories/edison-figure-analysis-round2.md:44:- Add explicit total program math: "200 alloys × ~$850 = ~$170K (FLAIME) vs. 200 × ~$50K = $10M+ (traditional)" — DOE reviewers want ROI quantified
edison-trajectories/edison-figure-analysis-round8.md:31:**Weaknesses:** The "~135× faster" claim compares "full qualification" (traditional, ~18 months) to "screening decision" (FLAIME, ~4 days)—non-equivalent endpoints. The math is correct (540/4 = 135×), but the asymmetric comparison is disclosed only in small footnote-level text. The ROI "50× cost reduction" uses only the lower traditional bound ($50K); the full range should read 50–500×. Panel (d) costs ($50+$100+$200+$300+$150+$200 = $1,000) are correct but require effort to verify visually.
edison-trajectories/edison-kpi3-acceleration-review.md:106:**Assessment**: The automation × AI × throughput decomposition proposed in FLAIME is a novel and useful framing, but it should be presented as a **proposed methodology** rather than a well-established standard. The proposal should: (a) clearly define measurement protocols for each factor independently (e.g., throughput = samples/week with automation vs manual; AI = iteration efficiency from BOFN benchmarking; automation = fraction of human-intervention-free operation time), and (b) address the non-independence of these factors (e.g., automation enables higher throughput, and AI value depends on throughput-limited batch sizes).

"""
v3-1: Fix FLAIME title and implement abstract inline citations.

1. Restore original FLAIME expansion in project title
2. Implement inline parenthetical (Author, Year) citations in abstract
3. Ensure narrative citation counter starts at [1]
"""

with open('genesis-mission-proposal/flaime-genesis-proposal.tex', 'r') as f:
    content = f.read()

# ===== 1. Restore FLAIME expansion in title =====
# Current title (both in abstract and title page):
old_title = "FLAIME: AI-Enabled Powder-to-Part Autonomous Discovery and Qualification of Critical-Mineral-Lean Alloys for Clean Energy"
# Restore to include the backronym expansion:
new_title = "FLAIME (Fast Learning AI for Mineral Efficiency): Autonomous Discovery and Qualification of Critical-Mineral-Lean Alloys for Clean Energy"

content = content.replace(old_title, new_title)

# Verify both occurrences updated (abstract line ~217 and title page line ~285)
count = content.count(new_title)
print(f"  Title updated in {count} locations (expected 2)")
assert count == 2, f"Expected 2 title occurrences, got {count}"

# ===== 2. Abstract inline citations =====
# Strategy: Use \bibentry or manual inline refs in abstract, then reset counter.
# Simplest robust approach: define the two specific citations as manual text
# in the abstract, and ensure the main bibliography counter starts fresh.
#
# The two abstract citations are:
#   \cite{usgs_mcs_2024} → (USGS, 2024)
#   \cite{conn_2025_apex} → (Conn et al., 2025)
#
# We'll replace \cite{} with manual parenthetical in abstract only,
# then the narrative's first \cite will naturally get [1].

# Replace in abstract section only (between \begin{document} and \newpage before title page)
# Find the abstract section boundaries
abstract_start = content.find(r'\section*{Project Summary / Abstract}')
abstract_end = content.find(r'\newpage', abstract_start)

abstract_section = content[abstract_start:abstract_end]

# Replace citations with inline parenthetical
abstract_section = abstract_section.replace(
    r'\cite{usgs_mcs_2024}',
    r'(USGS, 2024)'
)
abstract_section = abstract_section.replace(
    r'\cite{conn_2025_apex}',
    r'(Conn et~al., 2025)'
)

content = content[:abstract_start] + abstract_section + content[abstract_end:]

# Verify no \cite{} remains in abstract
abstract_check = content[abstract_start:content.find(r'\newpage', abstract_start)]
import re
remaining_cites = re.findall(r'\\cite\{', abstract_check)
print(f"  Remaining \\cite in abstract: {remaining_cites} (expected [])")
assert len(remaining_cites) == 0

# ===== 3. Verify narrative citation counter =====
# Since we removed \cite{} from the abstract, the first \cite in the narrative
# will naturally get [1] (natbib/bibtex numbers by order of first appearance).
# No counter reset needed — the abstract section is excluded from the
# submission PDF (\ifsubmission\else ... \fi), and even in draft mode,
# removing \cite{} from the abstract means no entries get numbered there.

# Let's verify the first \cite in the narrative
narrative_start = content.find(r'\section{Background')
if narrative_start == -1:
    narrative_start = content.find(r'\section*{DOE Title Page}')
first_cite_in_narrative = content.find(r'\cite{', narrative_start)
cite_end = content.find('}', first_cite_in_narrative)
first_cite_key = content[first_cite_in_narrative:cite_end+1]
print(f"  First narrative citation: {first_cite_key}")

with open('genesis-mission-proposal/flaime-genesis-proposal.tex', 'w') as f:
    f.write(content)

print("\n✓ v3-1: Title restored, abstract citations made inline parenthetical")
PYEOF
