$ cd /workspaces/digital-alloy-lab-private && python3 << 'PYEOF'
"""v3-4: Numerical consistency audit — check ALL key numbers across documents."""
import re

def read(path):
    with open(path) as f:
        return f.read()

tex = read('genesis-mission-proposal/flaime-genesis-proposal.tex')
plan = read('genesis-mission-proposal/proposal-population-plan.md')

findings = []

# === Budget ===
# Check $750K total
if tex.count('750') < 1:
    findings.append(("CRITICAL", "NUMERICAL", "Total budget $750K not found in tex"))
# Check BYU allocation
byu_refs = re.findall(r'BYU.*?\$?(\d+)K', tex)
print(f"BYU budget refs: {byu_refs}")
[partner-specific budget detail removed]
val_refs = re.findall(r'Valimet.*?\$(\d+)K', tex)
print(f"Valimet budget refs: {val_refs}")
[partner-specific budget detail removed]
amz_refs = re.findall(r'AMAZEMET.*?\$(\d+)K', tex)
print(f"AMAZEMET budget refs: {amz_refs}")
# Activity budgets
act1 = re.findall(r'Activity.?1.*?\$(\d+)K', tex)
act2_byu = re.findall(r'Activity.?2.*?BYU.*?\$(\d+)K', tex)
print(f"Activity 1: {act1}, Activity 2 BYU: {act2_byu}")

# === Personnel ===
ms_refs = re.findall(r'(\d+)\s*MS\s*student', tex)
ug_refs = re.findall(r'(\d+)\s*U[Gg]', tex)
print(f"MS students: {ms_refs}, UG: {ug_refs}")

# === Element palette ===
palette_match = re.search(r'\\elementpalette\{([^}]+)\}', tex)
if palette_match:
    elements = [e.strip() for e in palette_match.group(1).split(',')]
    print(f"Element palette: {len(elements)} elements: {elements}")
    if len(elements) != 15:
        findings.append(("CRITICAL", "NUMERICAL", f"Element palette has {len(elements)} elements, expected 15"))

# === Sub-system count ===
subsys_match = re.search(r'\\subsystemcountraw\{(\d+)\}', tex)
if subsys_match:
    subsys = int(subsys_match.group(1))
    # Verify: sum C(15,k) for k=2..8
    from math import comb
    expected = sum(comb(15, k) for k in range(2, 9))
    print(f"Sub-system count: {subsys} (expected {expected})")
    if subsys != expected:
        findings.append(("CRITICAL", "NUMERICAL", f"Sub-system count {subsys} != expected {expected}"))

# === kmin/kmax ===
kmin_match = re.search(r'\\kmin\{(\d+)\}', tex)
kmax_match = re.search(r'\\kmax\{(\d+)\}', tex)
if kmin_match and kmax_match:
    kmin, kmax = int(kmin_match.group(1)), int(kmax_match.group(1))
    print(f"kmin={kmin}, kmax={kmax}")
    # Check "ternary" language matches k=2 (binary) vs k=3 (ternary)
    if kmin == 2:
        # k=2 means binary, so text should say "binary" or at least not "ternary"
        ternary_refs = [(i+1, line) for i, line in enumerate(tex.split('\n')) if 'ternary' in line.lower() and 'binary' not in line.lower()]
        for lineno, line in ternary_refs:
            if 'e.g.' in line and 'Al--Fe--Si' in line:
                findings.append(("WARNING", "NUMERICAL", f"Line {lineno}: Says 'ternary (e.g., Al--Fe--Si)' but kmin=2 means we start at binary (2-component)"))

# === Composition targets ===
comp_refs = re.findall(r'(\d+)--(\d+)\s*compositions', tex)
print(f"Composition range refs: {comp_refs}")
geq200 = re.findall(r'geq.*?200.*?composition', tex)
if geq200:
    findings.append(("WARNING", "NUMERICAL", f"Still found >=200 composition refs (may be mechanical targets): {len(geq200)}"))

# === Discovery yield ===
yield_refs = re.findall(r'(\d+)\\?%.*?discovery', tex, re.IGNORECASE)
yield_refs2 = re.findall(r'discovery.*?(\d+)\\?%', tex, re.IGNORECASE)
print(f"Discovery yield refs: {yield_refs + yield_refs2}")

# === Acceleration ===
accel_refs = re.findall(r'(\d+)\$?\\times\$?.*?(?:acceleration|faster)', tex, re.IGNORECASE)
print(f"Acceleration refs: {accel_refs}")

# === Mineral burden ===
mb_refs = re.findall(r'(\d+)\\?%.*?mineral.burden\|mineral.burden.*?(\d+)\\?%', tex, re.IGNORECASE)
mb_refs2 = re.findall(r'(\d+)\\?%.*?(?:mineral|MBS|supply.risk)', tex, re.IGNORECASE)
print(f"Mineral burden refs: {mb_refs2}")
# Check specifically for 30% vs 40%
if '30\\%' in tex and 'mineral' in tex:
    lines_30 = [i+1 for i, l in enumerate(tex.split('\n')) if '30' in l and 'mineral' in l.lower()]
    print(f"  30% mineral lines: {lines_30}")
if '40\\%' in tex and 'mineral' in tex:
    lines_40 = [i+1 for i, l in enumerate(tex.split('\n')) if '40' in l and 'mineral' in l.lower()]
    print(f"  40% mineral lines: {lines_40}")

# === TRL ===
trl_refs = re.findall(r'TRL.?(\d)', tex)
print(f"TRL refs: {trl_refs}")

# === Gate months ===
gate_months = re.findall(r'[Gg](?:ate|1|2|3).*?month\s*(\d+)', tex)
print(f"Gate month refs: {gate_months}")

# === Throughput ===
throughput = re.findall(r'(\d+)\s*(?:unique\s*)?compositions?/day', tex)
print(f"Throughput refs: {throughput}")

# === CALPHAD databases ===
tcal_refs = re.findall(r'TCAl?\d+', tex, re.IGNORECASE)
print(f"TCAL refs: {tcal_refs}")
if any('8' in r for r in tcal_refs):
    findings.append(("WARNING", "NUMERICAL", f"Found TCAL8 reference: {[r for r in tcal_refs if '8' in r]}"))

# === Print findings ===
print("\n=== FINDINGS ===")
for sev, cat, msg in findings:
    print(f"  [{sev}] [{cat}] {msg}")
if not findings:
    print("  No numerical issues found")
PYEOF

"""v3-6: FOA compliance and reference audit."""
import re

def read(path):
    with open(path) as f:
        return f.read()

tex = read('genesis-mission-proposal/flaime-genesis-proposal.tex')
lines = tex.split('\n')

findings = []

# === Buy America statement ===
buy_america_line = None
for i, line in enumerate(lines):
    if 'Buy America' in line:
        buy_america_line = i + 1
        break
print(f"Buy America at line: {buy_america_line}")
# Check if it's within the first narrative section
narrative_start = None
for i, line in enumerate(lines):
    if '\\section{' in line and 'Background' in line:
        narrative_start = i + 1
        break
print(f"Narrative starts at line: {narrative_start}")

# === AI tool disclosure ===
ai_disclosure = None
for i, line in enumerate(lines):
    if 'AI' in line and ('tool' in line.lower() or 'disclosure' in line.lower() or 'generative' in line.lower()):
        ai_disclosure = i + 1
        break
if not ai_disclosure:
    for i, line in enumerate(lines):
        if 'Edison' in line or 'ChatGPT' in line or 'Claude' in line or 'Copilot' in line:
            ai_disclosure = i + 1
            break
print(f"AI disclosure near line: {ai_disclosure}")

# === Teaming: 2-of-3 categories ===
# (1) DOE/NNSA National Labs or Scientific User Facilities
# (2) Industry
# (3) Institutions of Higher Education/non-profits/other
# BYU = category 3, Valimet = category 2, AMAZEMET = category 2, Thermo-Calc = category 2
# Need at least 2 of 3 categories → we have (2) and (3) ✓
categories = set()
if re.search(r'BYU|Brigham Young|university', tex, re.IGNORECASE):
    categories.add(3)
if re.search(r'Valimet|AMAZEMET|Thermo.Calc|industry', tex, re.IGNORECASE):
    categories.add(2)
if re.search(r'National Lab|DOE.*lab|NNSA', tex, re.IGNORECASE):
    categories.add(1)
print(f"Team categories: {categories}")
if len(categories) < 2:
    findings.append(("CRITICAL", "FOA-COMPLIANCE", f"Team has only {len(categories)} of 2 required categories"))

# === DMSP ===
dmsp_refs = [i+1 for i, l in enumerate(lines) if 'DMSP' in l or 'Data Management' in l]
print(f"DMSP references at lines: {dmsp_refs[:5]}")

# === Label/ref integrity ===
all_labels = re.findall(r'\\label\{([^}]+)\}', tex)
all_refs = re.findall(r'\\ref\{([^}]+)\}', tex)
undefined = set(all_refs) - set(all_labels)
if undefined:
    findings.append(("CRITICAL", "REFERENCE", f"Undefined \\ref targets: {undefined}"))
    print(f"Undefined refs: {undefined}")
else:
    print("All \\ref targets defined ✓")

duplicates = [l for l in all_labels if all_labels.count(l) > 1]
if duplicates:
    findings.append(("WARNING", "REFERENCE", f"Duplicate labels: {set(duplicates)}"))
    print(f"Duplicate labels: {set(duplicates)}")

# === Placeholder figures ===
placeholders = [(i+1, line.strip()) for i, line in enumerate(lines) if 'Placeholder' in line or 'placeholder' in line]
print(f"\nPlaceholder items ({len(placeholders)}):")
for ln, text in placeholders:
    print(f"  Line {ln}: {text[:100]}")

# === Math checks ===
# Throughput: 2/day × 6 days/wk × ~39 weeks ≈ 468
theoretical_max = 2 * 6 * 39
print(f"\nTheoretical max compositions: {theoretical_max}")
# Check if "468" appears
if '468' in tex:
    print("  468 found in tex ✓")
else:
    print("  468 NOT found (check if mentioned)")

# Combinatorics: sum C(15,k) for k=2..8
from math import comb
subsys_expected = sum(comb(15, k) for k in range(2, 9))
print(f"Expected sub-systems (k=2..8): {subsys_expected}")

# Check sub-system formula text
subsys_formula = re.search(r'sum.*binom.*elementcount.*k.*k=(\d+)', tex)
if subsys_formula:
    print(f"  Formula starts at k={subsys_formula.group(1)}")

# Budget math: [activity/partner budget breakdown removed]
print(f"Budget check: [budget check removed]")

# === FOA section references ===
foa_refs = re.findall(r'FOA\s*(?:\\S|§)\s*([IVX]+(?:\.[A-Z])?)', tex)
print(f"\nFOA section refs: {set(foa_refs)}")

# === Print findings ===
print("\n=== FINDINGS ===")
for sev, cat, msg in findings:
    print(f"  [{sev}] [{cat}] {msg}")
if not findings:
    print("  No issues found")
PYEOF

CALPHAD thermodynamic data are drawn from Thermo-Calc's TCAl10 (aluminum) and
TCMG6 (magnesium) databases via the TC-Python API under BYU's HPC license
(Thermo-Calc collaboration letter, Appendix~7).
DFT-computed formation energies from the Materials Project augment CALPHAD
features as surrogate-model inputs; experimental benchmarks follow the MMPDS
handbook.
All \flaime{}-generated data will be published on Zenodo/Figshare with
persistent DOIs; the PI's MPTS-52 dataset, heavily reused by the
crystal-structure generative-AI community, evidences this open-data commitment.

\textbf{AI models.}
Bayesian Optimization over Function Networks (\bofn{}) with the partial
Knowledge Gradient (pKGFN) acquisition function drives cost-aware experiment
selection atop GPyTorch/BoTorch Gaussian-process surrogates.
\bofn{}/pKGFN code will be released as open-source Python packages with
Honegumi tutorials and integrated into BoTorch's tutorial ecosystem (Meta
letter of support, Appendix~7).

\textbf{Genesis Mission integration.}
\flaime{} is designed for integration with the American Science Cloud (AmSC)
and will host its digital thread, alloy database, and \bofn{}/pKGFN models on
the platform as it becomes available, participating in GM coordination
activities.  All datasets are simultaneously deposited on Zenodo/Figshare with
persistent DOIs, ensuring immediate FAIR-compliant open access to the broader
materials science community.  \bofn{}/pKGFN will be released as a domain-specific
``plug-and-play'' capability per the GM framework.

1. ---
2. name: proposal-consistency-check
3. description: >
4.   Automated consistency checker for the FLAIME Genesis Mission proposal.
5.   Runs a Python script that cross-checks numerical claims, terminology,
6.   and key facts across the LaTeX source, population plan, and checklist.
7.   Use when asked to check proposal consistency, find inconsistencies,
8.   or audit the proposal before submission.
9. allowed-tools: shell
10. ---
11. 
12. # Proposal Consistency Check Skill
13. 
14. This skill runs an automated consistency check across the FLAIME Genesis
15. Mission proposal documents. It catches numerical mismatches, terminology
16. drift, and missing required content.
17. 
18. ## Usage
19. 
20. Run the checker script from the skill's directory:
21. 
22. ```bash
23. python3 .github/skills/proposal-consistency-check/check_consistency.py
24. ```
25. 
26. The script outputs a structured report with severity levels:
27. - **CRITICAL**: Must fix before submission
28. - **WARNING**: Should review
29. - **INFO**: Minor / stylistic
30. 
31. ## What It Checks
32. 
33. 1. **Numerical claims** — budget totals, personnel counts, composition targets,
34.    throughput rates, timeline months, KPI thresholds, TRL levels
35. 2. **Terminology** — FLAIME acronym expansion, database names (TCAL10 not TCAL8),
36.    consistent partner names, consistent abbreviations
37. 3. **Cross-references** — LaTeX `\ref`/`\label` pairs, figure numbering
38. 4. **Required content** — Buy America statement, AI disclosure, team composition
39. 5. **Math validation** — combinatorics (22,698 sub-systems), throughput arithmetic
40. 
41. ## After Running
42. 
43. Review the output and address findings in order of severity. The script
44. is conservative — it may flag items that are technically correct but worth
45. a human double-check.
46.
````

1. #!/usr/bin/env python3
2. """
3. FLAIME Genesis Mission Proposal — Cross-Document Consistency Checker
4. 
5. Scans the LaTeX source, population plan, and checklist for inconsistencies
6. in numbers, terminology, cross-references, and FOA compliance.
7. 
8. Usage:
9.     python3 .github/skills/proposal-consistency-check/check_consistency.py
10. """
11. 
12. import os
13. import re
14. import sys
15. from dataclasses import dataclass, field
16. from math import comb
17. from pathlib import Path
18. from typing import Optional
19. 
20. # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
21. # Configuration
22. # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
23. 
24. REPO_ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[3]  # .github/skills/…/script → repo root
25. TEX_FILE = REPO_ROOT / "genesis-mission-proposal" / "flaime-genesis-proposal.tex"
26. PLAN_FILE = REPO_ROOT / "genesis-mission-proposal" / "proposal-population-plan.md"
27. CHECKLIST_FILE = REPO_ROOT / "genesis-mission-proposal" / "proposal-checklist.md"
28. 
29. 
30. # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
31. # Data model
32. # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
33. 
34. @dataclass
35. class Finding:
36.     severity: str  # CRITICAL, WARNING, INFO
37.     category: str  # NUMERICAL, TERMINOLOGY, CROSS-DOC, FOA-COMPLIANCE, REFERENCE, LOGIC
38.     message: str
39.     details: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
40. 
41. 
42. findings: list[Finding] = []
43. 
44. 
45. def add(severity: str, category: str, message: str, details: Optional[list[str]] = None):
46.     findings.append(Finding(severity, category, message, details or []))
47. 
48. 
49. # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
50. # Helpers
51. # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
52. 
53. def read(path: Path) -> str:
54.     if not path.exists():
55.         add("CRITICAL", "CROSS-DOC", f"Missing file: {path.relative_to(REPO_ROOT)}")
56.         return ""
57.     return path.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")
58. 
59. 
60. def count_occurrences(text: str, pattern: str, flags: int = 0) -> list[str]:
61.     return re.findall(pattern, text, flags)
62. 
63. 
64. def line_numbers_of(text: str, pattern: str, flags: int = 0) -> list[int]:
65.     result = []
66.     for i, line in enumerate(text.splitlines(), 1):
67.         if re.search(pattern, line, flags):
68.             result.append(i)
69.     return result
70. 
71. 
72. # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
73. # Load files
74. # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
75. 
76. tex = read(TEX_FILE)
77. plan = read(PLAN_FILE)
78. checklist = read(CHECKLIST_FILE)
79. all_text = tex + "\n" + plan + "\n" + checklist
80.
```

317. def check_references():
318.     labels = set(re.findall(r"\\label\{([^}]+)\}", tex))

327.     # Labels never referenced (info only)

329.     if unused:

333. 
334.     # Check for \lipsum usage

340. 
341.     # Check for placeholder text

366.

372.

## Critical Design Notes

### Element palette and sub-system counting

The palette has 15 **non-Al** alloying elements: Mn, Cr, Zr, Mg, Si, Cu, Ti, Fe,
Ni, Ce, Sc, Li, Er, Zn, Sn. **Aluminum is always the base element** and is NOT
counted in the binomial coefficient.

- `k` = number of alloying elements chosen from the 15-element palette
- **k=2 → ternary system** (2 chosen + Al = 3 components), e.g., Al-Fe-Si
- **k=3 → quaternary system** (3 chosen + Al = 4 components), e.g., Al-Mn-Cr-Zr
- **k=8 → 9-component system** (8 chosen + Al = 9 components)
- Total sub-systems: Σ C(15,k) for k=2..8 = **22,803**
- The `\kmin` and `\kmax` LaTeX variables control the range

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
FLAIME Genesis Mission Proposal — Cross-Document Consistency Checker

Scans the LaTeX source, population plan, and checklist for inconsistencies
in numbers, terminology, cross-references, and FOA compliance.

Usage:
    python3 .github/skills/proposal-consistency-check/check_consistency.py
"""

import os
import re
import sys
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from math import comb
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Optional

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Configuration — CANONICAL PROPOSAL PARAMETERS
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

REPO_ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[3]
TEX_FILE = REPO_ROOT / "genesis-mission-proposal" / "flaime-genesis-proposal.tex"
PLAN_FILE = REPO_ROOT / "genesis-mission-proposal" / "proposal-population-plan.md"
CHECKLIST_FILE = REPO_ROOT / "genesis-mission-proposal" / "proposal-checklist.md"

# Budget (current as of April 2026)
BUDGET_TOTAL = 750_000
BUDGET_BYU = 650_000          # $200K Act1 + $350K Act2 + $100K Act3
BUDGET_VALIMET = 50_000       # funded partner (own application)
BUDGET_AMAZEMET = 50_000      # funded partner (own application)

# Personnel
EXPECTED_MS = 2
EXPECTED_UG = 10

# Element palette — 15 NON-Al elements; Al is always the base
PALETTE_ELEMENTS = {"Mn", "Cr", "Zr", "Mg", "Si", "Cu", "Ti", "Fe", "Ni",
                    "Ce", "Sc", "Li", "Er", "Zn", "Sn"}
N_ELEMENTS = 15  # len(PALETTE_ELEMENTS)

# Sub-system counting: k = number of alloying elements chosen (NOT total components)
# k=2 → ternary (Al + 2 elements), k=3 → quaternary, ..., k=8 → 9-component
K_MIN = 2
K_MAX = 8
EXPECTED_SUBSYSTEMS = sum(comb(N_ELEMENTS, k) for k in range(K_MIN, K_MAX + 1))  # 22,803

# Composition targets (softened per Kosmos review April 2026)
COMPOSITION_RANGE = (100, 200)

# Other KPIs
MINERAL_BURDEN_REDUCTION = 40  # percent
DISCOVERY_YIELD = 3            # percent
ACCELERATION_FACTOR = 3        # times vs random baseline
GATE_MONTHS = {1: 3, 2: 5, 3: 7}
EXPECTED_TRLS = {2, 4, 6}     # entry, Phase I exit, Phase II

# FLAIME acronym
FLAIME_EXPANSION = "Fast Learning AI for Mineral Efficiency"


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Data model
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

@dataclass
class Finding:
    severity: str   # CRITICAL, WARNING, INFO
    category: str   # NUMERICAL, TERMINOLOGY, CROSS-DOC, FOA-COMPLIANCE, REFERENCE, LOGIC
    message: str
    details: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)


findings: list[Finding] = []


def add(severity: str, category: str, message: str, details: Optional[list[str]] = None):
    findings.append(Finding(severity, category, message, details or []))


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Helpers
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def read(path: Path) -> str:
    if not path.exists():
        add("CRITICAL", "CROSS-DOC", f"Missing file: {path.relative_to(REPO_ROOT)}")
        return ""
    return path.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")


def line_numbers_of(text: str, pattern: str, flags: int = 0) -> list[int]:
    result = []
    for i, line in enumerate(text.splitlines(), 1):
        if re.search(pattern, line, flags):
            result.append(i)
    return result


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Load files
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

tex = read(TEX_FILE)
plan = read(PLAN_FILE)
checklist = read(CHECKLIST_FILE)
all_text = tex + "\n" + plan + "\n" + checklist


# ===========================================================================
# CHECK 1: Numerical consistency
# ===========================================================================

def check_numerical():
    # --- Budget ---
    budget_section = re.search(
        r"Summary Budget Information.*?\\end\{tabularx\}", tex, re.DOTALL
    )
    if budget_section:
        budget_text = budget_section.group(0)
        budget_totals = re.findall(r"\\textbf\{Total\}.*?(\d[\d,]+)", budget_text)
        for bt in budget_totals:
            val = int(bt.replace(",", ""))
            if val != BUDGET_TOTAL:
                add("CRITICAL", "NUMERICAL",
                    f"Budget total in summary table is ${val:,} — expected ${BUDGET_TOTAL:,}",
                    [f"Found: {bt}"])

        byu_budget = re.findall(r"BYU.*?(\d[\d,]+)", budget_text)
        for b in byu_budget:
            val = int(b.replace(",", ""))
            if val not in (BUDGET_BYU,):
                add("WARNING", "NUMERICAL",
                    f"BYU budget in summary table is ${val:,} — expected ${BUDGET_BYU:,}")

        val_budget = re.findall(r"Valimet.*?(\d[\d,]+)", budget_text)
        for v in val_budget:
            val = int(v.replace(",", ""))
            if val not in (BUDGET_VALIMET,):
                add("WARNING", "NUMERICAL",
                    f"Valimet budget is ${val:,} — expected ${BUDGET_VALIMET:,}")

    # --- Personnel ---
    ms_matches = re.findall(r"(\d+)\s*MS\s*student", tex, re.IGNORECASE)
    ug_matches = re.findall(r"(\d+)\s*U[GR]\s*(?:researcher|student|undergrad)", tex, re.IGNORECASE)

    for m in ms_matches:
        if m != str(EXPECTED_MS):
            add("CRITICAL", "NUMERICAL",
                f"MS student count is {m} — expected {EXPECTED_MS}")
    for u in ug_matches:
        if u != str(EXPECTED_UG):
            add("CRITICAL", "NUMERICAL",
                f"UG researcher count is {u} — expected {EXPECTED_UG}")

    ms_plan = re.findall(r"(\d+)\s*MS", plan)
    ug_plan = re.findall(r"(\d+)\s*UG", plan)
    for m in ms_plan:
        if m not in (str(EXPECTED_MS),):
            add("WARNING", "NUMERICAL",
                f"Population plan mentions {m} MS students — expected {EXPECTED_MS}")
    for u in ug_plan:
        if u not in (str(EXPECTED_UG),):
            add("WARNING", "NUMERICAL",
                f"Population plan mentions {u} UGs — expected {EXPECTED_UG}")

    # --- Sub-systems count ---
    # Match the \subsystemcountraw LaTeX variable
    subsys_raw = re.search(r"\\subsystemcountraw\{(\d+)\}", tex)
    if subsys_raw:
        val = int(subsys_raw.group(1))
        if val != EXPECTED_SUBSYSTEMS:
            add("CRITICAL", "NUMERICAL",
                f"\\subsystemcountraw is {val:,} — expected {EXPECTED_SUBSYSTEMS:,}")

    # Also check free-text mentions
    subsys_mentions = re.findall(
        r"(\d[\d,]{2,})\s*(?:sub-?systems|element combinations)", all_text, re.IGNORECASE
    )
    for s in subsys_mentions:
        val = int(s.replace(",", ""))
        if val != EXPECTED_SUBSYSTEMS:
            add("CRITICAL", "NUMERICAL",
                f"Sub-system count {val:,} doesn't match Σ C({N_ELEMENTS},k) for k={K_MIN}..{K_MAX} = {EXPECTED_SUBSYSTEMS:,}")

    # Verify the combinatorial formula in LaTeX
    tex_formula = re.search(r"\\sum_\{k=(\d+)\}\^\{(\d+)\}", tex)
    if tex_formula:
        k_lo, k_hi = int(tex_formula.group(1)), int(tex_formula.group(2))
        if k_lo != K_MIN or k_hi != K_MAX:
            add("CRITICAL", "NUMERICAL",
                f"LaTeX formula uses k={k_lo}..{k_hi} — expected k={K_MIN}..{K_MAX}")

    # Also look for \binom{\elementcount}{k} and verify elementcount
    elem_count_match = re.search(r"\\elementcount.*?(\d+)", tex)

    # --- Composition targets ---
    # Accept 100-200 range or individual mentions of 100, 200 near "composition"
    geq200_comp = re.findall(r"\\geq\$?\s*200.*?composition", tex, re.IGNORECASE)
    if geq200_comp:
        add("WARNING", "NUMERICAL",
            f"Found '≥200 compositions' — should be '100–200' range (softened per Kosmos)",
            [f"Matches: {len(geq200_comp)}"])

    # --- Throughput ---
    throughput_max = 2 * 6 * 39  # ~468
    if "468" not in all_text:
        add("INFO", "NUMERICAL",
            "Throughput theoretical max (~468) not found in documents")

    # --- Discovery yield ---
    yields = re.findall(r"[≥>]\s*(\d+(?:\.\d+)?)\s*%.*?discovery\s*yield", all_text, re.IGNORECASE)
    yield_vals = set(float(y) for y in yields)
    if len(yield_vals) > 1:
        add("WARNING", "NUMERICAL",
            f"Multiple discovery yield targets: {yield_vals} (expected ≥{DISCOVERY_YIELD}%)")

    # --- Mineral-burden reduction ---
    mbr_30 = line_numbers_of(tex, r"[≥>\\geq]\s*30\s*\\?%.*?(?:mineral|reduction|MBS)", re.IGNORECASE)
    mbr_40 = line_numbers_of(tex, r"[≥>\\geq]\s*40\s*\\?%.*?(?:mineral|reduction|MBS)", re.IGNORECASE)
    if mbr_30 and mbr_40:
        add("WARNING", "NUMERICAL",
            f"Both 30% and 40% mineral-burden reduction mentioned",
            [f"30% at lines {mbr_30}", f"40% at lines {mbr_40}",
             f"Expected: ≥{MINERAL_BURDEN_REDUCTION}% consistently"])
    elif mbr_30 and not mbr_40:
        add("WARNING", "NUMERICAL",
            f"Mineral-burden reduction is 30% — should be {MINERAL_BURDEN_REDUCTION}%")

    # --- TRL levels ---
    trl_set = set(int(x) for x in re.findall(r"TRL\s*[~]?\s*(\d)", all_text))
    unexpected = trl_set - EXPECTED_TRLS - {9}  # TRL 9 may appear as CMI reference
    if unexpected:
        add("INFO", "NUMERICAL",
            f"Unexpected TRL values: {unexpected} (expected {EXPECTED_TRLS})")

    # --- Go/No-Go gate months ---
    gate_months = {}
    for m in re.finditer(r"^(\d+)\s*&\s*M\d+/G(\d)", tex, re.MULTILINE):
        month = int(m.group(1))
        gate = int(m.group(2))
        gate_months[gate] = month

    for g, expected_mo in GATE_MONTHS.items():
        if g in gate_months and gate_months[g] != expected_mo:
            add("WARNING", "NUMERICAL",
                f"G{g} is at month {gate_months[g]} — expected month {expected_mo}")


# ===========================================================================
# CHECK 2: Terminology consistency
# ===========================================================================

def check_terminology():
    # --- FLAIME acronym ---
    flaime_tex = re.findall(r"FLAIME.*?Fast Learning AI for (\w+ \w+)", tex)
    for exp in flaime_tex:
        if exp.lower() != "mineral efficiency":
            add("CRITICAL", "TERMINOLOGY",
                f"FLAIME expansion mismatch: 'Fast Learning AI for {exp}'",
                [f"Expected: '{FLAIME_EXPANSION}'"])

    # --- Database name TCAl10 vs TCAL8 ---
    tcal8_refs = line_numbers_of(tex, r"TCAl?8\b", re.IGNORECASE)
    if tcal8_refs:
        add("CRITICAL", "TERMINOLOGY",
            f"TCAL8 referenced in .tex (should be TCAl10)",
            [f"Lines: {tcal8_refs}"])

    tcal8_plan = line_numbers_of(plan, r"TCAl?8\b", re.IGNORECASE)
    if tcal8_plan:
        add("WARNING", "TERMINOLOGY",
            f"TCAL8 referenced in population plan (should be TCAl10)",
            [f"Lines: {tcal8_plan}"])

    # --- LPBF vs L-PBF ---
    lpbf_count = len(re.findall(r"\bLPBF\b", tex))
    l_pbf_count = len(re.findall(r"\bL-PBF\b", tex))
    if lpbf_count > 0 and l_pbf_count > 0:
        add("WARNING", "TERMINOLOGY",
            f"Mixed LPBF/L-PBF usage: LPBF={lpbf_count}, L-PBF={l_pbf_count}")

    # --- Thermo-Calc spelling ---
    bad_tc = []
    if re.search(r"ThermoCalc", tex, re.IGNORECASE):
        bad_tc.append("ThermoCalc")
    if re.search(r"Thermocalc(?![\w-])", tex):
        bad_tc.append("Thermocalc")
    if bad_tc:
        add("WARNING", "TERMINOLOGY",
            f"Non-standard Thermo-Calc spelling: {bad_tc}")

    # --- AMAZEMET casing ---
    amazemet_lower = line_numbers_of(tex, r"(?<![A-Z])Amazemet(?![A-Z])")
    if amazemet_lower:
        add("WARNING", "TERMINOLOGY",
            f"'Amazemet' (lowercase) found — should be 'AMAZEMET'",
            [f"Lines: {amazemet_lower}"])

    # --- pycalphad casing ---
    bad_pycalphad = re.findall(r"PyCalphad|PYCALPHAD|Pycalphad", tex)
    if bad_pycalphad:
        add("INFO", "TERMINOLOGY",
            f"pycalphad should be lowercase: found {bad_pycalphad}")

    # --- Sub-size vs subsize ---
    subsize_variants = {
        "sub-size": len(re.findall(r"sub-size", tex, re.IGNORECASE)),
        "subsize": len(re.findall(r"(?<!-)subsize", tex, re.IGNORECASE)),
        "sub size": len(re.findall(r"sub size", tex, re.IGNORECASE)),
    }
    active = {k: v for k, v in subsize_variants.items() if v > 0}
    if len(active) > 1:
        add("INFO", "TERMINOLOGY", f"Mixed 'sub-size' variants: {active}")

    # --- $TBD budget placeholders ---
    tbd_lines = line_numbers_of(tex, r"\$TBD")
    if tbd_lines:
        add("WARNING", "NUMERICAL",
            f"Budget placeholder '$TBD' still present",
            [f"Lines: {tbd_lines}"])

    # --- MVS defined before first use ---
    mvs_first = tex.find("MVS")
    mvs_def = tex.find("minimum-viable-specimen (MVS)")
    if mvs_def == -1:
        mvs_def = tex.find("Minimum Viable Specimen (MVS)")
    if mvs_first != -1 and mvs_def != -1 and mvs_first < mvs_def:
        first_line = tex[:mvs_first].count('\n') + 1
        def_line = tex[:mvs_def].count('\n') + 1
        add("WARNING", "TERMINOLOGY",
            f"MVS used at line ~{first_line} before definition at line ~{def_line}")


# ===========================================================================
# CHECK 3: LaTeX cross-references
# ===========================================================================

def check_references():
    labels = set(re.findall(r"\\label\{([^}]+)\}", tex))
    refs = set(re.findall(r"\\ref\{([^}]+)\}", tex))

    broken = refs - labels
    if broken:
        add("CRITICAL", "REFERENCE",
            f"Broken \\ref references (no matching \\label): {broken}")

    unused = labels - refs
    if unused:
        add("INFO", "REFERENCE",
            f"Labels defined but never \\ref'd: {unused}",
            ["May be intentional for appendix figures"])

    # \lipsum placeholder text
    lipsum_lines = line_numbers_of(tex, r"\\lipsum")
    if lipsum_lines:
        add("CRITICAL", "CROSS-DOC",
            f"\\lipsum still present (placeholder text!)",
            [f"Lines: {lipsum_lines}"])

    # Placeholder content
    placeholder_lines = line_numbers_of(tex, r"Placeholder:")
    if placeholder_lines:
        add("WARNING", "CROSS-DOC",
            f"Placeholder content still in .tex",
            [f"Lines: {placeholder_lines}",
             "Replace with actual figures/content before submission"])


# ===========================================================================
# CHECK 4: FOA compliance
# ===========================================================================

def check_foa_compliance():
    # Buy America statement in first 2 pages of narrative
    if "Buy America" not in tex:
        add("CRITICAL", "FOA-COMPLIANCE",
            "Buy America Act compliance statement missing")

    # AI tool disclosure
    if not re.search(r"AI\s*[Tt]ool\s*[Dd]isclosure", tex):
        add("CRITICAL", "FOA-COMPLIANCE",
            "AI Tool Disclosure section missing",
            ["FOA §IV.C requires disclosure of AI tools used"])

    # Team 2-of-3 categories
    has_ihe = bool(re.search(r"BYU|Brigham Young|universit", tex, re.IGNORECASE))
    has_industry = bool(re.search(r"Valimet|AMAZEMET", tex))
    categories = sum([has_ihe, has_industry])
    if categories < 2:
        add("WARNING", "FOA-COMPLIANCE",
            f"Team has {categories}/2 required institution categories")

    # Abstract: "Application Stage: Phase I"
    abstract_end = tex.find(r"\newpage")
    abstract_section = tex[:abstract_end] if abstract_end > 0 else tex[:5000]
    if "Application Stage" not in abstract_section:
        add("CRITICAL", "FOA-COMPLIANCE",
            "Abstract missing 'Application Stage: Phase I'",
            ["FOA §IV.C requires application stage in abstract header"])

    # Abstract: no \cite{} (must be self-contained)
    abstract_start = tex.find(r"\section*{Project Summary")
    if abstract_start >= 0:
        abstract_text = tex[abstract_start:abstract_end] if abstract_end > abstract_start else ""
        cite_in_abstract = re.findall(r"\\cite\{", abstract_text)
        if cite_in_abstract:
            add("WARNING", "FOA-COMPLIANCE",
                f"Abstract contains {len(cite_in_abstract)} \\cite commands — abstract must be self-contained",
                ["Use inline parenthetical (Author, Year) instead"])

    # Abstract: coinvestigators listed
    if abstract_start >= 0:
        abstract_header = tex[abstract_start:abstract_start + 2000]
        if not re.search(r"Senior.*Key.*Personnel|[Cc]oinvestigator|Partner.*:.*\w+\.\s*\w+", abstract_header):
            add("INFO", "FOA-COMPLIANCE",
                "Abstract may not list coinvestigator names (FOA wants names + affiliations)")

    # DMSP not required at submission
    if "not required" not in tex.lower() and "NOT required" not in tex:
        add("INFO", "FOA-COMPLIANCE",
            "Consider noting DMSP is not required at Phase I submission")


# ===========================================================================
# CHECK 5: Cross-document consistency
# ===========================================================================

def check_cross_doc():
    # Element palette
    tex_elements = set(re.findall(
        r"\b(Mn|Cr|Zr|Mg|Si|Cu|Ti|Fe|Ni|Ce|Sc|Li|Er|Zn|Sn)\b", tex
    ))
    tex_missing = PALETTE_ELEMENTS - tex_elements
    if tex_missing:
        add("WARNING", "CROSS-DOC",
            f"Elements missing from .tex: {tex_missing}")

    plan_elements = set(re.findall(
        r"\b(Mn|Cr|Zr|Mg|Si|Cu|Ti|Fe|Ni|Ce|Sc|Li|Er|Zn|Sn)\b", plan
    ))
    plan_missing = PALETTE_ELEMENTS - plan_elements
    if plan_missing:
        add("INFO", "CROSS-DOC",
            f"Elements missing from population plan: {plan_missing}")

    # Figure count
    tex_fig_count = len(re.findall(r"\\begin\{figure\}", tex))
    if tex_fig_count == 0:
        add("WARNING", "CROSS-DOC", "No figures found in .tex")

    # Word count estimate for narrative
    narrative_match = re.search(
        r"\\setcounter\{page\}\{1\}(.*?)(?=\\newpage\s*\\section\*\{Appendix|$)",
        tex, re.DOTALL
    )
    if narrative_match:
        narrative = narrative_match.group(1)
        stripped = re.sub(r"\\[a-zA-Z]+\{[^}]*\}", " ", narrative)
        stripped = re.sub(r"\\[a-zA-Z]+", " ", stripped)
        stripped = re.sub(r"\{[^}]*\}", " ", stripped)
        stripped = re.sub(r"%.*$", "", stripped, flags=re.MULTILINE)
        stripped = re.sub(r"\\begin\{.*?\\end\{[^}]+\}", " ", stripped, flags=re.DOTALL)
        words = len(stripped.split())
        if words > 2000:
            add("WARNING", "CROSS-DOC",
                f"Estimated narrative word count: ~{words} (target: ~1,570)")
        elif words < 1000:
            add("INFO", "CROSS-DOC",
                f"Estimated narrative word count: ~{words} (may be under-developed)")


# ===========================================================================
# CHECK 6: Logic validation
# ===========================================================================

def check_logic():
    # Verify combinatorics
    computed = sum(comb(N_ELEMENTS, k) for k in range(K_MIN, K_MAX + 1))
    if computed != EXPECTED_SUBSYSTEMS:
        add("CRITICAL", "LOGIC",
            f"Internal error: Σ C({N_ELEMENTS},{K_MIN}..{K_MAX}) = {computed}, expected {EXPECTED_SUBSYSTEMS}")

    # Individual binomial coefficients
    expected_by_k = {k: comb(N_ELEMENTS, k) for k in range(K_MIN, K_MAX + 1)}
    for k, exp in expected_by_k.items():
        plan_vals = re.findall(rf"C\(15,{k}\)\s*=\s*(\d[\d,]*)", plan)
        for pv in plan_vals:
            if int(pv.replace(",", "")) != exp:
                add("CRITICAL", "LOGIC",
                    f"Population plan: C(15,{k}) = {pv}, should be {exp:,}")

    # k=2 → ternary check (NOT binary!)
    # Since Al is always the base, k=2 means 2 alloying elements + Al = ternary
    ternary_lines = line_numbers_of(tex, r"ternary", re.IGNORECASE)
    binary_lines = line_numbers_of(tex, r"binary", re.IGNORECASE)
    # If kmin=2 and text says "binary" for k=2 systems, that's wrong
    for bl in binary_lines:
        line = tex.splitlines()[bl - 1]
        if "k=2" in line or "kmin" in line.lower():
            add("WARNING", "LOGIC",
                f"Line {bl}: 'binary' used for k=2 — should be 'ternary' (Al + 2 elements = 3 components)")

    # Throughput max
    throughput_max = 2 * 6 * 39  # ~468
    if "468" not in all_text and str(throughput_max) not in all_text:
        add("INFO", "LOGIC",
            "Throughput max (~468) not found in documents")

    # Budget arithmetic: 200 + 350 + 50 + 50 + 100 = 750
    budget_sum = 200 + 350 + 50 + 50 + 100
    if budget_sum != BUDGET_TOTAL // 1000:
        add("CRITICAL", "LOGIC",
            f"Budget items sum to ${budget_sum}K, expected ${BUDGET_TOTAL // 1000}K")


# ===========================================================================
# Main
# ===========================================================================

def main():
    print("=" * 70)
    print("FLAIME Proposal Consistency Checker")
    print(f"  Elements: {N_ELEMENTS} | k: {K_MIN}..{K_MAX} | Sub-systems: {EXPECTED_SUBSYSTEMS:,}")
    print(f"  Budget: ${BUDGET_TOTAL:,} | Personnel: {EXPECTED_MS} MS + {EXPECTED_UG} UG")
    print(f"  Compositions: {COMPOSITION_RANGE[0]}–{COMPOSITION_RANGE[1]} | MB: ≥{MINERAL_BURDEN_REDUCTION}%")
    print("=" * 70)
    print()

    check_numerical()
    check_terminology()
    check_references()
    check_foa_compliance()
    check_cross_doc()
    check_logic()

    severity_order = {"CRITICAL": 0, "WARNING": 1, "INFO": 2}
    findings.sort(key=lambda f: severity_order.get(f.severity, 3))

    if not findings:
        print("✅ No inconsistencies found!")
        return 0

    critical = [f for f in findings if f.severity == "CRITICAL"]
    warnings = [f for f in findings if f.severity == "WARNING"]
    infos = [f for f in findings if f.severity == "INFO"]

    print(f"Found {len(findings)} issues: "
          f"{len(critical)} critical, {len(warnings)} warnings, {len(infos)} info\n")

    if critical:
        print("## CRITICAL (must fix before submission)")
        print("-" * 50)
        for i, f in enumerate(critical, 1):
            print(f"  {i}. [{f.category}] {f.message}")
            for d in f.details:
                print(f"     → {d}")
        print()

    if warnings:
        print("## WARNING (should review)")
        print("-" * 50)
        for i, f in enumerate(warnings, 1):
            print(f"  {i}. [{f.category}] {f.message}")
            for d in f.details:
                print(f"     → {d}")
        print()

    if infos:
        print("## INFO (minor / stylistic)")
        print("-" * 50)
        for i, f in enumerate(infos, 1):
            print(f"  {i}. [{f.category}] {f.message}")
            for d in f.details:
                print(f"     → {d}")
        print()

    return 1 if critical else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

# Proposal Consistency Check Skill

This skill runs an automated consistency check across the FLAIME Genesis
Mission proposal documents. It catches numerical mismatches, terminology
drift, and missing required content.

## Usage

Run the checker script from the skill's directory:

```bash
python3 .github/skills/proposal-consistency-check/check_consistency.py
```

The script outputs a structured report with severity levels:
- **CRITICAL**: Must fix before submission
- **WARNING**: Should review
- **INFO**: Minor / stylistic

## What It Checks

[partner-specific budget detail removed]
[partner-specific budget detail removed]
   sub-system count (22,803 = Σ C(15,k) for k=2..8), KPI thresholds, TRL levels
2. **Terminology** — FLAIME = "Fast Learning AI for Mineral Efficiency",
   TCAl10 (not TCAL8), AMAZEMET (all caps), consistent LPBF/Thermo-Calc/pycalphad
3. **Cross-references** — LaTeX `\ref`/`\label` pairs, unreferenced figures, placeholders
4. **FOA compliance** — Buy America, AI disclosure, abstract self-contained (no `\cite{}`),
   "Application Stage: Phase I" in abstract, team 2-of-3 categories
5. **Math validation** — combinatorics, budget arithmetic, throughput

## Key Design Note: Element Palette

The palette has 15 **non-Al** alloying elements. Al is always the base.
- k=2 → **ternary** system (2 chosen + Al = 3 components)
- k=3 → **quaternary** system (3 chosen + Al = 4 components)
- This is NOT a bug — do not "fix" ternary to binary for k=2.

## Canonical Parameters (update these when proposal changes)

The script header contains all canonical parameter values. When the proposal
evolves, update the constants at the top of `check_consistency.py` to match.

## After Running

Review the output and address findings in order of severity. The script
is conservative — it may flag items that are technically correct but worth
a human double-check.

Add AM scale-up validation test structures analysis with modular proposal figure, structure schematics, and Topic 3B framing
Research deliverable answering: what are the standard test structures ("benchy" of metal AM) for validating new alloys, and what evaluations are performed — with Al alloy focus. Complements the powder-level GA scale-up plan from PR #26. **Updated for DOE Genesis Mission Topic 3B** (AI-Enabled Materials Discovery and Engineering, AMMTO, DE-FOA-0003612).

### `edison-trajectories/am-scaleup-test-structures.md`

- **Metal AM has no single "benchy"** — practitioners use a staged progression: single tracks → thin walls → density cubes → tensile bars → ISO/ASTM 52902 geometric artifact
- **8-stage validation funnel** from powder QA through production freeze, with standards mapping (ISO/ASTM 52902/52904/52907/52930, ASTM E8, SAE AMS 7003)
- **Topic 3B target alloy systems**: Al-Zr (Sc-free L1₂ strengthening, YS≥280 MPa aged), Al-Mn-Cr-Zr (multi-component Sc-free, YS≥250 MPa, EL≥5%), Cu-Cr-Zr stretch goal (YS≥200 MPa, ≥50% IACS conductivity) — all targeting critical mineral demand reduction (CMDRI ≥25% vs incumbent)
- **Al-specific defect hierarchy**: hot cracking (critical for 2xxx/7xxx), H₂ porosity, Al₂O₃ oxide inclusions — with Al-Zr peritectic solidification notes distinct from eutectic Al-Si systems
- **BOFN DAG with mineral-burden objective**: MB = Σᵢ wᵢ·xᵢ with USGS supply-risk weights; partner-specific nodes (Valimet GA, AMAZEMET UA, Thermo-Calc CALPHAD)
- **Concrete targets**: AlSi10Mg ≥99.5–99.9% relative density (baseline), Al-Zr ≥99.0% (novel), Ra 5–23 µm as-built
- **HT screening shortcuts** for FLAIME's ~200 comp/9mo throughput: combinatorial builds (Weaver 2021, 5× speedup), HT-READ mini-libraries (Vecchio 2021), miniature tensile mass screening
- **Minimum viable set for a new Al alloy**: ~15–30 features, ~$1,000, ~4 days — fail-fast ordering (cracks at step 2, density at step 3)

### Topic 3B Conversion and Partnership Context

- **Partnership structure**: Letters of collaboration from Valimet (gas atomization), AMAZEMET (ultrasonic atomization), Thermo-Calc (CALPHAD/AM Module). Letters of support from Ames National Lab (Ames Lab contacts), Fehrmann Alloys, Taylor Sparks (U of Utah), Ashley Speer, Adam Clare, Chris Stiles (JHU APL), Jae Hattrick-Simpers (autonomous experimentation), Keith Brown (Boston University SDL)
- **Preliminary results section**: AMAZEMET atomizer installed at BYU, AlSi10Mg tensile specimens (U of Utah + 3D Powder Tech), SEM/EDS of precursor powders and atomized mixture, high-T tensile data, Thermo-Calc AM Module simulations + BYU HPC runs, full pKGFN pipeline implementation, automated powder dispensing demonstration
- **Edison-validated** through 3 rounds of Topic 3B-specific review (B+/A- → B+ → A-)

# Preliminary Results Roadmap for FLAIME Genesis Mission Phase I Proposal

*Assessment of what preliminary results to collect by April 28, 2026*

## Overview

This document synthesizes input from three Edison Scientific queries — (1) mock PO/reviewer panel feedback, (2) asset readiness assessment, and (3) experimental capability evidence assessment — combined with the existing body of work across 17+ open PRs and the DOE Genesis Mission (DE-FOA-0003612) **Topic 3B (Critical Minerals and Materials — AI-Enabled Materials Discovery, AMMTO)** requirements. It identifies the highest-impact preliminary results to generate in the 19 days before the April 28 deadline, specifying exactly what would appear in the proposal: figures, figure captions, tables, and narrative text placement. Four rounds of Edison mock review informed this roadmap: two rounds (tasks `567c7816`, `97b09434`) refined structure and content, a third round (task `1e791f42`, score 7.0/10) incorporated after the comprehensive partnership and evidence update, and a fourth round (task `a039dc08`, score 8.0/10) harmonized figure numbering and reconciled cross-references.

> **Terminology note**: FLAIME uses **Bayesian Optimization over Function Networks (BOFN)** as the decision-making framework, with the **partial Knowledge Gradient for Function Networks (pKGFN)** as the primary acquisition function. In this document, "pKGFN" refers to the specific acquisition function implementation, while "BOFN" refers to the broader framework. Both are used throughout; they are not interchangeable but are complementary.

### Partnership Structure

**Letters of Collaboration (formal team members):**
- **Valimet** (Stockton, CA) — gas atomization service contract for Phase I scale-up powders
- **AMAZEMET** (Warsaw, Poland) — ultrasonic atomization equipment and rePOWDER service; returning atomized powder batches with controlled composition adjustments
- **Thermo-Calc** (McMurray, PA / Stockholm) — CALPHAD screening via TC-Python/TCAl10 and AM Module simulations; providing sample AM Module calculations and advisory support

**Letters of Support:**
- **Ames National Laboratory** — CMI Hub expertise, Phase II GARS pathway
- **Fehrmann Alloys** — feedstock validation and alloy supply chain
- **Taylor Sparks** (University of Utah) — LPBF printing capability; printed AlSi10Mg tensile specimens for baseline characterization
- **Ashley Speer** — characterization and materials science expertise
- **Adam Clare** (University of British Columbia / University of Nottingham, FREng) — additive manufacturing process expertise
- **Chris Stiles** (JHU/APL connection) — AM process engineering
- **Jae Hattrick-Simpers** — autonomous experimentation and SDL methodology
- **Keith Brown** (Boston University) — SDL validation and Bayesian optimization expertise

### Phase I Target Alloy System

**Phase I will focus on Al alloys processed by LPBF, targeting critical-mineral-lean compositions in the Al-Zr and Al-Mn-Cr-Zr families.** The primary objective is to discover and qualify printable Al alloys that eliminate dependence on critical minerals (Mg, Sc, REE) commonly used in high-performance Al-alloy feedstocks. AlSi10Mg serves as the baseline for benchmarking and initial BOFN validation because it is the most commercially mature and data-rich LPBF aluminum alloy — baseline tensile specimens have been printed at the University of Utah and by 3D Powder Tech, with tensile data collected. Novel compositions explored via CALPHAD-guided search will target the Al-Zr-X and Al-Mn-Cr-Zr spaces, where Zr provides grain refinement and Mn/Cr contribute corrosion resistance and strength. While Mn, Cr, and Zr appear on the 2022 USGS Critical Minerals List, they generally carry lower supply-chain risk than Sc and REE — which often exhibit high single-nation supply concentration (USGS, *2022 Final List of Critical Minerals*, 87 FR 10381) — and are typically used at lower concentrations than many Mg-based or Sc-bearing alloy formulations. FLAIME's mineral-burden objective uses a weighted criticality index that accounts for both supply-risk severity and required mass fraction, enabling the optimizer to quantitatively minimize aggregate critical mineral exposure rather than treating all listed minerals as equivalent. **Cu-Cr-Zr alloys are a secondary complement (~20% Phase I effort)** for Be-Cu replacement in high-conductivity applications, demonstrating platform generality. This alloy strategy aligns with AMMTO's Critical Minerals Strategy (CMS) Pillars 2 (Secure and Diversify Supply) and 5 (Invest in Workforce and Innovation), and with collaborator capabilities (U of Utah LPBF printing, Thermo-Calc CALPHAD/AM Module, AMAZEMET ultrasonic atomization, Valimet gas atomization) and available CALPHAD databases (TCAl10, Scheil-Gulliver solidification modeling on BYU HPC).

### Proposal Narrative Arc

The proposal argues that **autonomous, cost-aware closed-loop experimentation can substantially accelerate the discovery and qualification of critical-mineral-lean LPBF alloys, reducing dependence on supply-chain-vulnerable elements (Mg, Sc, REE) in structural aluminum applications**. The evidence chain is: (1) BOFN selects experiments that maximize information per dollar across a multi-stage workflow → (2) CALPHAD-informed constraints prevent exploration of unprintable compositions and enforce mineral-efficiency objectives → (3) stage-gated characterization (SEM, EDS, tensile) provides the physical ground truth that updates the surrogate → (4) the loop closes when qualification-relevant properties meet targets with minimal critical mineral content. The key differentiator is cost-aware multi-fidelity optimization over the full powder-to-property chain (not just process parameters) with an explicit mineral-burden objective. The Phase I deliverable is a validated closed-loop framework demonstrated on Al alloys with real experimental data, producing a shortlist of critical-mineral-lean compositions ready for Phase II scale-up. Preliminary results already in hand include: baseline AlSi10Mg tensile data from University of Utah and 3D Powder Tech printed specimens, SEM/EDS characterization of precursor powders and AMAZEMET-atomized powder, high-temperature tensile data on a standard aluminum specimen, Thermo-Calc AM Module simulations, CALPHAD screening runs on BYU HPC, a full pKGFN (partial Knowledge Gradient for Function Networks) pipeline implementation, and a demonstration of automated powder dispensing. *(ACTION ITEM: Insert quantified acceleration factor (X× fewer experiments, Y× lower cost vs. EI/random baselines) from closed-loop demo. Target: Day 9. Owner: Computational lead. If demo incomplete, state 'projected' with confidence interval.)*

### Page Budget Strategy

DOE Genesis Mission Phase I Project Narrative is capped at **5 pages** (§IV.C). Figures and tables count against this limit. Appendices (Facilities, Equipment, etc.) do not count. Preliminary results must be impactful but extremely concise — every figure and sentence must earn its space.

| Proposal Section | Target Pages | Max Figures/Tables |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| Background/Intro | ~1.0 | 1 figure |
| Project Objectives | ~0.5 | — |
| Proposed Research/Methods | ~1.5 | 1 figure |
| Milestones | ~1.0 | 1 table |
| Data Sources/Models | ~0.5 | — |
| Decision Gate Metrics | ~0.5 | 1 table |
| **Total (narrative)** | **5.0** | **~4 figures/tables** |
| *Appendix 2: Facilities (≤0.5p)* | *0.5* | *1 figure (atomizer)* |
| *Appendix 3: Equipment (≤0.5p)* | *0.5* | *1 table* |

Given the 5-page limit, preliminary results must be woven into Background/Intro and Research/Methods sections rather than occupying a dedicated section. The figure triage below identifies which evidence items to include in the narrative vs. appendices.

### Figure Triage for Preliminary Results (within 5-page narrative)

Given the extremely tight 5-page narrative limit, a maximum of 3 figures and 1 table fit in the narrative itself (~1.5 pages). The remaining experimental evidence is described in text with quantitative metrics, and supporting images go to Appendices (Facilities, Equipment).

| Figure # | Content | Proposal Section | Size |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Fig. 1** | Closed-loop pKGFN pipeline schematic + convergence plot | Research/Methods | Full-width, ~0.5 page |
| **Fig. 2** | Combined CALPHAD screening funnel + SEM/EDS multi-panel (2×3 compact) | Background/Prelim Results | Full-width, ~0.5 page |
| **Fig. 3** | Tensile data summary (stress–strain + YS/UTS/elongation bar chart) | Research/Methods | Half-width, ~0.25 page |
| **Table 1** | KPI/go-no-go dashboard (5 KPIs, triggered actions) | Milestones | Full-width, ~0.25 page |

**Moved to Appendices:** BOFN ablation (reference in text, full figure in supplementary); atomizer photo → Facilities appendix; detailed EDS maps → Facilities/Equipment appendix.
**Described in text only:** Real-data benchmark results (report MAE and cost-to-target numbers inline); automated powder dispensing (one sentence + metric); high-T tensile (report numbers in text alongside ambient tensile figure).

*See Edison provenance log at end of document for query details.*

Key reviewer-facing interpretation: The BOFN synthetic MAE and cost-savings are *necessary but not sufficient*. Without a real-data benchmark and at least one closed-loop pilot, they will be perceived as algorithm development decoupled from LPBF reality. The test-structure/validation schematic and parameter-space structuring are already strong because they signal execution readiness and digital-thread thinking. The LLM warmstart is the highest-risk preliminary result: unless it demonstrates it does *not* collapse exploration into known-alloy neighborhoods, reviewers may interpret it as novelty-harming.

Good context gathered. Here's my analysis and recommendation:

**MVS progression in abstract**: Yes — the abstract currently jumps from "LPBF" straight to "ASTM E8 sub-size tensile testing," hiding the staged fail-fast logic that reviewers value. Adding "single tracks → density cubes → tensile bars" shows execution sophistication within a short phrase.

**High-T tensile**: The facilities section (line 1093) already mentions "room- and elevated-temperature tensile testing per ASTM E8/E8M." PR #30's trajectory notes high-T testing is "relevant to aged-condition validation of Al-Zr alloys (aging at 350–400°C)" — this is significant because Al-Zr's L1₂ precipitate coarsening resistance at elevated temps is its key differentiator over conventional Al alloys and directly relevant to DOE clean-energy applications (engine components, heat exchangers). I recommend a brief mention in the narrative Methods section (Activity 2, where the MVS pipeline is described), noting that top-performing Al-Zr candidates will undergo elevated-temperature tensile evaluation to validate thermal stability. It shouldn't go in the abstract — too tight.

genesis-mission-proposal/edison-references.bib:9874:  title = {Materials Science Optimization Benchmark Dataset for High-dimensional, Multi-objective, Multi-fidelity Optimization of CrabNet Hyperparameters},
genesis-mission-proposal/edison-references.bib:9880:  abstract = {Benchmarks are crucial for driving progress in scientific disciplines. To be effective, benchmarks should closely mimic real-world tasks while being computationally efficient, allowing for accessibility and repeatability. Developing surrogate models that can be indistinguishable from the ground truth observation within the explored dataset bounds dramatically reduces the computational burden of running benchmarks without sacrificing quality, but this requires a large amount of initial data. In the fields of materials science and chemistry, relevant optimization tasks can be challenging due to their complexity, which includes hierarchical, noisy, multi-fidelity, multi-objective, high-dimensional, and non-linearly correlated variables. Additionally, they may include mixed numerical and categorical variables that are subject to linear and non-linear constraints. Simulating or experimentally verifying such tasks can be difficult, which is why benchmarks are essential. This study aimed to overcome these challenges by generating 173219 quasi-random hyperparameter combinations across 23 hyperparameters and using them to train CrabNet on the Matbench experimental band gap dataset (Computational runtime: 387 RTX-2080-Ti GPU days). The results were stored in a free-tier shared MongoDB Atlas dataset, creating a regression dataset that maps hyperparameter combinations to metrics such as MAE, RMSE, computational runtime, and model size for the CrabNet model trained on the Matbench experimental band gap benchmark task. To simulate the actual simulations, heteroskedastic noise was incorporated into the regression dataset, and bad hyperparameter combinations were excluded. Percentile ranks were computed within each group of identical parameter sets to capture heteroskedastic noise, rather than assuming Gaussian noise as is done in traditional approaches. This approach can be applied to other benchmark datasets, bridging the gap between optimization benchmarks with low computational overhead and realistically complex, real-world optimization scenarios.},

1849:  abstract = {AbstractWe present a benchmark test suite and an automated machine learning procedure for evaluating supervised machine learning (ML) models for predicting properties of inorganic bulk materials. The test suite, Matbench, is a set of 13 ML tasks that range in size from 312 to 132k samples and contain data from 10 density functional theory-derived and experimental sources. Tasks include predicting optical, thermal, electronic, thermodynamic, tensile, and elastic properties given a material’s composition and/or crystal structure. The reference algorithm, Automatminer, is a highly-extensible, fully automated ML pipeline for predicting materials properties from materials primitives (such as composition and crystal structure) without user intervention or hyperparameter tuning. We test Automatminer on the Matbench test suite and compare its predictive power with state-of-the-art crystal graph neural networks and a traditional descriptor-based Random Forest model. We find Automatminer achieves the best performance on 8 of 13 tasks in the benchmark. We also show our test suite is capable of exposing predictive advantages of each algorithm—namely, that crystal graph methods appear to outperform traditional machine learning methods given \textasciitilde{}104or greater data points. We encourage evaluating materials ML algorithms on the Matbench benchmark and comparing them against the latest version of Automatminer.},
4375:  abstract = {AbstractBayesian optimization (BO) has been leveraged for guiding autonomous and high-throughput experiments in materials science. However, few have evaluated the efficiency of BO across a broad range of experimental materials domains. In this work, we quantify the performance of BO with a collection of surrogate model and acquisition function pairs across five diverse experimental materials systems. By defining acceleration and enhancement metrics for materials optimization objectives, we find that surrogate models such as Gaussian Process (GP) with anisotropic kernels and Random Forest (RF) have comparable performance in BO, and both outperform the commonly used GP with isotropic kernels. GP with anisotropic kernels has demonstrated the most robustness, yet RF is a close alternative and warrants more consideration because it is free from distribution assumptions, has smaller time complexity, and requires less effort in initial hyperparameter selection. We also raise awareness about the benefits of using GP with anisotropic kernels in future materials optimization campaigns.},
8030:  abstract = {Many real-world optimisation problems such as hyperparameter tuning in machine learning or simulation-based optimisation can be formulated as expensive-to-evaluate black-box functions. A popular approach to tackle such problems is Bayesian optimisation, which builds a response surface model based on the data collected so far, and uses the mean and uncertainty predicted by the model to decide what information to collect next. In this article, we propose a generalisation of the well-known Knowledge Gradient acquisition function that allows it to handle constraints. We empirically compare the new algorithm with four other state-of-the-art constrained Bayesian optimisation algorithms and demonstrate its superior performance. We also prove theoretical convergence in the infinite budget limit.},
9032:  abstract = {Artificial intelligence is approaching the point at which it can complete the scientific cycle, from hypothesis generation to experimental design and validation, within a closed loop that requires little human intervention. Yet, the loop is not fully autonomous: humans still curate data, set hyperparameters, adjudicate interpretability, and decide what counts as a satisfactory explanation. As models scale, they begin to explore regions of hypothesis and solution space that are inaccessible to human reasoning because they are too intricate or alien to our intuitions. Scientists may soon rely on AI strategies they do not fully understand, trusting goals and empirical payoffs rather than derivations. This prospect forces a choice about how much control to relinquish to accelerate discovery while keeping outputs human relevant. The answer cannot be a blanket policy to deploy LLMs or any single paradigm everywhere. It demands principled matching of methods to domains, hybrid causal and neurosymbolic scaffolds around generative models, and governance that preserves plurality and counters recursive bias. Otherwise, recursive training and uncritical reuse risk model collapse in AI and an epistemic collapse in science, as statistical inertia amplifies flaws and narrows the investigation. We argue for graded autonomy in AI-conducted science: systems that can close the loop at machine speed, while remaining anchored to human priorities, verifiable mechanisms, and domain-appropriate forms of understanding.},
9874:  title = {Materials Science Optimization Benchmark Dataset for High-dimensional, Multi-objective, Multi-fidelity Optimization of CrabNet Hyperparameters},
9880:  abstract = {Benchmarks are crucial for driving progress in scientific disciplines. To be effective, benchmarks should closely mimic real-world tasks while being computationally efficient, allowing for accessibility and repeatability. Developing surrogate models that can be indistinguishable from the ground truth observation within the explored dataset bounds dramatically reduces the computational burden of running benchmarks without sacrificing quality, but this requires a large amount of initial data. In the fields of materials science and chemistry, relevant optimization tasks can be challenging due to their complexity, which includes hierarchical, noisy, multi-fidelity, multi-objective, high-dimensional, and non-linearly correlated variables. Additionally, they may include mixed numerical and categorical variables that are subject to linear and non-linear constraints. Simulating or experimentally verifying such tasks can be difficult, which is why benchmarks are essential. This study aimed to overcome these challenges by generating 173219 quasi-random hyperparameter combinations across 23 hyperparameters and using them to train CrabNet on the Matbench experimental band gap dataset (Computational runtime: 387 RTX-2080-Ti GPU days). The results were stored in a free-tier shared MongoDB Atlas dataset, creating a regression dataset that maps hyperparameter combinations to metrics such as MAE, RMSE, computational runtime, and model size for the CrabNet model trained on the Matbench experimental band gap benchmark task. To simulate the actual simulations, heteroskedastic noise was incorporated into the regression dataset, and bad hyperparameter combinations were excluded. Percentile ranks were computed within each group of identical parameter sets to capture heteroskedastic noise, rather than assuming Gaussian noise as is done in traditional approaches. This approach can be applied to other benchmark datasets, bridging the gap between optimization benchmarks with low computational overhead and realistically complex, real-world optimization scenarios.},
9935:  abstract = {Deep learning models are full of hyperparameters, which are set manually before the learning process can start. To find the best configuration for these hyperparameters in such a high dimensional space, with time-consuming and expensive model training / validation, is not a trivial challenge. Bayesian optimization is a powerful tool for the joint optimization of hyperparameters, efficiently trading off exploration and exploitation of the hyperparameter space. In this paper, we discuss Bayesian hyperparameter optimization, including hyperparameter optimization, Bayesian optimization, and Gaussian processes. We also review BoTorch, GPyTorch and Ax, the new open-source frameworks that we use for Bayesian optimization, Gaussian process inference and adaptive experimentation, respectively. For experimentation, we apply Bayesian hyperparameter optimization, for optimizing group weights, to weighted group pooling, which couples unsupervised tiered graph autoencoders learning and supervised graph prediction learning for molecular graphs. We find that Ax, BoTorch and GPyTorch together provide a simple-to-use but powerful framework for Bayesian hyperparameter optimization, using Ax's high-level API that constructs and runs a full optimization loop and returns the best hyperparameter configuration.},
10023:  abstract = {Bayesian optimization (BO) is a powerful paradigm for efficient optimization of black-box objective functions. High-dimensional BO presents a particular challenge, in part because the curse of dimensionality makes it difficult to define -- as well as do inference over -- a suitable class of surrogate models. We argue that Gaussian process surrogate models defined on sparse axis-aligned subspaces offer an attractive compromise between flexibility and parsimony. We demonstrate that our approach, which relies on Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for inference, can rapidly identify sparse subspaces relevant to modeling the unknown objective function, enabling sample-efficient high-dimensional BO. In an extensive suite of experiments comparing to existing methods for high-dimensional BO we demonstrate that our algorithm, Sparse Axis-Aligned Subspace BO (SAASBO), achieves excellent performance on several synthetic and real-world problems without the need to set problem-specific hyperparameters.},
10045:  abstract = {When hyperparameter optimization of a machine learning algorithm is repeated for multiple datasets it is possible to transfer knowledge to an optimization run on a new dataset. We develop a new hyperparameter-free ensemble model for Bayesian optimization that is a generalization of two existing transfer learning extensions to Bayesian optimization and establish a worst-case bound compared to vanilla Bayesian optimization. Using a large collection of hyperparameter optimization benchmark problems, we demonstrate that our contributions substantially reduce optimization time compared to standard Gaussian process-based Bayesian optimization and improve over the current state-of-the-art for transfer hyperparameter optimization.},
10285:  abstract = {This paper presents the results and insights from the black-box optimization (BBO) challenge at NeurIPS 2020 which ran from July-October, 2020. The challenge emphasized the importance of evaluating derivative-free optimizers for tuning the hyperparameters of machine learning models. This was the first black-box optimization challenge with a machine learning emphasis. It was based on tuning (validation set) performance of standard machine learning models on real datasets. This competition has widespread impact as black-box optimization (e.g., Bayesian optimization) is relevant for hyperparameter tuning in almost every machine learning project as well as many applications outside of machine learning. The final leaderboard was determined using the optimization performance on held-out (hidden) objective functions, where the optimizers ran without human intervention. Baselines were set using the default settings of several open-source black-box optimization packages as well as random search.},
10318:  abstract = {Bayesian optimization is popular for optimizing time-consuming black-box objectives. Nonetheless, for hyperparameter tuning in deep neural networks, the time required to evaluate the validation error for even a few hyperparameter settings remains a bottleneck. Multi-fidelity optimization promises relief using cheaper proxies to such objectives --- for example, validation error for a network trained using a subset of the training points or fewer iterations than required for convergence. We propose a highly flexible and practical approach to multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization, focused on efficiently optimizing hyperparameters for iteratively trained supervised learning models. We introduce a new acquisition function, the trace-aware knowledge-gradient, which efficiently leverages both multiple continuous fidelity controls and trace observations --- values of the objective at a sequence of fidelities, available when varying fidelity using training iterations. We provide a provably convergent method for optimizing our acquisition function and show it outperforms state-of-the-art alternatives for hyperparameter tuning of deep neural networks and large-scale kernel learning.},
11024:  abstract = {This study presents novel predictive models using Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for simulating thermal dynamics in Laser Powder Bed Fusion (L-PBF) processes. By developing and validating Single-Laser GNN (SL-GNN) and Multi-Laser GNN (ML-GNN) surrogates, the research introduces a scalable data-driven approach that learns fundamental physics from small-scale Finite Element Analysis (FEA) simulations and applies them to larger domains. Achieving a Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) of 3.77\\% with the baseline SL-GNN model, GNNs effectively learn from high-resolution simulations and generalize well across larger geometries. The proposed models capture the complexity of the heat transfer process in L-PBF while significantly reducing computational costs. For example, a thermomechanical simulation for a 2 mm x 2 mm domain typically requires about 4 hours, whereas the SL-GNN model can predict thermal distributions almost instantly. Calibrating models to larger domains enhances predictive performance, with significant drops in MAPE for 3 mm x 3 mm and 4 mm x 4 mm domains, highlighting the scalability and efficiency of this approach. Additionally, models show a decreasing trend in Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) when tuned to larger domains, suggesting potential for becoming geometry-agnostic. The interaction of multiple lasers complicates heat transfer, necessitating larger model architectures and advanced feature engineering. Using hyperparameters from Gaussian process-based Bayesian optimization, the best ML-GNN model demonstrates a 46.4\\% improvement in MAPE over the baseline ML-GNN model. In summary, this approach enables more efficient and flexible predictive modeling in L-PBF additive manufacturing.},
<exited with exit code 0>

3013:  abstract = {AbstractThe final part density in laser powder bed fusion is influenced by the powder particle size distribution. Too fine powders are not spreadable, and too coarse powders cause porosity. Powder blends, especially bimodal ones, can exhibit higher packing densities and changes in flowability compared to their monomodal constituents. These properties can influence final part density. Therefore, the influence of bimodal powder on final part density was investigated. Two gas atomized 316L (1.4404) powders with a D50 of 20.3 µm and 60.3 µm were blended at weight ratios of 3:1, 1:1, and 1:3, and the original and blended powders were processed. The results show that the final part porosity increases almost linearly with an increasing volume fraction of coarse powder. Furthermore, the final part density is independent of powder bulk density and flowability. Measurements of the top surface show that an increase of part porosity by coarse powder is caused by an increase in melt pool fluctuation, which in turn causes irregular solidified scan tracks. Additionally, the results show that the powder segregation during coating is stronger for the bimodal powder; however, no influence of the segregation on the part density could be found.},
8863:  abstract = {The adoption of additive manufacturing (AM) has driven extensive research into metal feedstocks, uncovering strong links between powder quality and the performance of printed parts. Poor powder characteristics, inadequate flowability or inconsistent packing, can significantly degrade the mechanical performance of the final 3D-printed components. This study investigates the effects of arc manipulator angle, electrical current, and vibration amplitude on AlSi12 powder quality via ultrasonic atomization (UA). Parameter adjustments significantly influenced particle size distribution, with span variations up to 37.5\%. Optimal rheological properties were achieved by increasing the vibration amplitude (from 75 to 80\%), decreasing the arc angle (from 5° to -5°), and reducing the current (from 150 A to 140 A). A modified AM suitability factor (AMS) was developed, incorporating logarithmic transformation and custom weighting to mitigate high-uncertainty parameter effects. Results revealed a non-linear relationship between powder suitability and arc angle, with a sharp worsening above 0°. Electrical current had the greatest impact on powder quality, followed by arc angle and vibration amplitude. Benchmarking showed that UA powder achieved suitability factors 21\% higher than commercial powder, with improved sphericity compared to the irregular, fused particles of commercial alternatives. These findings underscore the potential of UA to enhance AM part reliability.},
<exited with exit code 0>
```

@misc{baird_2021_chemrxiv,
  author = {Baird, Sterling and Diep, Tran and Sparks, Taylor},
  title = {DiSCoVeR: a Materials Discovery Screening Tool for High Performance, Unique Chemical Compositions},
  year = {2021},
  month = {10},
  publisher = {American Chemical Society (ACS)},
  doi = {10.26434/chemrxiv-2021-5l2f8-v3},
  url = {https://doi.org/10.26434/chemrxiv-2021-5l2f8-v3},
  abstract = {We present Descending from Stochastic Clustering Variance Regression (DiSCoVeR), a Python tool for identifying high-performing, chemically unique compositions relative to existing compounds using a combination of a chemical distance metric, density-aware dimensionality reduction, and clustering. We introduce several new metrics for materials discovery and validate DiSCoVeR on Materials Project bulk moduli using compound-wise and cluster-wise validation methods. We visualize these via multiobjective Pareto front plots and assign a weighted score to each composition where this score encompasses the trade-off between performance and density-based chemical uniqueness. We explore an additional uniqueness proxy related to property gradients in chemical space. We demonstrate that DiSCoVeR can successfully screen materials for both performance and uniqueness in order to extrapolate to new chemical spaces.},
}

@misc{balandat_2019_19100640,
  author = {Maximilian Balandat and Brian Karrer and Daniel R. Jiang and Samuel Daulton and Benjamin Letham and Andrew Gordon Wilson and Eytan Bakshy},
  title = {{BoTorch: A Framework for Efficient Monte-Carlo Bayesian Optimization}},
  year = {2019},
  eprint = {1910.06403},
  archiveprefix = {arXiv},
  doi = {10.48550/arxiv.1910.06403},
  url = {https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.06403},
  abstract = {Bayesian optimization provides sample-efficient global optimization for a broad range of applications, including automatic machine learning, engineering, physics, and experimental design. We introduce BoTorch, a modern programming framework for Bayesian optimization that combines Monte-Carlo (MC) acquisition functions, a novel sample average approximation optimization approach, auto-differentiation, and variance reduction techniques. BoTorch's modular design facilitates flexible specification and optimization of probabilistic models written in PyTorch, simplifying implementation of new acquisition functions. Our approach is backed by novel theoretical convergence results and made practical by a distinctive algorithmic foundation that leverages fast predictive distributions, hardware acceleration, and deterministic optimization. We also propose a novel "one-shot" formulation of the Knowledge Gradient, enabled by a combination of our theoretical and software contributions. In experiments, we demonstrate the improved sample efficiency of BoTorch relative to other popular libraries.},
}
