5605:  abstract = {Next-generation autonomous laboratories that combine machine learning (ML), robotic synthesis, and in situ characterization is rapidly emerging as one of the key directions in modern materials science. By integrating active and deep learning algorithms with multi-level datasets ranging from quantum mechanical simulations to high-throughput flow-based experiments, these platforms establish closed-loop frameworks that guide complex nanofabrication processes in real time. Such AI-driven systems lower material and energy consumption, enable the precise design of nanostructures with tailored optical, electronic, and mechanical properties, and create research opportunities that were previously difficult to realize. This review provides a comprehensive overview of self-driving laboratories (SDLs), including their architectures, algorithmic strategies, and practical demonstrations such as the optimization of perovskite nanostructures, the development of nanoparticles for targeted drug delivery, and the synthesis of quantum dots with controlled emission. It also discusses existing methodological limitations, the need for standardized data practices, and challenges related to the integration of in situ techniques, while highlighting the prospects for creating fully digital pipelines for material production, as evidenced by recent autonomous laboratory demonstrations that progressed from initial hypotheses to functional prototypes within remarkably short timeframes. Furthermore, the self-driving lab paradigm is beginning to transition from academic laboratories into industrial research and development. This emerging trend suggests that SDL techniques will soon accelerate discovery and development in sectors such as pharmaceutical research and chemical manufacturing.},
5758:  abstract = {AbstractIn real-world materials research, machine learning (ML) models are usually expected to predict and discover novel exceptional materials that deviate from the known materials. It is thus a pressing question to provide an objective evaluation of ML model performances in property prediction of out-of-distribution (OOD) materials that are different from the training set. Traditional performance evaluation of materials property prediction models through the random splitting of the dataset frequently results in artificially high-performance assessments due to the inherent redundancy of typical material datasets. Here we present a comprehensive benchmark study of structure-based graph neural networks (GNNs) for extrapolative OOD materials property prediction. We formulate five different categories of OOD ML problems for three benchmark datasets from the MatBench study. Our extensive experiments show that current state-of-the-art GNN algorithms significantly underperform for the OOD property prediction tasks on average compared to their baselines in the MatBench study, demonstrating a crucial generalization gap in realistic material prediction tasks. We further examine the latent physical spaces of these GNN models and identify the sources of CGCNN, ALIGNN, and DeeperGATGNN’s significantly more robust OOD performance than those of the current best models in the MatBench study (coGN and coNGN) as a case study for the perovskites dataset, and provide insights to improve their performance.},
6921:  abstract = {We must accelerate the pace at which we make technological advancements to address climate change and disease risks worldwide. This swifter pace of discovery requires faster research and development cycles enabled by better integration between hypothesis generation, design, experimentation, and data analysis. Typical research cycles take months to years. However, data-driven automated laboratories, or self-driving laboratories, can significantly accelerate molecular and materials discovery. Recently, substantial advancements have been made in the areas of machine learning and optimization algorithms that have allowed researchers to extract valuable knowledge from multidimensional data sets. Machine learning models can be trained on large data sets from the literature or databases, but their performance can often be hampered by a lack of negative results or metadata. In contrast, data generated by self-driving laboratories can be information-rich, containing precise details of the experimental conditions and metadata. Consequently, much larger amounts of high-quality data are gathered in self-driving laboratories. When placed in open repositories, this data can be used by the research community to reproduce experiments, for more in-depth analysis, or as the basis for further investigation. Accordingly, high-quality open data sets will increase the accessibility and reproducibility of science, which is sorely needed.In this Account, we describe our efforts to build a self-driving lab for the development of a new class of materials: organic semiconductor lasers (OSLs). Since they have only recently been demonstrated, little is known about the molecular and material design rules for thin-film, electrically-pumped OSL devices as compared to other technologies such as organic light-emitting diodes or organic photovoltaics. To realize high-performing OSL materials, we are developing a flexible system for automated synthesis via iterative Suzuki-Miyaura cross-coupling reactions. This automated synthesis platform is directly coupled to the analysis and purification capabilities. Subsequently, the molecules of interest can be transferred to an optical characterization setup. We are currently limited to optical measurements of the OSL molecules in solution. However, material properties are ultimately most important in the solid state (e.g., as a thin-film device). To that end and for a different scientific goal, we are developing a self-driving lab for inorganic thin-film materials focused on the oxygen evolution reaction.While the future of self-driving laboratories is very promising, numerous challenges still need to be overcome. These challenges can be split into cognition and motor function. Generally, the cognitive challenges are related to optimization with constraints or unexpected outcomes for which general algorithmic solutions have yet to be developed. A more practical challenge that could be resolved in the near future is that of software control and integration because few instrument manufacturers design their products with self-driving laboratories in mind. Challenges in motor function are largely related to handling heterogeneous systems, such as dispensing solids or performing extractions. As a result, it is critical to understand that adapting experimental procedures that were designed for human experimenters is not as simple as transferring those same actions to an automated system, and there may be more efficient ways to achieve the same goal in an automated fashion. Accordingly, for self-driving laboratories, we need to carefully rethink the translation of manual experimental protocols.},

edison-trajectories/calphad_hpc.md:34:For scaling beyond a single node, Message Passing Interface (MPI) parallelization provides near-linear speedup. Studies on parallelized equilibrium solvers using MPI have demonstrated close-to-linear scaling up to approximately 24–48 cores, at which point inter-core data-transfer overhead begins to dominate (roos2022acceleratingcomplexchemical pages 6-8). The equilipy package provides a dedicated `equilib_batch()` function that treats each NPT (composition–pressure–temperature) condition as an independent calculation and distributes work across processors using `mpi4py` (kwon2024equilipyapython pages 1-3, kwon2024equilipyapython pages 5-7, kwon2024equilipyapython pages 3-5). By default, equilipy uses all available processors on a single node; for multi-node runs, users configure OpenMPI or MPICH environments. Its core Fortran equilibrium solver, interfaced with Python via F2PY, achieves computation speeds comparable to TC-Python and PanPython in benchmarks on 8,096 equilibrium calculations (kwon2024equilipyapython pages 1-3). GPU acceleration with mixed-precision strategies (single precision for most work, double for refinement) has also been explored for equilibrium solvers, yielding approximately 3× speedup in test cases (roos2022acceleratingcomplexchemical pages 6-8).
[partner-specific budget detail removed]
edison-trajectories/calphad_licensing.md:43:Equilipy is an open-source Python package developed at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, released under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 license, and specifically designed for high-throughput CALPHAD calculations on high-performance computing systems (kwon2024equilipyapython pages 1-3). Its key features include phase equilibrium calculation, parallel batch computations via the `equilib_batch()` function (embarrassingly parallel across input conditions), Scheil-Gulliver solidification, and metastable phase stability calculations (kwon2024equilipyapython pages 3-5). Equilipy leverages all available processors by default and supports multi-node environments via MPI through mpi4py, with no license-imposed processor limits—directly addressing a limitation of commercial tools like TC-Python (kwon2024equilipyapython pages 1-3, kwon2024equilipyapython pages 5-7). Benchmark tests demonstrate that Equilipy's computation speed is comparable to TC-Python and PanPython for equivalent calculations (kwon2024equilipyapython pages 1-3). Its results have been validated against FactSage for multiphase equilibrium and Scheil-Gulliver solidification calculations (kwon2024equilipyapython pages 3-5).

  - **Equilipy** (v0.2.1): 81 equilibrium calculations (0 errors) using AlCuMgSi_ORNL ChemSage database — single-point, temperature sweep (10.1 calcs/sec), composition sweep (18.3 calcs/sec), and batch mode (**26.9 calcs/sec** with 2 CPUs via built-in parallelism).
  - **OpenCalphad** (v6.106): 3 Cr-Fe equilibria compiled from source — correctly predicts BCC+SIGMA two-phase at 800K; per-calc speed of **0.4–1.1 ms** (1000–2500 calcs/sec/core, ~100x faster than pycalphad).

  - **Accuracy / Quality** — All three tools implement the same CALPHAD formalism; given identical thermodynamic parameters they produce identical results. Quality depends on the database, not the software.

TDBDB's 766 files are independent assessments that cannot be mixed; TCFE has ~350+ binary and ~175+ ternary mutually consistent subsystems; TCHEA4 has 307 binary and 493 higher-order subsystems for 26 elements. Published comparison studies cited: Ravi &amp; Wolverton (2005, 36 cit.), Wertz et al. (2018, 29 cit.), Gorsse &amp; Senkov (2018, 131 cit.).

  - **Why CALPHAD assessments stop at ternary** — Explains the Muggianu geometric extrapolation principle: higher-order (4+ element) Gibbs energies are mathematically constructed from assessed binary and ternary subsystems, so quaternary+ parameters are rarely needed. 41:10. [Free Thermodynamic Databases](#free-thermodynamic-databases)
265:All three tools implement the same underlying CALPHAD formalism — minimizing Gibbs energy using sublattice models (Compound Energy Formalism). **Given identical thermodynamic parameters as input, they produce the same equilibrium results.** The speed differences come from implementation language and solver strategy, not from thermodynamic accuracy.
297:There are **766+ freely available TDB files** indexed by TDBDB (van de Walle et al. 2018), covering a wide range of alloy systems from published literature. pycalphad and OpenCalphad can read any of these. Equilipy's ChemSage .dat format has far fewer freely available databases (ORNL provides a handful: AlCuMgSi, AlFeSi), making it less flexible for exploring new alloy systems unless you already have .dat files from FactSage.
301:#### TDBDB vs. commercial databases (TCFE, TCHEA)
303:The key distinction is **scope and consistency**, not fundamental methodology. Both free and commercial databases use the same CALPHAD formalism — the difference is how many systems have been rigorously assessed and how well they work together in multicomponent predictions.
319:**When free TDB files are sufficient**: For binary and ternary phase diagram calculations within the scope of a single published assessment, free TDB files can be just as accurate as commercial databases — the parameters come from the same CALPHAD methodology and are fitted to the same types of experimental data. Many published HT-CALPHAD screening studies (e.g., Wang & Xiong 2020, 450K compositions) use free TDB files successfully for ternary systems.

19:**Consistency and Quality Assurance.** Commercial databases undergo rigorous internal consistency checks: phase models, sublattice descriptions, and naming conventions are harmonized across all subsystems, and unassessed interaction parameters are explicitly estimated rather than defaulted to zero (fries2005developmentofmulticomponent pages 1-2, fries2005developmentofmulticomponent pages 2-4). Open TDB files assembled from disparate literature assessments frequently suffer from format variations across software implementations, ambiguous notation, limited metadata and provenance tracking, and conversion-induced errors (mianiUnknownyearperspectivestudyfor pages 1-4, mianiUnknownyear…forthe pages 1-4). The TDBDB project, which indexed 766 data entries from 528 publications, required a dedicated utility (ocutil) to fix common formatting problems such as truncated lines, nonprintable characters, and misordered keywords (walle2018thethermodynamicdatabase pages 2-3, walle2018thethermodynamicdatabase pages 1-2).
110:**OpenCalphad (OC)** is a GNU-licensed, open-source CALPHAD implementation developed by Sundman et al. that provides multicomponent equilibrium calculations, parallelized computation, and a programming interface for coupling to simulation codes. At the time of its publication, it was described as the first high-quality open-source software for multicomponent CALPHAD calculations (sundman2015opencalphada pages 1-3). OC implements core CALPHAD models but relies on external databases; it does not itself provide a comprehensive assessed database (kattner2016thecalphadmethod pages 11-13).

Question: How can pycalphad be used for high-throughput thermodynamic calculations? # Pycalphad for High-Throughput Thermodynamic Calculations: Parallelization Strategies and Freely Available Databases

## 1. Overview of Pycalphad for High-Throughput Thermodynamic Calculations

Pycalphad is a free and open-source Python library (MIT license) for designing thermodynamic models, calculating phase diagrams, and solving multicomponent, multi-phase Gibbs energy minimization problems using the CALPHAD (CALculation of PHAse Diagrams) method (otis2024pycalphadcalphadbasedcomputational pages 1-3, liu2018oceanofdata pages 6-8). Several architectural features make pycalphad particularly well-suited for high-throughput (HT) thermodynamic workflows:

**Symbolic model representation and runtime flexibility.** Pycalphad decouples phase models from the equilibrium solver using symbolic representations (via SymPy). Models can be programmatically created, manipulated, and overridden at runtime without changing solver code, enabling automated batch workflows and custom model development (olson2024genomicmaterialsdesign pages 29-34, otis2024pycalphadcalphadbasedcomputational pages 1-3). Users can define custom phase models by subclassing the `Model` class and passing them directly to `calculate()` and `equilibrium()` functions.

**Vectorized inputs and labeled result arrays.** The `equilibrium()` function accepts multi-dimensional arrays of shape (P, T, y) for pressure, temperature, and site-fraction grids, returning results as xarray datasets with named dimensions (e.g., temperature, composition, internal degrees of freedom, vertex). For example, a single call can compute equilibria at 170 temperatures and 100 compositions simultaneously (otis2024pycalphadcalphadbasedcomputational pages 4-7). Slicing results is straightforward—e.g., `eq.MU.sel(component='AL', T=600)` retrieves all Al chemical potentials at 600 K. Datasets support reading/writing to disk for storing long-running calculations (otis2024pycalphadcalphadbasedcomputational pages 4-7).

**Integration with ESPEI and automated workflows.** Pycalphad serves as the computational engine for ESPEI, which implements an automated two-step procedure: (1) fit model parameters using thermochemical data from DFT-based first-principles calculations, and (2) refine using experimental phase-equilibrium data via Bayesian MCMC optimization (otis2017highthroughputthermodynamicmodeling pages 1-2, liu2018oceanofdata pages 6-8). This enables rapid, systematic construction of multicomponent thermodynamic descriptions suitable for ICME pipelines (otis2017highthroughputthermodynamicmodeling pages 5-7).

**Scheil-Gulliver solidification simulations.** The open-source `scheil` Python package, built on pycalphad, implements Scheil-Gulliver solidification simulations and is designed explicitly for high-throughput screening, capable of performing multiple simulations by looping over a series of compositions in multicomponent composition space (bocklund2020scheilgulliversimulationsfor pages 6-10).

**MaterialsMap for systematic alloy design.** The MaterialsMap tool uses pycalphad as one of its computational engines for high-throughput equilibrium calculations and Scheil-Gulliver simulations across systematically sampled composition grids, with parallel computations built in (sun2024materialsmapacalphadbased pages 6-10, sun2024materialsmapacalphadbased pages 10-15).

## 2. Parallelization Strategies for Pycalphad Calculations

### 2.1 Native Capabilities

Pycalphad itself supports vectorized calculations internally: by passing large arrays of conditions to `equilibrium()`, many temperature-composition points can be evaluated in a single function call (otis2024pycalphadcalphadbasedcomputational pages 4-7). Pycalphad lists **Dask** as a dependency, positioning it as an available backend for parallel and distributed computation (otis2024pycalphadcalphadbasedcomputational pages 4-7).

### 2.2 Multiprocessing (as used in MaterialsMap)

The MaterialsMap package employs the **Python multiprocessing Pool library** to accelerate equilibrium calculations and Scheil-Gulliver simulations using multicore processors. The `pycalphad_eq()` and `pycalphad_scheil()` functions are designed for seamless integration into parallel computing, with enhancements to display time and process information during parallel execution (sun2024materialsmapacalphadbased pages 10-15).

### 2.3 Distributed Task Management (Malac-Distmas)

For large-scale HT-CALPHAD computations, the Malac-Distmas system implements a server-client distributed computing architecture that partitions massive calculation tasks into independent subtasks. Each subtask (an independent equilibrium or Scheil calculation at specific conditions) is dispatched to computing nodes, with SQL-based task management, exception handling, and results aggregation. This approach couples with both commercial and open-source CALPHAD software including pycalphad (gao2022amachinelearning pages 1-2, gao2022amachinelearning pages 2-3, gao2022amachinelearning pages 3-5).

### 2.4 Equilipy: Built-in Parallel Computations

Equilipy, a related open-source Python package for phase equilibria calculations, was specifically developed for high-throughput CALPHAD with built-in parallel computations across multiple processors and nodes. Its `equilib_batch()` function processes each NPT condition independently, ensuring consistent computation speed regardless of input sequence (kwon2024equilipyapython pages 3-5, kwon2024equilipyapython pages 1-3).

### 2.5 Code Examples for Parallelizing Pycalphad

The following code demonstrates three parallelization approaches (multiprocessing, joblib, and Dask) applied to pycalphad's `equilibrium()` API, based on the published code structure from the pycalphad paper (otis2024pycalphadcalphadbasedcomputational media b99aade9) and the parallelization strategy documented in MaterialsMap (sun2024materialsmapacalphadbased pages 10-15):

```python
import numpy as np
from pycalphad import Database, equilibrium
import pycalphad.variables as v
from multiprocessing import Pool
from joblib import Parallel, delayed
import dask
from dask import delayed as dask_delayed

# --- 1. Setup System based on COST507 (Al-Fe) ---
# Citations: (otis2024pycalphadcalphadbasedcomputational media b99aade9, otis2024pycalphadcalphadbasedcomputational pages 10-11)
# Load the thermodynamic database (assumes file exists)
db_alfe = Database("alfe_sei.TDB")
components = ["AL", "FE", "VA"]
phases = ["LIQUID", "BCC_A2", "FCC_A1", "AL13FE4"]

# --- 2. Define Calculation Helper ---
def calculate_point(temp, comp_al):
    """
    Wraps pycalphad equilibrium for a single condition.
    This function is pickled and sent to workers.
    """
    # Create conditions dictionary (Pressure, Temperature, Composition)
    # v.X('AL') specifies the mole fraction of Aluminum
    conds = {v.P: 101325, v.T: temp, v.X("AL"): comp_al}

    # Perform equilibrium calculation
    # Note: pycalphad supports vectorized inputs natively, which is efficient.
    # Parallelization wrappers are useful for complex workflows or distributed clusters.
    eq_result = equilibrium(db_alfe, components, phases, conds)

    # Return a lightweight result (e.g., Minimum Gibbs Energy) to reduce IPC overhead
    return eq_result.GM.values.flat[0]

# Create a grid of conditions (Task List)
temps = np.linspace(700, 2000, 20)  # 20 Temperature points
compositions = np.linspace(0.01, 0.99, 20) # 20 Composition points
tasks = [(T, X) for T in temps for X in compositions]

# --- 3. Parallelization Approach A: Multiprocessing ---
# Strategy used in MaterialsMap (sun2024materialsmapacalphadbased pages 10-15)
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Pool creates separate processes (bypassing GIL)
    with Pool(processes=4) as pool:
        # starmap executes the function with arguments from the list
        results_mp = pool.starmap(calculate_point, tasks)
    print(f"Multiprocessing: Computed {len(results_mp)} points.")

# --- 4. Parallelization Approach B: Joblib ---
# Common for scientific computing arrays
results_joblib = Parallel(n_jobs=4)(
    delayed(calculate_point)(T, X) for T, X in tasks
)
print(f"Joblib: Computed {len(results_joblib)} points.")

# --- 5. Parallelization Approach C: Dask ---
# PyCalphad dependency for distributed computing (otis2024pycalphadcalphadbasedcomputational pages 4-7)
# Create a graph of lazy tasks
lazy_results = [dask_delayed(calculate_point)(T, X) for T, X in tasks]
<exited with exit code 0>
````

<sub>⏱️ 154m 31s</sub>

### 💬 Copilot

Here's my analysis of your three concerns:

---

### 1. Two-Level Hierarchical Search

The narrative currently frames it as a computational structure (Level 1 = element selection across 22,803 sub-systems, Level 2 = composition optimization within top 3–6). Your insight about **atomization contamination** is a strong practical justification — staying within the same sub-system for multiple compositions avoids full cleaning between runs. However, I agree this is operationally complex to encode in the acquisition function (you'd need a "switching cost" penalty in pKGFN). **Recommendation**: Keep the two-level framing but add a brief sentence noting the practical benefit (reduced contamination overhead). Don't oversell the implementation — it's a natural consequence of the search structure, not a separate algorithm.

### 2. pycalphad Concern

**Current framing problem**: Lines 743–747 describe pycalphad as "Sobol/LHS coarse sampling" for "all 22,803 sub-systems" — this reads like screening/filtering, which could invite the red-herring critique you're worried about.

**What line 767 already says** (but could be stronger): "All CALPHAD outputs flow as features to downstream GP nodes." This is the right idea — pycalphad outputs are **contextual input features** to the GP, not hard filters.

**The fix**: Explicitly state that Fidelity 1 outputs are used as contextual features (not pass/fail screening), and that the multi-fidelity GP learns the systematic bias between fidelity levels. The Kennedy–O'Hagan autoregressive framework handles exactly this. Edison query submitted to get quantitative comparisons.

### 3. BO Scalability

The narrative **partially addresses this** (lines 769–774): SVDKL for 15K–54K compositions, exact GP for ≤3,876. But it doesn't address:
- What happens beyond 54K compositions (the 119M figure at line 734 is enormous)
- How the GP handles growing observation count over 9 months of async BO
- The practical HPC fairshare constraint / data-driven scheduling

PR #14 had a detailed discussion about this (RF pre-screen → SVDKL → exact GP tiered architecture). The narrative should mention the tiered surrogate strategy more explicitly.

690. The \flaime{} optimizer is a \bofn{} directed acyclic graph (Fig.~\ref{fig:bofn-dag}) whose nodes
691. mirror the physical pipeline: CALPHAD evaluation (Thermo-Calc
692. TCAl10/TCMG6 via TC-Python), powder properties, LPBF process window, and
693. mechanical response.  The pKGFN acquisition function selects the most
694. cost-informative next experiment at each iteration, routing cheap CALPHAD
695. queries (negligible cost on university HPC) before committing to expensive builds
696. ({$\sim$}\$500/composition).  A mineral-burden node encodes a
697. composition-weighted supply-risk index
698. $\mathrm{MBS}(\mathbf{x})=\sum_i w_i\,x_i$ (weights from USGS
699. import-reliance data), enabling multi-objective optimization of strength
700. \emph{and} critical mineral reduction simultaneously.
701. An asynchronous, cost-aware multi-fidelity framework deploys three
702. CALPHAD fidelity levels---\texttt{pycalphad} ({$\sim$}0.1\,CPU-sec/eval),
703. TC-Python/TCAl10 ({$\sim$}1--5\,CPU-min/eval), and the Thermo-Calc
704. AM~Module ({$\sim$}0.5--2\,CPU-hr/eval)---in parallel at maximum HPC
705. capacity (fairshare-limited, not algorithm-sequenced).  All fidelity
706. outputs flow continuously as input features to the unified GP surrogate:
707. Node~0 CALPHAD outputs (phase fractions, solidification range, CSI)
708. inform every downstream model node.  The pKGFN acquisition function
709. computes value-of-information per CPU-hour, naturally prioritizing cheap
710. evaluations first while deciding which expensive assessments to request
711. next given all data already collected.  Preliminary results confirm
712. pKGFN convergence on a manufacturing benchmark (Fig.~\ref{fig:pipeline}) and active

229. \textbf{Project Title:} FLAIME (Fast Learning AI for Mineral Efficiency): Autonomous Discovery and Qualification of Critical-Mineral-Lean Alloys for Clean Energy
230. 
231. \textbf{PI:} Sterling G.\ Baird, Ph.D., Brigham Young University
232. 
233. \textbf{Application Stage:} Phase I
234. 
235. \textbf{Senior/Key Personnel and Partner Organizations:}
236. Valimet Inc.\ (funded): Valimet's CTO, Valimet's technical manager---gas atomization;
237. AMAZEMET (funded): Amazemet's CEO, Amazemet's application engineer---ultrasonic atomization;
238. Thermo-Calc AB (unfunded): a Thermo-Calc specialist, Thermo-Calc's account manager---CALPHAD databases
239. 
240. \bigskip
241. 
242. The United States imports 100\% of its manganese, 100\% of its zirconium
243. mineral concentrates, and 74\% of its chromium~(USGS, 2024)---elements
244. central to high-performance aluminum alloys for advanced manufacturing. A single supply disruption could idle domestic
245. additive-manufacturing production dependent on these materials. FLAIME (Fast
246. Learning AI for Mineral Efficiency) addresses this vulnerability with an
247. AI-autonomous closed-loop platform that discovers and qualifies aluminum alloys
248. meeting structural performance targets while minimizing critical mineral
249. content, directly supporting DOE Critical Materials Strategy Pillars~2
250. (Develop Alternatives) and~3 (Materials and Manufacturing Efficiency).
251. 
252. FLAIME integrates Bayesian Optimization over Function Networks (BOFN) with
253. the partial Knowledge Gradient for Function Networks (pKGFN) acquisition
254. function to jointly optimize alloy composition, printability, and mechanical
255. properties across the full powder-to-part pipeline---from CALPHAD evaluation
256. through ultrasonic and gas atomization, laser powder bed fusion (LPBF),
257. and a staged minimum-viable-specimen (MVS) progression---single tracks,
258. density cubes ($\geq$99\% relative density gate), and ASTM~E8 sub-size
259. tensile bars. By modeling every manufacturing stage as a node in
260. a cost-aware function-network DAG with an embedded mineral-burden objective,
261. BOFN selects maximally informative experiments at each stage, reducing
262. powder-to-tensile cycle time by an estimated 10$\times$ versus conventional
263. sequential campaigns ($\geq$3$\times$ from AI-guided experiment
264. selection $\times$ closed-loop execution speedup)---software-orchestrated with human operators in Phase~I,
265. architected for direct robotic integration in Phase~II.  No existing
266. platform closes this complete composition-discovery and
267. manufacturing-qualification loop: the closest structural-alloy SDL
268. automates printing through testing but not the full
269. powder-to-property pipeline~(Conn et~al., 2025).
270. 
271. Phase~I explores \subsystemcount{} element combinations---$\sum_{k=2}^{8}\binom{\elementcount}{k}$
272. sub-systems spanning ternary (e.g., Al--Fe--Si) through 9-component alloys---drawn from a
273. \elementcount-element Al-alloy palette via an asynchronous, cost-aware multi-fidelity
274. framework (\texttt{pycalphad}, TC-Python/TCAl10, Thermo-Calc AM~Module)
275. that evaluates CALPHAD thermodynamics, Scheil solidification, and
276. printability in parallel at maximum high-performance computing (HPC) capacity,
277. then focuses experimental validation on the top 3--6 sub-systems---including
278. the Al--Mn--Cr--Zr and Al--Zr anchors---characterizing 100--200 compositions
279. (up to 2~unique compositions/day, 6~days/week) through the full
280. powder-to-tensile pipeline with a discovery yield $\geq$3\% (at least 3--6 high-performing alloys). All
281. experimental data and BOFN models will be shared as a FAIR-compliant
282. digital thread via the Genesis Mission platform and open repositories
283. (Zenodo/Figshare with DOIs). The project enters Phase~I at
284. TRL~2 (concept formulated) and targets TRL~4 (closed-loop validated in
285. laboratory) at the conclusion of the 9-month, \$750K effort.
286.

449. % --- 1. Background / Introduction (~1 page) --------------------------------
450. \section{Background and Introduction}\pagebudget{1}
451. \label{sec:background}
452. 
453. \guidance{FOA: ``Explain the importance and relevance of the proposed
454. work and clearly articulate which aspect of the chosen challenge will be
455. addressed and solved.  Set the proposed research in perspective to other
456. efforts in the field.  Highlight novel or unique aspects of the proposed
457. work.  Cite relevant literature.''  CRITICAL: Lead with the platform
458. need and AI advantage, not the alloy system.  Frame for Focus Area B
459. (AMMTO): autonomous discovery platforms, closed-loop AI, accelerated
460. qualification, reducing demand for critical minerals.}
461. 
462. \note{Buy America compliance statement below --- required within the
463. first 2 pages of the Project Narrative (FOA \S IV.C).}
464. 
465. \textbf{Overview.}
466. The U.S.\ depends on foreign sources for 100\% of its manganese, 100\%
467. of its zirconium mineral concentrates, and 74\% of its
468. chromium~\cite{usgs_mcs_2024}---elements central to high-performance
469. aluminum alloys for advanced manufacturing.
470. \flaime{} (Fast Learning AI for Mineral Efficiency) is an
471. AI-autonomous closed-loop platform that discovers aluminum alloys meeting
472. structural performance targets while minimizing critical mineral content.
473. By integrating AI-guided optimization with a complete
474. powder-to-print-to-test manufacturing pipeline---the first to unify
475. computational evaluation, powder atomization, laser powder bed fusion
476. (LPBF), and mechanical testing in one loop---\flaime{} targets
477. $\geq$3$\times$ acceleration over conventional alloy development
478. approaches.%
479. \footnote{Buy America Act compliance: this project does not involve
480. construction, alteration, maintenance, or repair of public
481. infrastructure (FOA \S III.F).}
482. 
483. \textbf{Critical minerals challenge.}
484. A single supply disruption in manganese or chromium could idle U.S.\
485. additive manufacturing production dependent on these elements.
486. Manganese is 100\% import-reliant; chromium and zirconium appear on the
487. USGS Critical Minerals List with high supply-concentration risk~\cite{bauer_2023_1998242}.
488. Beryllium is equally vulnerable:
489. ${\sim}$347{,}000~kg~Be/yr enters alloy production, 84\% from one mine,
490. sustaining a \$250--400M/yr Cu-Be market with $<$1\% recycling~\cite{unknown_2025_3001694}.
491. The DOE Critical Materials Strategy calls for action
492. across Pillar~2 (Develop Alternatives), Pillar~3 (Materials and
493. Manufacturing Efficiency), and Pillar~5 (Enabling Activities)~\cite{bauer_2023_1998242}.
494. AMMTO's CMI Hub at Ames National Laboratory has
495. invested $>$\$80M in follow-on R\&D and advanced Al-Ce alloys to TRL~9~\cite{lograsso_2024_2338076},
496. establishing direct precedent for this work.
497. 
498. Despite this momentum, no existing platform unifies
499. powder production, LPBF printing, and tensile testing under a single AI
500. decision loop.  The closest structural-alloy SDL (APEX) automates DED
501. printing through mechanical characterization but remains
502. human-monitored with no peer-reviewed end-to-end
503. validation~\cite{conn_2025_apex}; A-Lab demonstrates fully robotic
504. powder synthesis but targets oxides, not structural
505. metals~\cite{szymanski_2023_s4158602}.  A recent two-dimensional
506. autonomy framework confirms this gap: high \emph{software} autonomy
507. (AI-directed experiment selection) and high \emph{hardware} autonomy
508. (robotic execution) have not yet been achieved
509. together for structural AM~\cite{tobias_2025_autonomy}.  The critical
510. unsolved problem is closing the \emph{decision} loop across this
511. pipeline, not physical automation alone.  All confirmed AM aluminum deployments---AlSi10Mg satellite
512. structures, Scalmalloy telecom parts ($>$100 in orbit), and the AL250C
513. engine demonstrator---use LPBF exclusively~\cite{hart_2021_s4157802},
514. validating \flaime{}'s focus on the qualification-relevant manufacturing
515. modality.
516.

571. \label{sec:objectives}
572. 
573. \guidance{FOA: ``Provide a clear and concise statement of the specific
574. objectives of the proposed project.  Address how the objectives align

577. 
578. \guidance{COMMERCIALIZATION (Review Criterion 4, FOA p.85): ``Does the

584. 
585. \begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{O\arabic*.},leftmargin=2em]
586.   \item Demonstrate a closed-loop BOFN/pKGFN platform for AI-autonomous,
587.         cost-aware alloy exploration across the full powder-to-property pipeline.
588.   \item Evaluate \subsystemcount{} element combinations ($k=2$--$8$ from a
589.         \elementcount-element palette) and 100--200 compositions within selected
590.         sub-systems via CALPHAD with an integrated mineral-burden objective.
591.   \item Validate 100--200 compositions experimentally through the minimum-viable-specimen (MVS)
592.         pipeline (2~compositions/day, 6~days/week, 9~months; $\sim$468
593.         theoretical max, 100--200 after ramp-up).
594.   \item Achieve overall discovery yield $\geq$3\%---i.e., at least 3--6
595.         high-performing alloys from the 100--200 experimentally validated
596.         compositions (meeting all family-specific mechanical and mineral-burden
597.         targets); complementary metric:
598.         $\geq$20\% Tier~1 pass rate among fully tested compositions.
599.   \item Demonstrate AI acceleration factor $\geq$3$\times$ vs.\ a
600.         pre-registered random baseline, with bootstrap confidence intervals
601.         across $\geq$20 seeds.
602. \end{enumerate}
603. 
604. \noindent Collectively, these objectives demonstrate that a
605. software-orchestrated, AI-autonomous closed-loop platform can
606. simultaneously accelerate alloy discovery \emph{and} reduce critical
607. mineral dependence---the dual mandate of Topic~3B. Phase~I focuses exclusively on Al alloys processed by LPBF,
608. with Cu-Cr-Zr as a stretch demonstration.
609. The broad \elementcount-element palette (Al~+~\elementlisttex{}) spans 0\% to 100\% USGS import reliance, ensuring the
610. mineral-burden objective produces genuine supply-risk tradeoffs rather than
611. trivially satisfied constraints.
612. 
613. \flaime{} advances from TRL~2 (BOFN DAG + CALPHAD pipeline designed)
614. to TRL~4 at Phase~I exit (closed-loop validated on real Al alloys)
615. to TRL~6 in Phase~II (system in relevant environment with
616. industry-scale powders).
617. 
618. The Be-Cu replacement market represents \$250--400M/yr; \flaime{}'s
619. industry pathway proceeds from powder production (Valimet) through
620. qualification to commercial feedstock supply (Fehrmann
621. Materials~GmbH). The platform will be released open-source; a Month-6
622. internal review will assess selective IP protection for top
623. compositions to best serve commercialization.
624. 
625. Phase~II will extend \flaime{} to AMMTO priority alloys---beginning with
626. Cu-Cr-Zr for clean-energy thermal management (heat exchangers, EV motor
627. components, power-electronics heat sinks) as a direct Be-Cu replacement
628. pathway, and 316H for nuclear structural applications---leveraging transfer
629. learning from Phase~I surrogates, and transition mechanical testing to
630. full-size ASTM~E8 specimens on larger-format LPBF systems
631. (${\geq}250$\,mm build plates), enabling direct qualification-grade
632. property data and resolving the known sub-size elongation sensitivity
633. documented for AM metals~\cite{wang_2020_17452759,karnati_2022_mpc20210136}.
634. Phase~I's software-orchestrated architecture provides a

637. (automated powder dispensing, specimen transfer, SEM prep, and mechanical
638. testing) drawn from the emerging ecosystem of self-driving materials
639. laboratories---a transition requiring dedicated automation engineers and
640. \$6--15M investment appropriate to Phase~II scope.

687. \textbf{Activity~1: AI-Guided Computational Exploration}
688. (\emph{PI, BYU; {$\sim$}\$200K}).
689. %
690. The \flaime{} optimizer is a \bofn{} directed acyclic graph (Fig.~\ref{fig:pipeline}, right) whose nodes
691. mirror the physical pipeline: CALPHAD evaluation (Thermo-Calc
692. TCAl10/TCMG6 via TC-Python), powder properties, LPBF process window, and
693. mechanical response.  The pKGFN acquisition function selects the most
694. cost-informative next experiment at each iteration, routing cheap CALPHAD
695. queries (negligible cost on university HPC) before committing to expensive builds
696. ({$\sim$}\$500/composition).  A mineral-burden node encodes a
697. composition-weighted supply-risk index
698. $\mathrm{MBS}(\mathbf{x})=\sum_i w_i\,x_i$ (weights from USGS
699. import-reliance data), enabling multi-objective optimization of strength
700. \emph{and} critical mineral reduction simultaneously.
701. An asynchronous, cost-aware multi-fidelity framework deploys three
702. CALPHAD fidelity levels---\texttt{pycalphad} ({$\sim$}0.1\,CPU-sec/eval),
703. TC-Python/TCAl10 ({$\sim$}1--5\,CPU-min/eval), and the Thermo-Calc
704. AM~Module ({$\sim$}0.5--2\,CPU-hr/eval)---in parallel at maximum HPC
705. capacity (fairshare-limited, not algorithm-sequenced).  All fidelity
706. outputs flow continuously as input features to the unified GP surrogate:
707. Node~0 CALPHAD outputs (phase fractions, solidification range, CSI)
708. inform every downstream model node.  The pKGFN acquisition function
709. computes value-of-information per CPU-hour, naturally prioritizing cheap
710. evaluations first while deciding which expensive assessments to request
711. next given all data already collected.  Preliminary results confirm
712. pKGFN convergence on a manufacturing benchmark (Fig.~\ref{fig:pipeline}, left) and active
713. CALPHAD evaluation on BYU HPC.
714.

730. \textbf{Two-Level Hierarchical Search.}
731. The search proceeds in two levels.
732. \emph{Level~1 (Element Combination Selection):}
733. \bofn{} explores all $\sum_{k=2}^{8}\binom{\elementcount}{k}=\subsystemcount{}$
734. sub-systems---from ternary (e.g., Al--Fe--Si) through 9-component
735. alloys---spanning ${\sim}$\num{119000000} unique compositions at
736. 1\,at.\% resolution (Al\,$\geq$\,85\,at.\%), via an asynchronous
737. multi-fidelity evaluation, a novel NChooseK element-selection problem
738. solved via Bayesian optimization.
739. All three CALPHAD fidelity levels run concurrently at maximum HPC
740. parallelism; since the binding constraint is fairshare rate (not cost),
741. asynchronous BO treats pending HPC jobs as fantasy samples, updating the
742. surrogate as each completes---no synchronous batch waits.
743. %
744. \emph{Fidelity~1} (\texttt{pycalphad}, \$0): Sobol/LHS coarse sampling
745. (${\sim}50$ compositions per sub-system, $\sim$\num{1130000} total)
746. computes equilibrium phase fractions, Scheil solidification curves,
747. crack-susceptibility index (CSI), and mineral-burden scores for all
748. \subsystemcount{} sub-systems.
749. At ${\sim}10$~calcs/sec/core on 64~cores, Fidelity~1 completes in under
750. one hour on a single BYU HPC node.
751. %
[Thermo-Calc licensing/pricing detail removed]
753. targeted sub-systems receive Scheil solidification with
754. back-diffusion (MOBAL8 solver), TC-PRISMA precipitation kinetics
755. (e.g., L$_{1\text{2}}$-Al$_3$Zr nucleation and coarsening), and fully
756. assessed multicomponent thermodynamics---capabilities that require
757. commercially assessed ternary interaction parameters unavailable in
758. free databases.
759. %
760. \emph{Fidelity~3} (Thermo-Calc AM~Module): selected compositions
761. receive steady-state printability maps (lack-of-fusion / stable /
762. keyhole regimes), melt-pool geometry, $G$/$R$ conditions overlaid on the
763. columnar-to-equiaxed transition (CET), and Scheil curves with the
764. solute-trapping extension at LPBF cooling rates
765. ($10^{4}$--$10^{6}$~K/s)---identifying unprintable candidates before any
766. powder is atomized.
767. %
768. All CALPHAD outputs flow as features to downstream GP nodes: Fidelity~1
769. phase fractions and CSI inform the Fidelity~2 and~3 models, and all
770. fidelity data feeds the unified surrogate continuously.  For large
771. composition spaces (6+ components, 15K--54K compositions), SVDKL deep
772. kernel GPs handle phase-boundary non-stationarity via learned features
773. while preserving the GP posterior interface needed by BOFN;
774. for small spaces (${\leq}5$ components, ${\leq}3{,}876$ compositions),
775. exact GPs suffice.  The cost-aware pKGFN acquisition function decides
776. which expensive evaluations to request next based on all available data.
777. %
778. \emph{Level~2 (Composition Optimization):}
779. pKGFN optimizes compositions within the top 3--6 sub-systems through
780. the full experimental pipeline.  Al--Mn--Cr--Zr and Al--Zr serve as
781. guaranteed ``anchor'' systems that receive experimental validation
782. regardless of Level~1 rankings, ensuring continuity with prior
783. results while enabling the AI to discover sub-systems a human
784. designer might not consider.
785.

854. Weekly PI--partner calls and monthly all-hands reviews maintain

856. as the single source of truth; datasets are shared via the Genesis

859. oversight, operate in shifts to sustain six-day/week throughput

861. experimental velocity.

863. \textbf{Risk Mitigation.}
864. Low atomization yield $\to$ Valimet gas-atomization fallback.  Modest
865. \bofn{} advantage $\to$ honest reporting via pre-registered time-ledger
866. decomposition.  LPBF access disrupted $\to$ 3D~Powder Tech backup.
867. Tiered screening (${\sim}50$ tensile + ${\sim}150$ density/hardness)
868. bounds characterization bottleneck risk.
869. 
870. \textbf{Relationship to Prior Work.}
871. \flaime{} builds on the PI's open-source SDL infrastructure (Honegumi)

927. \textbf{Data sources.}
928. CALPHAD thermodynamic data are drawn from Thermo-Calc's TCAl10 (aluminum) and

930. (Thermo-Calc collaboration letter, Appendix~7).

932. features as surrogate-model inputs; experimental benchmarks follow the MMPDS
933. handbook.

935. persistent DOIs; the PI's MPTS-52 dataset, heavily reused by the
936. crystal-structure generative-AI community, evidences this open-data commitment.
937. 
938. \textbf{AI models.}
939. Bayesian Optimization over Function Networks (\bofn{}) with the partial
940. Knowledge Gradient (pKGFN) acquisition function drives cost-aware experiment
941. selection atop GPyTorch/BoTorch Gaussian-process surrogates.
942. \bofn{}/pKGFN code will be released as open-source Python packages with
943. Honegumi tutorials and integrated into BoTorch's tutorial ecosystem (Meta
944. letter of support, Appendix~7).
945. 
946. \textbf{Genesis Mission integration.}
947. \flaime{} is designed for integration with the American Science Cloud (AmSC)
948. and will host its digital thread, alloy database, and \bofn{}/pKGFN models on
949. the platform as it becomes available, participating in GM coordination
950. activities.  All datasets are simultaneously deposited on Zenodo/Figshare with
951. persistent DOIs, ensuring immediate FAIR-compliant open access to the broader
952. materials science community.  \bofn{}/pKGFN will be released as a domain-specific
953. ``plug-and-play'' capability per the GM framework.
954. Bidirectionally, \flaime{} will leverage other GM teams' validated
955. data---shared characterization databases and benchmark property
956. sets---to accelerate CALPHAD surrogate training.

990. Three quantitative metrics define Phase~I go/no-go evaluation.
991. %
992. \textbf{(1)~AI Acceleration Factor.}
993. $\mathrm{AF}(y) = n_{\mathrm{baseline}} / n_{\mathrm{BOFN}}$ measures the
994. iteration reduction \bofn{} achieves relative to each of four pre-registered
995. baselines---random search~(B1), expert DOE~(B2), standard BO~(B3), and a
996. \bofn{} ablation without the mineral-burden objective~(B4)---with $\geq$20
997. replicate seeds, bootstrap confidence intervals, and win-rate reporting.
998. Phase~I target: AF\,$\geq$\,3$\times$ vs.\ random (conservative; the
999. cross-study SDL median is $\sim$6$\times$~\cite{sabanzagil_2025_s4358802}).
1000. %
1001. \textbf{(2)~Discovery Yield.}
1002. Fraction of BOFN-proposed compositions satisfying all family-specific
1003. mechanical thresholds (e.g., Al-Mn-Cr-Zr: YS\,$\geq$\,250\,MPa,
1004. EL\,$\geq$\,5\%; verified per ASTM E8 sub-size) \emph{and} supply-risk reduction
1005. versus the Scalmalloy incumbent.  The \elementcount-element palette creates genuine
1006. supply-risk variance---constituent elements span 0\% (Fe) to 100\% (Sc)
1007. USGS import reliance---ensuring mineral-burden scores reflect real
1008. supply-chain tradeoffs rather than trivially low baselines.
1009. Phase~I target: $\geq$\,3\%.
1010. %
1011. \textbf{(3)~Mineral-Burden Reduction.}
1012. Weighted critical-mineral content (wt\,\%) of the best-performing \flaime{}
1013. alloy versus the Scalmalloy incumbent (Al-Mg-Sc-Zr).
1014. Phase~I target: $\geq$\,40\% reduction.
1015. 
1016. \textbf{Scaling behavior.}
1017. BOFN surrogate accuracy (cross-validated MAE) and acquisition efficiency
1018. improve monotonically as CALPHAD-screened and experimentally validated
1019. compositions accumulate, demonstrating increasing performance with additional
1020. data.
1021.

abstract = {Powder bed fusion (PBF) is a widely adopted additive manufacturing (AM) process category that enables high-resolution fabrication across metals, polymers, ceramics, and composites. However, its inherent process complexity demands robust modeling to ensure quality, reliability, and scalability. This review provides a critical synthesis of advances in physics-based simulations, machine learning, and digital twin frameworks for PBF. We analyze progress across scales—from micro-scale melt pool dynamics and mesoscale track stability to part-scale residual stress predictions—while highlighting the growing role of hybrid physics–data-driven approaches in capturing process–structure–property (PSP) relationships. Special emphasis is given to the integration of real-time sensing, multi-scale modeling, and AI-enhanced optimization, which together form the foundation of emerging PBF digital twins. Key challenges—including computational cost, data scarcity, and model interoperability—are critically examined, alongside opportunities for scalable, interpretable, and industry-ready digital twin platforms. By outlining both the current state-of-the-art and future research priorities, this review positions digital twins as a transformative paradigm for advancing PBF toward reliable, high-quality, and industrially scalable manufacturing.},
  title = {Development of New Aluminium Alloys for Future Automotive Structural Components With Less Criticality and Higher Casting Processability},
  abstract = {Abstract The linear economy follows a “take-make-dispose model, while the circular economy aims for closed-loop system where resources are reused, recycled and regenerated, minimizing waste and environmental impact. Following that, the surge in integration from linear economy to circular economy has been widely witnessed in various European industries for past few years. In automotive industry, aluminium and its alloys are defined as the most suitable candidates, that meets circular economy principles along with technical requirements. However, as per publication by European Commission (EC) on Critical Raw Materials (CRMs), aluminium and its major alloying elements, i.e. silicon and magnesium are declared as CRMs. This poses new constraints to usage of these elements in various automotive structural components. Under these premises, the aim of this work is to implement an innovative roadmap for the development of high-performance aluminium alloys with low content of CRMs and enhanced casting processability. The presented approach shows that by incorporating low criticality concept with high casting processability, it is possible to come up with advanced aluminium alloys with higher mechanical performance that fulfills the requirements of todays manufacturing while addressing global resource challenges. This work also envisioned that researchers in foundry could utilize the descripted approach in designing new aluminium alloys for future applications. Graphic Abstract},
  abstract = {Abstract In alignment with the Materials Genome Initiative and as the product of a workshop sponsored by the US National Science Foundation, we define a vision for materials laboratories of the future in alloys, amorphous materials, and composite materials; chart a roadmap for realizing this vision; identify technical bottlenecks and barriers to access; and propose pathways to equitable and democratic access to integrated toolsets in a manner that addresses urgent societal needs, accelerates technological innovation, and enhances manufacturing competitiveness. Spanning three important materials classes, this article summarizes the areas of alignment and unifying themes, distinctive needs of different materials research communities, key science drivers that cannot be accomplished within the capabilities of current materials laboratories, and open questions that need further community input. Here, we provide a broader context for the workshop, synopsize the salient findings, outline a shared vision for democratizing access and accelerating materials discovery, highlight some case studies across the three different materials classes, and identify significant issues that need further discussion. Graphical abstract},
  abstract = {Sustainable feedstock management remains a major challenge in laser beam powder bed fusion (PBF-LB), where conventional reuse strategies are typically limited to sieving and blending rather than full material regeneration. Ultrasonic atomization (UA) offers a fundamentally different powder production route based on capillary-wave instabilities induced at the surface of a molten metal by high-frequency vibrations. In contrast to turbulence-driven atomization, droplet formation in UA is primarily governed by ultrasonic frequency and intrinsic thermophysical properties of the melt, enabling quasi-deterministic particle formation with high sphericity and reduced satellite formation. In this study, ultrasonic atomization was investigated as a closed-loop route for converting PBF-LB-manufactured 316L stainless steel parts into reusable powder. Printed rods were remelted and atomized under controlled variation of electric current and vibration amplitude. The resulting powders were characterized in terms of morphology, internal microstructure, particle size distribution, chemical composition, and gas impurity content. UA produced highly spherical particles with reduced internal porosity and improved flowability compared to the initial gas-atomized powder, while preserving the principal alloying elements. An increase in oxygen content was observed after recycling, attributed to selective high-temperature oxidation under residual oxygen in nominally inert conditions. The results establish a mechanistic framework for transforming consolidated PBF-LB material into secondary feedstock and identify key parameters governing structural and compositional stability in closed-loop recycling.},
  title = {Alloy Development from Sustainable Materials – Close-Loop of Materials Using Ultrasonic Atomization},
  title = {Raw material criticality assessment as a complement to environmental life cycle assessment: Examining methods for product‐level supply risk assessment},
  abstract = {Summary The diversity of raw materials used in modern products, compounded by the risk of supply disruptions—due to uneven geological distribution of resources, along with socioeconomic factors like production concentration and political (in)stability of raw material producing countries—has drawn attention to the subject of raw material “criticality.” In this article, we review the state of the art regarding the integration of criticality assessment, herein termed “product‐level supply risk assessment,” as a complement to environmental life cycle assessment. We describe and compare three methods explicitly developed for this purpose—Geopolitical Supply Risk (GeoPolRisk), Economic Scarcity Potential (ESP), and the Integrated Method to Assess Resource Efficiency (ESSENZ)—based on a set of criteria including considerations of data sources, uncertainties, and other contentious methodological aspects. We test the methods on a case study of a European‐manufactured electric vehicle, and conclude with guidance for appropriate application and interpretation, along with opportunities for further methodological development. Although the GeoPolRisk, ESP, and ESSENZ methods have several limitations, they can be useful for preliminary assessments of the potential impacts of raw material supply risks on a product system (i.e., “outside‐in” impacts) alongside the impacts of a product system on the environment (i.e., “inside‐out” impacts). Care is needed to not overlook critical raw materials used in small amounts but nonetheless important to product functionality. Further methodological development could address regional and firm‐level supply risks, multiple supply‐chain stages, and material recycling, while improving coverage of supply risk characterization factors.},
  abstract = {In a selective laser melting process, it is common to reuse the powder in consecutive cycles of the route because it is more sustainable and cost effective. However, it is unknown whether reusing the material has an influence on the process. In this paper, Inconel 718, Ti6Al4V, AlSi10Mg and Scalmalloy are characterized to determine the impact of reusing powders on the additive manufacturing (AM) process under an argon high-purity atmosphere. Virgin powders were taken from the suppliers and compared to powders that had been used in the process for a long period of time with periodic ‘rejuvenation’. A well-structured characterization procedure, combining many existing techniques, is proposed, determining changes in the morphology, composition (chemical and microstructure) and flowability. Clear differences between the virgin and used state are revealed by the characterizations; AlSi10Mg, appears to be the most sensitive to reuse with changes in particle size distribution and morphology, and with an increase in the oxygen content. The main contribution of this paper is providing insight into the effects of reuse for four commonly used AM powders, by means of a simple but well-structured method that links the particle feature characterization process to the flowability of metal AM powders. The provided insights enable enhanced decision-making on recycling and reuse of powder for specific AM processes.},
  abstract = {Fundamentals of critical minerals and their paramount role in the successful deployment of clean energy technologies in future transportation are assessed along with current global efforts to satisfy the needs of automotive supply chains and environmental concerns. An implementation of large quantities of minerals, in particular metals, into the manufacturing of strategic components of zero-emission vehicles will bring new challenges to energy security. As a result, a reduced dependency on conventional hydrocarbon resources may lead to new and unexpected interdependencies, including dependencies on raw materials. It is concluded that to minimize the impact of a metal-intensive transition to clean transportation, in addition to overcoming challenges with minerals mining and processing, further progress in understanding the properties of critical materials will be required to better correlate them with intended applications, to identify potential substitutions and to optimize their use through the sustainable exploration of their resources and a circular economy.},
  abstract = {AbstractHigh-performance conductors are essential for economically and environmentally sustainable ways of electricity transfer in modern infrastructure, manufacturing and transportation, including electric vehicles. This report reviews the aluminum conductors, their fundamentals, classification and utilization markets, focusing on metallurgical characteristics of present commercial solutions and the strategy of future development directions. The inherent features of aluminum, both beneficial and detrimental, for electrical engineering are emphasized along with alloying concepts that provide the accelerated decomposition of matrix solid solution to minimize the electron scattering. Development activities are assessed of new generation of aluminum conductors that in addition to alloying utilize novel processing techniques such as ultra-fast crystallization, severe plastic deformation and complex thermomechanical treatments aiming at grain reduction to nanometer scale, crystallographic texture control and grain boundary engineering. Transition metals and rare earths are considered as the promising alloying candidates for high-strength conductors having superior thermal stability with extra importance given to immiscible systems of Al–Ce, Al–La and Al–Y along with multiply additions, combined to generate the synergy effects. The composites with cladding configuration and particulate reinforcement including via carbon-type strengtheners are discussed as the effective solutions of advanced conductors. A variety of strategies that aim at overcoming the strength–conductivity trade-off in conductor materials are presented throughout the report.Graphical abstract},
  title = {Research Acceleration in Self‐Driving Labs: Technological Roadmap toward Accelerated Materials and Molecular Discovery},
  title = {Alloy Substitution in a Critical Raw Materials Perspective},
  abstract = {Since many years, the European Community has been monitoring some raw materials because of their high importance to the European Union economy and their high supply risk. Such raw materials, classified as critical, form a strong industrial base, producing a lot of goods and applications used in everyday life and modern technologies. Many critical raw materials are used to produce alloys and their high supply risk may constitute a serious problem for the future world economy and technological progress. Mitigating actions are therefore needed such as recycling, material efficiency improvements and, when possible, material substitution. In the present work, a systematic approach for alloy substitution in a critical raw materials perspective is developed. The method is illustrated with an example.},
  title = {Materials selection in a critical raw materials perspective},
  abstract = {Abstract Critical Raw Materials (CRMs) are those raw materials that are economically and strategically important for the European economy but have a high-risk associated with their supply. Used in environmental technologies, consumer electronics, health, steel-making, defence, space exploration, and aviation, these materials are not only ‘critical’ for key industry sectors and future applications, but also for the sustainable functioning of the European economy. In this scenario, ‘mitigating actions’ need to be developed to reduce criticalities linked to the use of those raw materials. Recycling and substitution, when possible, are strategic solutions but a more efficient use of such CRMs in design, obtained by a correct alloy selection, is become nowadays mandatory. A method for metallic alloys selection in a CRMs perspective, based on the definition of the alloy critical index, is described. The proposed method allows selecting the alloy for the current application that minimizes its criticality associated to CRMs. The method is illustrated with examples.},
  title = {Design for Recycling in a Critical Raw Materials Perspective},
  abstract = {The European Union (EU) identified a number of raw materials that are strategic for its economy but suffer at the same time from a high supply risk. Such critical raw materials (CRMs) are used in a wide range of commercial and governmental applications: green technology, telecommunications, space exploration, aerial imaging, aviation, medical devices, micro-electronics, transportation, defense, and other high-technology products and services. As a result, the industry, the environment, and our quality and modern way of life are reliant on the access and use of them. In this scenario, recycling may be a strategic mitigating action aimed at reducing the critical raw materials supply risks. In this work, a design strategy is proposed for alloys selection that minimizes the number of CRMs with the lowest end-of-life recycling input rate. The method is illustrated with an example.},
  title = {How to apply mitigating actions against critical raw materials issues in mechanical design},
  abstract = {Circular economy, sustainability and design for environment are some of the keywords that identify new formidable challenges to be faced in the next years. Raw materials have a dominant role in reaching that goal. Green energy, electric vehicles, communication, etc. depends on raw materials labeled as critical because of their economic importance coupled with high supply risk. For this reason, mitigating actions need to be used in materials selection and design such as material substitution, materials efficiency improvement and recycling. In this work, a method to implement raw materials criticality issues in materials selection for mechanical design is described according to the recent literature. The strategy is based on Ashby’s approach and the definition of the alloy criticality index quantifying the criticality per unit of mass of the material.},

edison-trajectories/edison-3b-deepdive-8-multiobjective-bofn-mineral.md:### B. Supply-risk / criticality-weighted metrics (more rigorous for “criticality”)
edison-trajectories/edison-3b-deepdive-8-multiobjective-bofn-mineral.md:Product-level “supply risk” methods in industrial ecology treat criticality as a set of characterization factors (CFs) applied to the bill of materials (BOM) / inventory flows:
edison-trajectories/edison-3b-deepdive-8-multiobjective-bofn-mineral.md:- **GeoPolRisk, ESP, ESSENZ** are explicitly reviewed as product-level supply risk/criticality methods that compute supply-risk metrics via CFs applied to inventory flows, and the authors caution not to overlook small-mass but functionally important materials (cimprich2019rawmaterialcriticality pages 1-2, cimprich2019rawmaterialcriticality pages 2-3). Differences include whether CFs effectively cancel out mass magnitude (GeoPolRisk) versus scaling with amounts used (ESP/ESSENZ) (cimprich2019rawmaterialcriticality pages 8-9).
edison-trajectories/edison-3b-deepdive-8-multiobjective-bofn-mineral.md:- Ferro & Bonollo define an **Alloy Criticality Index (CIA)** and abundance-risk scoring (ARL based on crustal abundance), aiming to quantify raw-material criticality per unit alloy mass and then per unit function (ferro2019materialsselectionin pages 1-2, ferro2019materialsselectionin pages 9-9).
edison-trajectories/edison-3b-deepdive-8-multiobjective-bofn-mineral.md:- Lütkehaus et al. propose **economic product importance (EPI)** combining material flows, cost share, substitutability and then combining with supply disruption probability to yield product-specific overall criticality (lutkehaus2022measuringrawmaterialcriticality pages 1-2).
edison-trajectories/edison-3b-deepdive-8-multiobjective-bofn-mineral.md:## 3. Pareto optimization for alloy composition with strength/ductility and criticality: precedent
edison-trajectories/edison-3b-deepdive-8-multiobjective-bofn-mineral.md:EHVI/qEHVI are powerful but can be computationally expensive as the number of objectives grows, and scaling issues are acknowledged in MOBO literature (daulton2020differentiableexpectedhypervolume pages 1-2, daulton2022multiobjectivebayesianoptimization pages 2-3). For 3 objectives ({UTS, elongation, criticality}) EHVI-family methods are commonly used in practice.
edison-trajectories/edison-3b-deepdive-8-multiobjective-bofn-mineral.md:- Compute M(x) directly from x (cheap, exact) using chosen definition (wt.% sum, CIA-like, CF-weighted supply risk, etc.) (cimprich2019rawmaterialcriticality pages 8-9, mancini2018characterizationofraw pages 1-2, ferro2019materialsselectionin pages 1-2).
edison-trajectories/edison-3b-deepdive-8-multiobjective-bofn-mineral.md:- Add a cheap deterministic node for mineral burden M(x) computed from composition (using supply-risk CFs or alloy criticality index), and then define U(x) as a known deterministic function of predicted performance and M(x) (e.g., U = performance − λ·M, or a Tchebycheff/Chimera-like scalarization). Scalarization is a standard MO-to-SO technique (tran2022srmobo3gpasequential pages 12-13, xu2025multiobjectiveoptimizationin pages 5-7).
edison-trajectories/edison-3b-deepdive-8-multiobjective-bofn-mineral.md:**Technical feasibility is high**: critical-mineral minimization can be added rigorously to FLAIME’s BOFN-based optimization by defining a defensible mineral-burden metric (mass-based or criticality-weighted) and either (i) incorporating it into a single-objective scalar utility to retain BOFN/p-KGFN unchanged, or (ii) extending BOFN to multi-objective outputs and using established MOBO acquisitions (EHVI/qEHVI) to identify Pareto-optimal trade-offs. There is strong precedent in the broader materials BO literature for optimizing sustainability, carbon footprint, and supply risk alongside performance, including a direct supply-risk-aware alloy MOBBO case study. The main limitation is that BOFN and p-KGFN, as published, are single-objective; therefore a multi-objective BOFN implementation is an extension project rather than a configuration option (astudillo2021bayesianoptimizationof pages 2-4, buathong2506fastbayesianoptimization pages 2-4, mulukutla2024supplyriskawarealloy pages 1-2, ament2310sustainableconcretevia pages 1-3).

edison-trajectories/materials_criticality_databases.md:Baird and Sparks developed multiple tools relevant to materials informatics including matbench-genmetrics for benchmarking crystal structure generative models, DiSCoVeR for materials discovery screening based on chemical uniqueness, and CrabNet for attention-based materials property prediction. edison-trajectories/edison-3b-deepdive-10-early-career-ammto-competitiveness.md:Context: PI is Sterling Baird, assistant professor at BYU Mechanical Engineering, with publication track record in self-driving labs and Bayesian optimization but no prior DOE funding as PI. Proposing for Topic 3B (Critical Minerals).
genesis-mission-proposal/edison-references.bib:  abstract = {The concept of “resource criticality” has recently emerged as a policy priority and research subject, usually referred to the risk of supply disruption for mineral resources, due to economic and geopolitical reasons. Different methodologies for assessing critical raw materials (CRM) have been developed in governmental and research contexts, and the possibility of including the resource security aspect in life cycle assessment (LCA) has been claimed by different authors. The present paper aims at integrating CRM considerations in LCA in order to address socio-economic and strategic aspects related to resource use. In this paper, we first explore how resource criticality could be interpreted, taking into account a wider perspective and a multidimensional concept. This includes the consideration of environmental and depletion aspects, in addition to the dominant interpretation, based on economic and geopolitical considerations. We then focus on the economic dimension of the resource criticality and propose the integration of this aspect in LCA through the use of characterization factors (CFs) based on the supply risk factors for Europe. Four different methodological options for resource security CFs are tested in the impact assessment of 50 processes and products. These options include the following: supply risk factors as such; two exponential functions of the supply risk factors, aimed at increasing the variability of the dataset, and the ratio between supply risk and production data, which reflect the size of the market, giving more importance to the materials used in small amounts in products and applications (like, e.g. specialty metals, that are often perceived as critical). The results show how the impact depends on the supply risk factors or on the mass depending on the algorithm used. Even if there is no objective way to establish how much importance should be given to one aspect or the other, we conclude that the use of the factors “supply risk/production” results might better reflect CRM importance and therefore could be used in LCA for an assessment of resource security impact for EU. Applying an exponent to the supply risk factors, the values are spread on a wider range and it is possible to spot the CRM among the resources within an inventory. The choice of the indicator is based rather on how important is the need of identifying a CRM in the inventory, e.g. in order to optimize CRM use, explore substitution options and enhance recovery in waste management.},

abstract = {Metal additive manufacturing (AM) has grown in recent years to supplement or even replace traditional fabrication methods. Specifically, the laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process has been used to manufacture components in support of sustainment issues, where obsolete components are hard to procure. While LPBF can be used to solve these issues, much work is still required to fully understand the metal AM technology to determine its usefulness as a reliable manufacturing process. Due to the complex physical mechanisms involved in the multiscale problem of LPBF, repeatability is often difficult to achieve and consequently makes meeting qualification requirements challenging. The purpose of this work is to provide a review of the physics of metal AM at the melt pool and part scales, thermomechanical simulation methods, as well as the available commercial software used for finite element analysis and computational fluid dynamics modeling. In addition, metal AM process qualification frameworks are briefly discussed in the context of the computational basis established in this work.},
}

@article{delgadolicona_2023_aisy2022,
  author = {Delgado-Licona, Fernando and Abolhasani, Milad},
  title = {Research Acceleration in Self‐Driving Labs: Technological Roadmap toward Accelerated Materials and Molecular Discovery},
  journal = {Advanced Intelligent Systems},
  year = {2023},
  month = {4},
  volume = {5},
  number = {4},
  pages = {2200331},
  publisher = {Wiley},
  doi = {10.1002/aisy.202200331},
  url = {https://doi.org/10.1002/aisy.202200331},
  issn = {2640-4567},
  abstract = {The urgency of finding solutions to global energy, sustainability, and healthcare challenges has motivated rethinking of the conventional chemistry and material science workflows. Self‐driving labs, emerged through integration of disruptive physical and digital technologies, including robotics, additive manufacturing, reaction miniaturization, and artificial intelligence, have the potential to accelerate the pace of materials and molecular discovery by 10–100X. Using autonomous robotic experimentation workflows, self‐driving labs enable access to a larger part of the chemical universe and reduce the time‐to‐solution through an iterative hypothesis formulation, intelligent experiment selection, and automated testing. By providing a data‐centric abstraction to the accelerated discovery cycle, in this perspective article, the required hardware and software technological infrastructure to unlock the true potential of self‐driving labs is discussed. In particular, process intensification as an accelerator mechanism for reaction modules of self‐driving labs and digitalization strategies to further accelerate the discovery cycle in chemical and materials sciences are discussed.},
}

  abstract = {Manufacturing is an important pillar of socio-economic development, but it has a large carbon footprint and causes serious damage to the ecosystem. There is significant pressure on the manufacturing sector to embrace eco-friendly manufacturing technologies to reduce its environmental burden. Metal Additive Manufacturing (MAM) is a rapidly evolving field with promising prospects to balance the economic and ecological concerns. Recently, manufacturing businesses started to examine MAM as a potential route to strengthen their eco-footprint and improve sustainability performance. The shift from Conventional Manufacturing (CM) processes to MAM requires significant capital investment, staff training, and possibly changing the business model. This may lead to hesitancy among enterprises to take on such risks without guaranteeing the sustainability benefits of MAM. This paper conducts a comprehensive review and critical evaluation of the environmental and economic impacts of MAM. The paper draws guidelines on the best production contexts that enable the fulfilment of environmental goals and maintain economic viability through MAM technologies. In general, Powder Bed Fusion (PBF) techniques are considered environmentally friendly and cost-effective for small-scale production of lightweight small parts with complex shapes and relatively high resolution. In contrast, Direct Energy Deposition (DED) processes are valuable for repairing and manufacturing large-scale parts that have medium shape complexity and relatively low resolution.},
}
