@misc{baird_2021_chemrxiv,
  author = {Baird, Sterling and Diep, Tran and Sparks, Taylor},
  title = {DiSCoVeR: a Materials Discovery Screening Tool for High Performance, Unique Chemical Compositions},
  year = {2021},
  month = {10},
  publisher = {American Chemical Society (ACS)},
  doi = {10.26434/chemrxiv-2021-5l2f8-v3},
  url = {https://doi.org/10.26434/chemrxiv-2021-5l2f8-v3},
  abstract = {We present Descending from Stochastic Clustering Variance Regression (DiSCoVeR), a Python tool for identifying high-performing, chemically unique compositions relative to existing compounds using a combination of a chemical distance metric, density-aware dimensionality reduction, and clustering. We introduce several new metrics for materials discovery and validate DiSCoVeR on Materials Project bulk moduli using compound-wise and cluster-wise validation methods. We visualize these via multiobjective Pareto front plots and assign a weighted score to each composition where this score encompasses the trade-off between performance and density-based chemical uniqueness. We explore an additional uniqueness proxy related to property gradients in chemical space. We demonstrate that DiSCoVeR can successfully screen materials for both performance and uniqueness in order to extrapolate to new chemical spaces.},
}

@misc{baird_2023_chemrxiv,
  author = {Baird, Sterling G. and Parikh, Jeet N. and Sparks, Taylor D.},
  title = {Materials Science Optimization Benchmark Dataset for High-dimensional, Multi-objective, Multi-fidelity Optimization of CrabNet Hyperparameters},
  year = {2023},
  month = {3},
  publisher = {American Chemical Society (ACS)},
  doi = {10.26434/chemrxiv-2023-9s6r7},
  url = {https://doi.org/10.26434/chemrxiv-2023-9s6r7},
  abstract = {Benchmarks are crucial for driving progress in scientific disciplines. To be effective, benchmarks should closely mimic real-world tasks while being computationally efficient, allowing for accessibility and repeatability. Developing surrogate models that can be indistinguishable from the ground truth observation within the explored dataset bounds dramatically reduces the computational burden of running benchmarks without sacrificing quality, but this requires a large amount of initial data. In the fields of materials science and chemistry, relevant optimization tasks can be challenging due to their complexity, which includes hierarchical, noisy, multi-fidelity, multi-objective, high-dimensional, and non-linearly correlated variables. Additionally, they may include mixed numerical and categorical variables that are subject to linear and non-linear constraints. Simulating or experimentally verifying such tasks can be difficult, which is why benchmarks are essential. This study aimed to overcome these challenges by generating 173219 quasi-random hyperparameter combinations across 23 hyperparameters and using them to train CrabNet on the Matbench experimental band gap dataset (Computational runtime: 387 RTX-2080-Ti GPU days). The results were stored in a free-tier shared MongoDB Atlas dataset, creating a regression dataset that maps hyperparameter combinations to metrics such as MAE, RMSE, computational runtime, and model size for the CrabNet model trained on the Matbench experimental band gap benchmark task. To simulate the actual simulations, heteroskedastic noise was incorporated into the regression dataset, and bad hyperparameter combinations were excluded. Percentile ranks were computed within each group of identical parameter sets to capture heteroskedastic noise, rather than assuming Gaussian noise as is done in traditional approaches. This approach can be applied to other benchmark datasets, bridging the gap between optimization benchmarks with low computational overhead and realistically complex, real-world optimization scenarios.},
}

abstract = {Abstract Integration of circular economy principles into additive manufacturing (AM) has emerged as a critical strategy for addressing economic and environmental challenges associated with the high-cost, resource-intensive production of NiTi shape memory alloys (SMAs). This review presents a comprehensive analysis of the ultrasonic plasma atomization (UPA) technique as an advanced recycling approach for converting NiTi AM waste into high-quality feedstock. Furthermore, UPA demonstrates significant potential as a dual-function method, enabling both alloying and fine powder production within a single integrated process. AM processes, such as powder bed fusion-laser beam (PBF-LB), binder jetting, and direct energy deposition (DED), often result in substantial material losses, exacerbated by powder degradation phenomena including oxidation, particle morphology changes, and loss of flowability. While conventional atomization techniques, such as gas and plasma atomization, offer partial solutions for powder production, they are limited by significant energy inefficiencies, high capital investment requirements, and increased risks of contamination. Moreover, powders produced via gas atomization typically exhibit inferior quality compared to those generated by UPA, including lower sphericity and a higher prevalence of surface satellites. In contrast, the UPA system, a hybrid technique combining high-frequency ultrasonic vibrations and plasma melting, offers precise control over droplet formation through acoustic cavitation, Faraday wave instabilities, and rapid solidification, enabling the production of highly spherical, homogeneous, and contamination-minimized NiTi powders. Drawing on thermofluidic principles, vibrational mechanics, and metallurgical kinetics, this review systematically deconstructs the UPA mechanism, highlighting key phenomena such as resonance-induced cavitation dynamics, ultrasonic capillary wave collapse, and non-equilibrium solidification. Furthermore, it investigates contamination pathways specific to UPA and proposes strategies for impurity mitigation, including sonotrode design optimization, inert atmosphere refinement, and post-atomization conditioning. Experimental findings are analyzed to demonstrate the feasibility of achieving high sphericity (> 0.9), compositionally stable, and thermally responsive NiTi powders from recycled feedstock. Finally, the review outlines a roadmap for industrial-scale deployment, advocating the integration of machine learning and closed-loop recycling models to enhance process predictability, quality control, and resource efficiency. The insights presented herein position UPA as a transformative solution for enabling sustainable, high-performance NiTi powder regeneration within AM workflows, advancing the circular economy in advanced manufacturing.},
<exited with exit code 0>
```

465. \textbf{Overview.}
466. The U.S.\ depends on foreign sources for 100\% of its manganese, 100\%
467. of its zirconium mineral concentrates, and 74\% of its
468. chromium~\cite{usgs_mcs_2024}---elements central to high-performance
469. aluminum alloys for advanced manufacturing.
470. \flaime{} (Fast Learning AI for Mineral Efficiency) is an
471. AI-autonomous closed-loop platform that discovers aluminum alloys meeting
472. structural performance targets while minimizing critical mineral content.
473. By integrating AI-guided optimization with a complete
474. powder-to-print-to-test manufacturing pipeline---the first to unify
475. computational evaluation, powder atomization, laser powder bed fusion
476. (LPBF), and mechanical testing in one loop---\flaime{} targets
477. $\geq$3$\times$ acceleration over conventional alloy development
478. approaches.%
479. \footnote{Buy America Act compliance: this project does not involve
480. construction, alteration, maintenance, or repair of public
481. infrastructure (FOA \S III.F).}
482. 
483. \textbf{Critical minerals challenge.}
484. A single supply disruption in manganese or chromium could idle U.S.\
485. additive manufacturing production dependent on these elements.
486. Manganese is 100\% import-reliant; chromium and zirconium appear on the
487. USGS Critical Minerals List with high supply-concentration risk~\cite{bauer_2023_1998242}.
488. Beryllium is equally vulnerable:
489. ${\sim}$347{,}000~kg~Be/yr enters alloy production, 84\% from one mine,
490. sustaining a \$250--400M/yr Cu-Be market with $<$1\% recycling~\cite{unknown_2025_3001694}.
491. The DOE Critical Materials Strategy calls for action
492. across Pillar~2 (Develop Alternatives), Pillar~3 (Materials and
493. Manufacturing Efficiency), and Pillar~5 (Enabling Activities)~\cite{bauer_2023_1998242}.
494. AMMTO's CMI Hub at Ames National Laboratory has
495. invested $>$\$80M in follow-on R\&D and advanced Al-Ce alloys to TRL~9~\cite{lograsso_2024_2338076},
496. establishing direct precedent for this work.
497. 
498. Despite this momentum, no existing platform unifies
499. powder production, LPBF printing, and tensile testing under a single AI
500. decision loop.  The closest structural-alloy self-driving laboratory (SDL), APEX, automates DED
501. printing through mechanical characterization but remains
502. human-monitored with no peer-reviewed end-to-end
503. validation~\cite{conn_2025_apex}; A-Lab demonstrates fully robotic
504. powder synthesis but targets oxides, not structural
505. metals~\cite{szymanski_2023_s4158602}.  A recent two-dimensional
506. autonomy framework confirms this gap: high \emph{software} autonomy
507. (AI-directed experiment selection) and high \emph{hardware} autonomy
508. (robotic execution) have not yet been achieved
509. together for structural AM~\cite{tobias_2025_autonomy}.  The critical
510. unsolved problem is closing the \emph{decision} loop across this
511. pipeline, not physical automation alone.  All confirmed AM aluminum deployments---AlSi10Mg satellite
512. structures, Scalmalloy telecom parts ($>$100 in orbit), and the AL250C
513. engine demonstrator---use LPBF exclusively~\cite{hart_2021_s4157802},
514. validating \flaime{}'s focus on the qualification-relevant manufacturing
515. modality.

730. \textbf{Two-Level Hierarchical Search.}
731. The search proceeds in two levels.
732. \emph{Level~1 (Element Combination Selection):}
733. \bofn{} explores all $\sum_{k=2}^{8}\binom{\elementcount}{k}=\subsystemcount{}$
734. sub-systems---from ternary (e.g., Al--Fe--Si) through 9-component
735. alloys---spanning ${\sim}$\num{119000000} unique compositions at
736. 1\,at.\% resolution (Al\,$\geq$\,85\,at.\%), via an asynchronous
737. multi-fidelity evaluation, a novel NChooseK element-selection problem
738. solved via Bayesian optimization.
739. All three CALPHAD fidelity levels run concurrently at maximum HPC
740. parallelism; since the binding constraint is fairshare rate (not cost),
741. asynchronous BO treats pending HPC jobs as fantasy samples, updating the
742. surrogate as each completes---no synchronous batch waits.
743. %
744. \emph{Fidelity~1} (\texttt{pycalphad}, {$\sim$}0.1\,CPU-sec/eval): Sobol/LHS coarse sampling
745. (${\sim}50$ compositions per sub-system, $\sim$\num{1130000} total)
746. computes equilibrium phase fractions, Scheil solidification curves,
747. crack-susceptibility index (CSI), and mineral-burden scores for all
748. \subsystemcount{} sub-systems.
749. At ${\sim}10$~calcs/sec/core on 64~cores, Fidelity~1 completes in under
750. one hour on a single BYU HPC node.
751. %

753. targeted sub-systems receive Scheil solidification with
754. back-diffusion (MOBAL8 solver), TC-PRISMA precipitation kinetics
755. (e.g., L$_{1\text{2}}$-Al$_3$Zr nucleation and coarsening), and fully
756. assessed multicomponent thermodynamics---capabilities that require
757. commercially assessed ternary interaction parameters unavailable in
758. free databases.
759. %
760. \emph{Fidelity~3} (Thermo-Calc AM~Module): selected compositions
761. receive steady-state printability maps (lack-of-fusion / stable /
762. keyhole regimes), melt-pool geometry, $G$/$R$ conditions overlaid on the
763. columnar-to-equiaxed transition (CET), and Scheil curves with the
764. solute-trapping extension at LPBF cooling rates
765. ($10^{4}$--$10^{6}$~K/s)---identifying unprintable candidates before any
766. powder is atomized.
767. %
768. All CALPHAD outputs flow as features to downstream GP nodes: Fidelity~1
769. phase fractions and CSI inform the Fidelity~2 and~3 models, and all
770. fidelity data feeds the unified surrogate continuously.  For large
771. composition spaces (6+ components, 15K--54K compositions), SVDKL deep
772. kernel GPs handle phase-boundary non-stationarity via learned features
773. while preserving the GP posterior interface needed by BOFN;
774. for small spaces (${\leq}5$ components, ${\leq}3{,}876$ compositions),
775. exact GPs suffice.  The cost-aware pKGFN acquisition function decides
776. which expensive evaluations to request next based on all available data.
777. %

779. pKGFN optimizes compositions within the top 3--6 sub-systems through
780. the full experimental pipeline.  Al--Mn--Cr--Zr and Al--Zr serve as
781. guaranteed ``anchor'' systems that receive experimental validation
782. regardless of Level~1 rankings, ensuring continuity with prior
783. results while enabling the AI to discover sub-systems a human
784. designer might not consider.

928. CALPHAD thermodynamic data are drawn from Thermo-Calc's TCAl10 (aluminum) and

930. (Thermo-Calc collaboration letter, Appendix~7).

932. features as surrogate-model inputs; experimental benchmarks follow the MMPDS
933. handbook.
934. All \flaime{}-generated data will be published on Zenodo/Figshare with
935. persistent DOIs; the PI's MPTS-52 dataset, heavily reused by the
936. crystal-structure generative-AI community, evidences this open-data commitment.
937. 
938. \textbf{AI models.}
939. Bayesian Optimization over Function Networks (\bofn{}) with the partial
940. Knowledge Gradient (pKGFN) acquisition function drives cost-aware experiment
941. selection atop GPyTorch/BoTorch Gaussian-process surrogates.
942. \bofn{}/pKGFN code will be released as open-source Python packages with
943. Honegumi tutorials and integrated into BoTorch's tutorial ecosystem (Meta
944. letter of support, Appendix~7).
945. 
946. \textbf{Genesis Mission integration.}
947. \flaime{} is designed for integration with the American Science Cloud (AmSC)
948. and will host its digital thread, alloy database, and \bofn{}/pKGFN models on
949. the platform as it becomes available, participating in GM coordination
950. activities.  All datasets are simultaneously deposited on Zenodo/Figshare with
951. persistent DOIs, ensuring immediate FAIR-compliant open access to the broader
952. materials science community.  \bofn{}/pKGFN will be released as a domain-specific
953. ``plug-and-play'' capability per the GM framework.
954. Bidirectionally, \flaime{} will leverage other GM teams' validated
955. data---shared characterization databases and benchmark property
956. sets---to accelerate CALPHAD surrogate training.

984. for this project: (1)~10x faster screening (5 days/composition vs.\
985. 8--32 weeks conventional), (2)~autonomous experimental campaigns that

987. timelines via digital thread.  The FOA uses ``AI advantage'' as a
988. central evaluation concept; your Decision Gate Metrics must quantify it.}
989. 
990. Three quantitative metrics define Phase~I go/no-go evaluation.
991. %
992. \textbf{(1)~AI Acceleration Factor.}
993. $\mathrm{AF}(y) = n_{\mathrm{baseline}} / n_{\mathrm{BOFN}}$ measures the
994. iteration reduction \bofn{} achieves relative to each of four pre-registered
995. baselines---random search~(B1), expert DOE~(B2), standard BO~(B3), and a
996. \bofn{} ablation without the mineral-burden objective~(B4)---with $\geq$20
997. replicate seeds, bootstrap confidence intervals, and win-rate reporting.
998. Phase~I target: AF\,$\geq$\,3$\times$ vs.\ random (conservative; the
999. cross-study SDL median is $\sim$6$\times$~\cite{sabanzagil_2025_s4358802}).
1000. %
1001. \textbf{(2)~Discovery Yield.}
1002. Fraction of BOFN-proposed compositions satisfying all family-specific
1003. mechanical thresholds (e.g., Al-Mn-Cr-Zr: YS\,$\geq$\,250\,MPa,
1004. EL\,$\geq$\,5\%; verified per ASTM E8 sub-size) \emph{and} supply-risk reduction
1005. versus the Scalmalloy incumbent.  The \elementcount-element palette creates genuine
1006. supply-risk variance---constituent elements span 0\% (Fe) to 100\% (Sc)
1007. USGS import reliance---ensuring mineral-burden scores reflect real
1008. supply-chain tradeoffs rather than trivially low baselines.
1009. Phase~I target: $\geq$\,3\%.
1010. %
1011. \textbf{(3)~Mineral-Burden Reduction.}
1012. Weighted critical-mineral content (wt\,\%) of the best-performing \flaime{}
1013. alloy versus the Scalmalloy incumbent (Al-Mg-Sc-Zr).
1014. Phase~I target: $\geq$\,40\% reduction.
1015. 
1016. \textbf{Scaling behavior.}
1017. BOFN surrogate accuracy (cross-validated MAE) and acquisition efficiency
1018. improve monotonically as CALPHAD-screened and experimentally validated
1019. compositions accumulate, demonstrating increasing performance with additional
1020. data.
1021.

@article{mamun_2025_ada47d,
  author = {Mamun, Osman and Bause, Markus and Ebna Hai, Bhuiyan Shameem Mahmood},
  title = {Accelerated development of multi-component alloys in discrete design space using Bayesian multi-objective optimisation},
  journal = {Machine Learning: Science and Technology},
  year = {2025},

  url = {https://doi.org/10.1088/2632-2153/ada47d},
  issn = {2632-2153},
  abstract = {Abstract Bayesian optimisation (BO) protocols grounded in active learning (AL) principles have gained significant recognition for their ability to efficiently optimize black-box objective functions. This capability is critical for advancing autonomous and high-throughput materials design and discovery processes. However, the application of these protocols in materials science, particularly in the design of novel alloys with multiple targeted properties, remains constrained by computational complexity and the absence of reliable and robust acquisition functions for multiobjective optimisation. Recent advancements have demonstrated that expected hypervolume-based geometrical acquisition functions outperform other multiobjective optimisation algorithms, such as Thompson Sampling Efficient Multiobjective optimisation and pareto efficient global optimisation (parEGO), in both performance and speed. This study evaluates several leading multiobjective BO acquisition functions–namely, parallel expected hypervolume improvement (qEHVI), noisy qEHVI, parallel parEGO, and parallel noisy parEGO (qNparEGO)–in optimizing the physical properties of multi-component alloys. Our findings highlight the superior performance of the qEHVI acquisition function in identifying the optimal Pareto front across 1-, 2-, and 3-objective aluminum alloy optimisation problems, all within a constrained evaluation budget and reasonable computational cost. Furthermore, we explore the impact of various surrogate model optimisation methods from both computational cost and efficiency perspectives. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of a pool-based AL protocol in expediting the discovery process by executing multiple computational and experimental campaigns in each iteration. This approach is particularly advantageous for deployment in massively parallel high-throughput synthesis facilities and advanced computing architectures.},
}

@article{graedel_2022_s4146702,
  author = {Graedel, T. E. and Reck, Barbara K. and Miatto, Alessio},
  title = {Alloy information helps prioritize material criticality lists},
  journal = {Nature Communications},
  year = {2022},
  month = {1},

  pages = {150},
  publisher = {Springer Science and Business Media LLC},
  doi = {10.1038/s41467-021-27829-w},
  url = {https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-021-27829-w},
  issn = {2041-1723},
  abstract = {AbstractMaterials scientists employ metals and alloys that involve most of the periodic table. Nonetheless, materials scientists rarely take material criticality and reuse potential into account. In this work, we expand upon lists of “critical materials” generated by national and regional governments by showing that many materials are employed predominantly as alloying elements, which can be a deterrent to recovery and reuse at end of product life and, likely as a consequence, have low functional end-of-life recycling rates, among other problematic characteristics. We thereby single out six metals for enhanced concern: dysprosium, samarium, vanadium, niobium, tellurium, and gallium. From that perspective, the use of critical metals in low concentrations in alloys unlikely to be routinely recycled should be avoided if possible. If not, provision should be made for better identification and more efficient recycling so that materials designated as critical can have increased potential for more than a single functional use.},
}

@misc{buathong_2025_25061145,
  author = {Poompol Buathong and Peter I. Frazier},
  title = {{Fast Bayesian Optimization of Function Networks with Partial Evaluations}},
  year = {2025},
  eprint = {2506.11456},
  archiveprefix = {arXiv},
  doi = {10.48550/arxiv.2506.11456},
  url = {https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.11456},
  abstract = {Bayesian optimization of function networks (BOFN) is a framework for optimizing expensive-to-evaluate objective functions structured as networks, where some nodes'outputs serve as inputs for others. Many real-world applications, such as manufacturing and drug discovery, involve function networks with additional properties - nodes that can be evaluated independently and incur varying costs. A recent BOFN variant, p-KGFN, leverages this structure and enables cost-aware partial evaluations, selectively querying only a subset of nodes at each iteration. p-KGFN reduces the number of expensive objective function evaluations needed but has a large computational overhead: choosing where to evaluate requires optimizing a nested Monte Carlo-based acquisition function for each node in the network. To address this, we propose an accelerated p-KGFN algorithm that reduces computational overhead with only a modest loss in query efficiency. Key to our approach is generation of node-specific candidate inputs for each node in the network via one inexpensive global Monte Carlo simulation. Numerical experiments show that our method maintains competitive query efficiency while achieving up to a 16x speedup over the original p-KGFN algorithm.},
}

---

@misc{balandat_2019_19100640,
  author = {Maximilian Balandat and Brian Karrer and Daniel R. Jiang and Samuel Daulton and Benjamin Letham and Andrew Gordon Wilson and Eytan Bakshy},
  title = {{BoTorch: A Framework for Efficient Monte-Carlo Bayesian Optimization}},
  year = {2019},
  eprint = {1910.06403},
  archiveprefix = {arXiv},
  doi = {10.48550/arxiv.1910.06403},
  url = {https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.06403},
  abstract = {Bayesian optimization provides sample-efficient global optimization for a broad range of applications, including automatic machine learning, engineering, physics, and experimental design. We introduce BoTorch, a modern programming framework for Bayesian optimization that combines Monte-Carlo (MC) acquisition functions, a novel sample average approximation optimization approach, auto-differentiation, and variance reduction techniques. BoTorch's modular design facilitates flexible specification and optimization of probabilistic models written in PyTorch, simplifying implementation of new acquisition functions. Our approach is backed by novel theoretical convergence results and made practical by a distinctive algorithmic foundation that leverages fast predictive distributions, hardware acceleration, and deterministic optimization. We also propose a novel "one-shot" formulation of the Knowledge Gradient, enabled by a combination of our theoretical and software contributions. In experiments, we demonstrate the improved sample efficiency of BoTorch relative to other popular libraries.},
}

  url = {https://doi.org/10.1201/9781003514466-18},
  abstract = {The pycalphad software package is a free and open-source Python library for designing thermodynamic models, calculating phase diagrams and investigating phase equilibria using the CALPHAD method. It provides routines for reading thermodynamic databases and solving the multi-component, multi-phase Gibbs energy minimization problem. The pycalphad software project advances the state of thermodynamic modeling by providing a flexible yet powerful interface for manipulating CALPHAD data and models. The key feature of the software is that the thermodynamic models of individual phases and their associated databases can be programmatically manipulated and overridden at run-time without modifying any internal solver or calculation code. Because the models are internally decoupled from the equilibrium solver and the models themselves are represented symbolically, pycalphad is an ideal tool for CALPHAD database development and model prototyping.},
}

@misc{bocklund_2020_20011161,
  author = {Brandon Bocklund and Lourdes D. Bobbio and Richard A. Otis and Allison M. Beese and Zi-Kui Liu},
  title = {{Scheil-Gulliver simulations for the design of functionally graded alloys by additive manufacturing using pycalphad}},
  year = {2020},
  eprint = {2001.11611},
  archiveprefix = {arXiv},
  doi = {10.48550/arxiv.2001.11611},
  url = {https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.11611},
  abstract = {Additive manufacturing (AM), through directed energy deposition, supports planned composition changes between locations within a single component, allowing for functionally graded materials (FGMs) to be developed and fabricated. The formation of deleterious phases along a particular composition path can cause significant cracking during the AM build process that makes the composition path unviable to produce these FGMs, but it is challenging to predict which phases will be present in as-built additively manufactured parts by analyzing only equilibrium phase relations. Solute segregation during solidification can lead to the formation of non-equilibrium phases that are stable at compositions far from the nominal composition of the melt, leading to crack formation. In this work, we developed a Scheil-Gulliver simulation tool based on pycalphad. We used this tool to compare the non-equilibrium phases predicted to form during solidification using the Scheil-Gulliver model with experimentally measured phases at several locations with different composition in a Ti-6Al-4V to Invar-36 FGM and a commercially pure Ti to Invar-36 FGM. We showed that the phases predicted to form by the Scheil-Gulliver model outperform the predictions made by assuming equilibrium solidification. Further, we demonstrated the use of our Scheil-Gulliver simulation tool as a method of screening potential FGM pathways by calculating the solidification phase fractions along the experimental gradient path in composition space.},
}

@misc{buathong_2023_23110214,
  author = {Poompol Buathong and Jiayue Wan and Sam Daulton and Raul Astudillo and M. Balandat and P. Frazier},
  title = {{Bayesian Optimization of Function Networks with Partial Evaluations}},
  year = {2023},
  eprint = {2311.02146},
  archiveprefix = {arXiv},
  doi = {10.48550/arxiv.2311.02146},
  url = {https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.02146},
  abstract = {Bayesian optimization is a powerful framework for optimizing functions that are expensive or time-consuming to evaluate. Recent work has considered Bayesian optimization of function networks (BOFN), where the objective function is given by a network of functions, each taking as input the output of previous nodes in the network as well as additional parameters. Leveraging this network structure has been shown to yield significant performance improvements. Existing BOFN algorithms for general-purpose networks evaluate the full network at each iteration. However, many real-world applications allow for evaluating nodes individually. To exploit this, we propose a novel knowledge gradient acquisition function that chooses which node and corresponding inputs to evaluate in a cost-aware manner, thereby reducing query costs by evaluating only on a part of the network at each step. We provide an efficient approach to optimizing our acquisition function and show that it outperforms existing BOFN methods and other benchmarks across several synthetic and real-world problems. Our acquisition function is the first to enable cost-aware optimization of a broad class of function networks.},
}

@misc{daulton_2022_22101019,
  author = {Sam Daulton and Xingchen Wan and David Eriksson and M. Balandat and Michael A. Osborne and E. Bakshy},
  title = {{Bayesian Optimization over Discrete and Mixed Spaces via Probabilistic Reparameterization}},
  year = {2022},
  eprint = {2210.10199},
  archiveprefix = {arXiv},
  doi = {10.48550/arxiv.2210.10199},
  url = {https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.10199},
  abstract = {Optimizing expensive-to-evaluate black-box functions of discrete (and potentially continuous) design parameters is a ubiquitous problem in scientific and engineering applications. Bayesian optimization (BO) is a popular, sample-efficient method that leverages a probabilistic surrogate model and an acquisition function (AF) to select promising designs to evaluate. However, maximizing the AF over mixed or high-cardinality discrete search spaces is challenging standard gradient-based methods cannot be used directly or evaluating the AF at every point in the search space would be computationally prohibitive. To address this issue, we propose using probabilistic reparameterization (PR). Instead of directly optimizing the AF over the search space containing discrete parameters, we instead maximize the expectation of the AF over a probability distribution defined by continuous parameters. We prove that under suitable reparameterizations, the BO policy that maximizes the probabilistic objective is the same as that which maximizes the AF, and therefore, PR enjoys the same regret bounds as the original BO policy using the underlying AF. Moreover, our approach provably converges to a stationary point of the probabilistic objective under gradient ascent using scalable, unbiased estimators of both the probabilistic objective and its gradient. Therefore, as the number of starting points and gradient steps increase, our approach will recover of a maximizer of the AF (an often-neglected requisite for commonly used BO regret bounds). We validate our approach empirically and demonstrate state-of-the-art optimization performance on a wide range of real-world applications. PR is complementary to (and benefits) recent work and naturally generalizes to settings with multiple objectives and black-box constraints.},
}

    m = re.search(r'\\section\{(.+?)\}', line)
    if m:
        if current_section:
            sections.append((current_section, current_cites.copy()))
        current_section = m.group(1)
        current_cites = set()
    for cite_match in re.finditer(r'\\cite\{([^}]+)\}', line):

12. # Databases, Datasets, and Data Sources for Materials Criticality Assessment and Critical Mineral Supply Risk Analysis
13. 
14. ## 1. Introduction
15. 
16. Materials criticality assessment is an inherently data-intensive endeavor that draws on geological, economic, geopolitical, and environmental data sources to quantify supply risk and economic importance of raw materials. This review identifies and characterizes the principal databases, datasets, characterization factor sets, alloy-level criticality methods, and ML-relevant tools available for constructing an AI-guided alloy design platform targeting critical minerals. The following comprehensive table summarizes all identified sources.
17.

42. 
43. ## 2. Government and Institutional Data Sources
44. 
45. ### 2.1 USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries and Critical Minerals Methodology
46. 
47. The USGS National Minerals Information Center maintains the most widely cited public database for mineral commodity data, publishing annual Mineral Commodity Summaries covering production, reserves, net import reliance, trade, and price context for over 80 mineral commodities (cimprich2019rawmaterialcriticality pages 3-5, cimprich2019rawmaterialcriticality pages 5-6, cimprich2019rawmaterialcriticality pages 11-11). These data serve as the primary production statistics input for virtually all criticality assessment methods, including GeoPolRisk, ESP, ESSENZ, and the Yale/Graedel methodology (cimprich2019rawmaterialcriticality pages 3-5, bach2019analyzingchangesin pages 3-5). The USGS 2025 critical minerals methodology introduced a probabilistic economic-effects assessment covering 84 commodities across more than 1,200 disruption scenarios, using price elasticities and input-output tables to quantify GDP impacts (nassar2025methodologyandtechnical pages 9-10). USGS production and reserves data are updated annually and recommended as a core data source for supply risk indicator construction (helbig2021anoverviewof pages 18-20).
48. 
49. ### 2.2 DOE 2023 Critical Materials Strategy
50. 
51. The DOE 2023 Critical Materials Strategy (CMS) provides short-term (2020–2025) and medium-term (2025–2035) criticality matrices that plot material criticality along two axes: importance to energy and supply risk (bauer20232023criticalmaterials pages 133-136, bauer20232023criticalmaterials pages 16-18). The 2023 assessment screened 38 materials across eight major energy technologies, deeply evaluating 23 materials and classifying them as critical, near-critical, or noncritical. Seven materials were identified as short-term critical (cobalt, dysprosium, gallium, natural graphite, iridium, neodymium, terbium), with nine classified as near-critical including lithium, nickel, and electrical steel (bauer20232023criticalmaterials pages 133-136). The CMS introduced a formal scoring rubric and expanded the definition of "materials" to include engineered materials such as silicon carbide and electrical steel (bauer20232023criticalmaterials pages 16-18).
52. 
53. ### 2.3 EU JRC Raw Materials Information System (RMIS)
54. 
55. The European Commission's JRC Raw Materials Information System (RMIS v3.0, released March 2023) is a comprehensive knowledge platform covering approximately 100 raw material profiles with dashboards containing 20+ indicators on reserves, production, EU trade, recycling, use, and sustainability (manfredi2024rawmaterialsinformation pages 1-2, manfredi2024rawmaterialsinformation pages 2-3). RMIS provides material-specific, country-level, and sector/technology profiles and supports the EU's triennial CRM assessment (delia2022buildingafricaeuraw pages 9-11). The EU criticality assessment methodology itself plots materials on an Economic Importance (EI) vs. Supply Risk (SR) space, with materials exceeding thresholds (EI ≥ 1 and SR ≥ 2.8) deemed critical (eynard2023criticalrawmaterials pages 32-36). The 2023 EU CRM list expanded to 34 critical raw materials and introduced a "strategic raw materials" category for materials essential to green/digital transitions (troster2024insearchof pages 11-13).
56. 
57. ### 2.4 British Geological Survey (BGS) Supply Risk Index
58. 
59. The BGS Supply Risk Index uses seven scored criteria—production concentration, reserve distribution, recycling rate, substitutability, governance of top producer/reserve holder, and companion metal fraction—aggregated and normalized to a 1–10 index (bachmann2022d1.4critical pages 121-124).
60. 
61. ## 3. Elemental Criticality Characterization Factor Methods
62. 
63. ### 3.1 GeoPolRisk
64. 
65. The Geopolitical Supply Risk (GeoPolRisk) method uses World Bank Worldwide Governance Indicators (specifically "Political Stability and Absence of Violence/Terrorism") weighted by import shares from the UN Comtrade database to produce region-specific characterization factors (cimprich2019rawmaterialcriticality pages 3-5, cimprich2019rawmaterialcriticality pages 2-3). The method uniquely accounts for domestic production as geopolitically "risk-free" and has been extended to an endpoint indicator (GeoPolEndpoint) that models socio-economic damage through price elasticity considerations (cimprich2019rawmaterialcriticality pages 8-9).
66. 
67. ### 3.2 ESSENZ
68. 
69. The ESSENZ method (Integrated Method to Assess Resource Efficiency) produces characterization factors for approximately 40 abiotic resources across 11 supply-risk categories, including political stability, demand growth, mining capacity, trade barriers, concentration of production and reserves, company concentration, co-production, price volatility, and feasibility of exploration (bach2019analyzingchangesin pages 1-3, bachmann2022d1.4critical pages 34-36). ESSENZ uses a distance-to-target approach normalized by global production amounts (bach2019analyzingchangesin pages 3-5). Data sources include USGS, World Bank WGI, World Economic Forum data, and the SNL metals and mining database for company concentration (bach2019analyzingchangesin pages 3-5). Updated ESSENZ characterization factors are published at the TU Berlin website: https://www.see.tu-berlin.de/menue/forschung/ergebnisse/essenz/parameter/en/ (bach2019analyzingchangesin pages 1-3).
70.

81. Helbig et al. (2021) systematically reviewed 88 criticality assessment methods published through 2020, documenting 618 individual applications of supply risk criteria with 98 unique criteria belonging to 10 indicator categories (helbig2021anoverviewof pages 2-4, helbig2021anoverviewof pages 1-2). The most frequently used categories are concentration, scarcity, and political instability, with the most common individual criteria being country concentration of production, depletion time of reserves, and geopolitical risk (helbig2021anoverviewof pages 1-2). The supplementary spreadsheets provide a structured meta-dataset that is valuable for ontology building and automated indicator selection (helbig2021anoverviewof pages 18-20).

96. *Table: This table compares alloy-level criticality and supply-risk quantification approaches, emphasizing how each method converts elemental criticality data into alloy-level scores. It is useful for selecting candidate methods and datasets for criticality-aware alloy optimization.*
97. 
98. ### 4.1 Ferro & Bonollo Alloy Criticality Index
99. 
100. Ferro and Bonollo (2019) define an Alloy Criticality Index (CIA) that quantifies supply risk per unit mass of alloy by aggregating element-level CICRM values weighted by composition (ferro2020alloysubstitutionin pages 7-9, ferro2019materialsselectionin pages 3-4). Their CICRM metric incorporates modified HHI indices combining governance (HHIWGI) and environmental performance (HHIEPI), supply risk (SR) computed from production concentration, substitutability, and recycling rate, economic importance (EI), and end-of-life recycling input rate (ferro2019materialsselectionin pages 3-4, ferro2023lightweightdesignversus pages 7-8, ferro2019materialsselectionin pages 9-9). The method uses EU CRM factsheet data as inputs and embeds CIA into Ashby-style material selection charts for multi-objective design (ferro2019materialsselectionin pages 1-2, ferro2023lightweightdesignversus pages 1-2).
101. 
102. ### 4.2 Helbig et al. Alloy-Level Supply Risk
103. 
104. Helbig et al. (2020) assess supply risk for 12 alloying elements in nickel-based superalloys using 12 indicators across four risk categories, then aggregate to alloy level via four methods: arithmetic mean, mass-share weighting, cost-share weighting, and maximum-element approach (helbig2020supplyriskconsiderations pages 9-12, helbig2020supplyriskconsiderations pages 5-7, helbig2020supplyriskconsiderations pages 7-9). The cost-share approach reveals the largest spread in alloy-level scores, primarily driven by rhenium introduction in second-generation single-crystal alloys (helbig2020supplyriskconsiderations pages 1-3). Supplementary data files include alloy compositions, element prices, and computed supply risk values (helbig2020supplyriskconsiderations pages 14-15).
105. 
106. ## 5. ML-Ready Datasets and Supply-Risk-Aware Alloy Optimization
107. 
108. ### 5.1 Mulukutla et al. SupplyRiskAwareDesign
109. 
110. Mulukutla et al. (2024) present the most directly relevant ML-ready resource for supply-risk-aware alloy design. Their open-source GitHub repository (https://github.com/mrinalinimulukutla/SupplyRiskAwareDesign) contains tabulated elemental supply risk data including Table S1 (Elemental Info), Table S2 (Calculation Detail), Table S3 (HHIL Calculation), and Table S4 (Element Price History) (mulukutla2024supplyriskawarealloy pages 16-18). The approach uses an LLM-based pipeline to automatically extract supply risk statistics from USGS Mineral Commodity Surveys, periodicals, and research papers via document retrieval, keyword-based data reduction, LLM classification and extraction, and validation steps (mulukutla2024supplyriskawarealloy pages 18-20, mulukutla2024supplyriskawarealloy pages 6-8, mulukutla2024supplyriskawarealloy pages 20-22). These indicators are then integrated into a multi-objective Batch Bayesian Optimization framework to identify Pareto-optimal high-entropy alloys balancing performance with minimized supply risk, demonstrated on the MoNbTiVW system (mulukutla2024supplyriskawarealloy pages 18-20).
111. 
112. ### 5.2 Matminer and Matbench
113. 
114. Matminer is an open-source Python toolkit for materials data mining with 47 featurization classes and data retrieval interfaces to the Materials Project, Materials Data Facility, and other databases (ward2018matmineranopen pages 2-3, ward2018matmineranopen pages 1-2). It provides standardized pandas DataFrame outputs compatible with scikit-learn pipelines (ward2018matmineranopen pages 2-3). Matbench provides 13 benchmark ML tasks spanning 312 to 132,752 samples covering optical, thermal, electronic, thermodynamic, tensile, and elastic properties (dunn2020benchmarkingmaterialsproperty pages 2-3, dunn2020benchmarkingmaterialsproperty pages 1-2). While not criticality-specific, these tools provide the essential materials informatics infrastructure for building composition-to-property surrogate models that can be combined with criticality objectives in multi-objective optimization.
115. 
116. ### 5.3 Taylor Sparks and Collaborators
117. 
118. Baird and Sparks developed multiple tools relevant to materials informatics including matbench-genmetrics for benchmarking crystal structure generative models, DiSCoVeR for materials discovery screening based on chemical uniqueness, and CrabNet for attention-based materials property prediction. Notably, Mohanty, Sayeed, and Sparks published a 2025 study in PRX Energy on comprehensive insights into global mineral commodities using analysis, visualization, and intelligent assistance applied to USGS mineral commodity data—a directly relevant tool for mineral criticality data exploration, though full details were not retrievable in this search.
119. 
120. ## 6. Underlying Data Sources Common Across Methods
121. 
122. Virtually all criticality assessment methods draw from a common set of underlying data sources (cimprich2019rawmaterialcriticality pages 3-5, cimprich2019rawmaterialcriticality pages 5-6, bakkerUnknownyearastudyon pages 44-45, bach2019analyzingchangesin pages 3-5):
123. 
124. - **Production data**: USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries (annually updated, 80+ commodities)
125. - **Trade data**: UN Comtrade (HS-coded bilateral trade flows)
126. - **Governance indicators**: World Bank Worldwide Governance Indicators (six dimensions, 200+ countries, annual)
127. - **Human development**: UNDP Human Development Index
128. - **Mining policy**: Fraser Institute Policy Perception Index
129. - **Environmental performance**: Yale Environmental Performance Index
130. - **Market/price data**: Bloomberg, Fastmarkets Metal Bulletin, S&P Global SNL (proprietary)
131. - **Recycling/substitution**: EU CRM factsheets, expert assessments
132. 
133. ## 7. Programmatic Access Considerations
134. 
135. For integration with Bayesian optimization platforms, the most directly programmatically accessible resources are: (1) the Mulukutla et al. GitHub repository with its LLM-based extraction pipeline and structured JSON indicator definitions (mulukutla2024supplyriskawarealloy pages 20-22); (2) Matminer's API-based data retrieval modules (ward2018matmineranopen pages 2-3); (3) USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries (downloadable annually but requiring ETL from PDF/tables) (helbig2021anoverviewof pages 18-20); (4) UN Comtrade API for trade data; (5) World Bank WGI data portal; and (6) ESSENZ characterization factors available at the TU Berlin website (bach2019analyzingchangesin pages 1-3). The EU JRC RMIS platform provides rich dashboard data but is more oriented toward interactive exploration than bulk API access (manfredi2024rawmaterialsinformation pages 3-5).
136. 
137. ## 8. Identified Gaps
138. 
139. No single, centralized, ML-ready criticality dataset exists that combines all relevant indicators across all elements in a standardized, versioned, and API-accessible format. The field remains fragmented across government reports (often PDF-first), academic supplementary materials, and proprietary commercial databases. The Mulukutla et al. (2024) LLM-extraction approach and the Helbig et al. (2021) meta-review of 88 methods with 618 indicators represent the most promising foundations for constructing such a unified resource (mulukutla2024supplyriskawarealloy pages 18-20, helbig2021anoverviewof pages 2-4). The Andrieu et al. (2025) global database of critical mineral lists across 206 jurisdictions, built with LLM-assisted discovery, represents an emerging resource for cross-country policy comparison but is at the preprint stage.
140.

# v3 LLAMBO-Style Warmstart for BOFN — Edison ANALYSIS Review

**Edison task**: `11e2d390-832c-4c47-841f-91c80dfe3c73` (ANALYSIS mode)
**Rating**: 7/10 (up from 6/10 in v2, 4/10 in v1)
**Files reviewed**: warmstart script v3, 3-panel convergence figure, results JSON, visualization script

---

## What v3 Fixed (Improvements Over v2)

1. **CRITICAL FIX: Paired process/print params** — All 3 arms per seed now share identical non-composition inputs (lines 724-727). This ensures composition initialization is the ONLY variable differing between arms. This was the most important fairness correction.

2. **Per-seed LLM perturbation** — `perturb_compositions(base_comps, seed, noise_scale=0.03)` creates meaningful per-seed variation. LLM initial_best std = 0.256, comparable to Random (0.219). No longer a constant set across seeds.

3. **Harder benchmark** — CALPHAD scale=15 (vs 8), softplus (vs sigmoid), noise_std=0.01. These make the problem more discriminative.

4. **Reduced n_initial=8** (from 15) — Extends the cold-start regime. BOFN standard is 2(d+1)=16 for 7D, so 8 is deliberately low, which is appropriate for testing warmstart.

5. **Diversity diagnostics** — Reports mean pairwise distance (LLM=0.193, Random=0.373, LHS=0.550) and min distances. Honest about LLM clustering.

6. **More honest reporting** — Win rates of 55% candidly reported.

---

## Quantitative Results Summary

### Cold-Start Advantage (Strong, Significant)
- LLM vs Random initial best: Δ = +0.356, t(19) = 6.00, **p < 0.00001**, Cohen's d = **1.34** (very large)
- LLM vs LHS initial best: Δ = +0.321, t(19) = 5.56, **p = 0.00002**, Cohen's d = **1.24**
- LLM compositions yield 75.6% of initial points with CALPHAD phase fraction > 0.5, vs 10.0% for Random and 13.8% for LHS

### Convergence Advantage (Negligible, Not Significant)
- LLM vs Random final best: Δ = +0.028, t(19) = 0.32, **p = 0.756**, Cohen's d = 0.07
- LLM vs LHS final best: Δ = +0.082, t(19) = 0.85, **p = 0.406**, Cohen's d = 0.19
- Win rate 55% (11/20) vs both baselines — binomial test p = 0.412, consistent with chance
- Would require ~1,600 seeds to detect d=0.07 at 80% power — the convergence effect is negligible

### Advantage Dissipation Timeline
- Significant (p<0.05) through **iteration 8** (8 BO iterations after init)
- Non-significant at iteration 9 (p=0.18) and iteration 10 (p=0.76)
- Effect size decays from d=1.34 (init) → d=0.07 (final) — complete dissipation

### Sample Efficiency (The Real Story)
- **AUC (Area Under Cumulative Best)**: LLM=21.04, Random=18.11, LHS=17.88
  - LLM vs Random: **+16.2%**, t(19)=3.99, **p=0.0008**, Cohen's d=0.89
  - LLM vs LHS: **+17.7%**, t(19)=4.20, **p=0.0005**, Cohen's d=0.94
- **Iterations to Y≥2.0**: LLM=2.6 (mean among reached), Random=6.5, LHS=6.2
  - LLM reaches threshold **~4 iterations sooner** than baselines

---

## Top 3 Remaining Issues

### Issue 1: Synthetic Benchmark Circularity (HIGH Severity)
The ground-truth optimum [0.7, 0.2, 0.1] is suspiciously aligned with well-known Al-Si-Mg alloy compositions. The fallback LLM compositions include points at L2 distance 0.071 from the optimum (CALPHAD output = 0.928). This creates a circular argument: the optimum was designed to match real metallurgy → the LLM suggests real metallurgical compositions → the LLM "wins" because the optimum was placed where domain knowledge would direct it. This cannot distinguish "LLM warmstart is useful" from "the benchmark was designed to reward LLM knowledge."

**Fix**: Add 2-3 benchmarks where the optimum is NOT aligned with domain knowledge (randomly shifted/rotated CALPHAD peaks, multi-modal objectives, or use Astudillo & Frazier's original benchmarks).

### Issue 2: No True BOFN Acquisition Function (MEDIUM-HIGH Severity)
The implementation uses Thompson sampling with 2000 random candidates, NOT the EI-FN or KG-FN acquisition functions from Astudillo & Frazier (2021). Thompson sampling over random candidates in 7D is weak (2000^(1/7) ≈ 3 points per dimension). Seeds 9 and 15 show complete exploration failure (stuck at ~1.5 for all 10 iterations). The original BOFN uses gradient-based optimization of EI-FN. You cannot claim to show "LLM warmstart helps BOFN" when you're running a different (simpler) algorithm. Additionally, the code comment on line 19 says "5000 candidates" while the actual code uses 2000.

**Fix**: Implement EI-FN from the BOFN paper, or at minimum use gradient-based Thompson sampling (L-BFGS-B on the Thompson sample). Use BoTorch's infrastructure for function networks.

### Issue 3: Results Framing — "Convergence Advantage" is Misleading (MEDIUM Severity)
The claimed "persistent advantage at convergence" (+0.028, 55% win rate) is statistically indistinguishable from zero. The honest finding is that LLM warmstart provides a **large, significant sample efficiency gain** (d=0.89 on AUC, d=1.34 on cold-start) that fully dissipates by iteration 10. This is actually a good and publishable result — it matches LLAMBO's theoretical prediction. But it must be framed as "sample efficiency" not "convergence advantage."

**Fix**: Report AUC and iterations-to-threshold as primary metrics. Frame the contribution as sample efficiency gain in the cold-start regime, consistent with LLAMBO's findings.

---

## Comparison to Astudillo & Frazier (2021)

Per the original BOFN paper and literature confirmation:
- BOFN uses **2(d+1) uniformly random** initial points (uninformed design)
- BOFN uses **EI-FN / KG-FN** acquisition functions with gradient-based optimization
- BOFN uses structured GPs that exploit the DAG to capture inter-node correlations

This v3 correctly implements: per-node GPs, DAG propagation through posteriors.
This v3 does NOT implement: BOFN's acquisition function, structured covariance, gradient-based candidate optimization.
<exited with exit code 0>
```

# LLM-Augmented Bayesian Optimization

*Edison Scientific LITERATURE_HIGH query*

Question: How are large language models (LLMs) being integrated into Bayesian optimization? Cover: (1) the Meta Adaptive Experimentation (AE) team's work on LLM+BO, specifically LILO (Language-in-the-Loop Optimization), (2) LLAMBO (LLM-augmented BO), (3) BORA (BO with LLM reasoning agents), (4) other approaches combining LLMs with surrogate-based optimization. What are the key mechanisms by which LLMs improve BO performance? What benchmarks and deployment contexts have been demonstrated?

# Integration of Large Language Models with Bayesian Optimization (2024–2025)

## Executive Summary

The integration of LLMs into Bayesian optimization represents a rapidly emerging frontier that leverages the broad scientific knowledge encoded in pretrained language models to improve BO's sample efficiency, prior specification, and interpretability. Five distinct integration paradigms have emerged: (1) LLM as surrogate/warmstarter (LLAMBO), (2) LLM as preference elicitor (LILO), (3) LLM as trust-weighted reasoning agent (BORA), (4) LLM as knowledge-graph builder (Reasoning BO), and (5) LLM as acquisition function selector (LMABO). These approaches address different bottlenecks in BO — cold-start, prior misspecification, human-in-the-loop feedback, and acquisition function design — and have been demonstrated on synthetic benchmarks, hyperparameter tuning, and production A/B testing at Meta.

| Method | Authors | Year | Venue | Key Mechanism | Citations |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| **LLAMBO** | Liu, Feng, et al. | 2024 | ICLR | LLM warmstarting, zero-shot surrogate, guided sampling | ~166 |
| **LILO** | Kobalczyk, Lin, Letham, Zhao, Balandat, Bakshy | 2025 | Meta AE | Natural-language feedback → pairwise preferences → GP utility model | ~15 |
| **BORA** | Cissé, Kégl, Fumagalli | 2025 | Preprint | Trust-weighted LLM intervention in BO loop; calibrated reliability | ~8 |
| **Reasoning BO** | Yang, Heng, Liu | 2025 | Preprint | Multi-agent LLM + knowledge graphs for structured scientific reasoning | ~5 |
| **LMABO** | Ngo, Hoang, et al. | 2025 | Preprint | LLM-based adaptive acquisition function selection | ~3 |
| **AlloyGPT** | CMU group | 2025 | Preprint | Domain-specific LLM fine-tuned on alloy literature for materials design | ~2 |

## 1. LILO — Language-in-the-Loop Optimization (Meta AE Team)

### Overview

LILO (Kobalczyk, Lin, Letham, Zhao, Balandat, Bakshy 2025) is the Meta Adaptive Experimentation team's approach to incorporating human domain expertise into BO through natural language feedback. It is the most practically deployed of the LLM+BO methods, having been used in production at Meta for A/B testing optimization.

### Mechanism

1. **Natural language feedback**: After observing BO's suggested experiments, a human expert provides feedback in natural language (e.g., "the notification frequency should be lower on weekends" or "users in region X prefer shorter content")
2. **LLM interpretation**: An LLM converts the natural-language feedback into structured **pairwise preferences** between candidate configurations
3. **Preference learning**: The pairwise preferences are incorporated into a GP-based **utility model** that augments the standard BO surrogate
4. **Acquisition function modification**: The utility model biases the acquisition function toward configurations consistent with expert feedback without overriding the data-driven component

### Key Technical Innovation

LILO uses a **preferential GP** (Chu & Ghahramani 2005) to model the expert's latent utility function. The LLM acts as a translator between unstructured human knowledge and the structured preference format required by the GP. This avoids the brittleness of directly using LLM outputs as surrogate predictions (as in LLAMBO) while still capturing rich expert knowledge.

### Deployment at Meta

LILO has been deployed for:
- A/B test parameter optimization (notification timing, content ranking)
- Accelerating convergence by 30–50% compared to standard BO in production settings
- Enabling non-technical stakeholders to influence optimization without specifying mathematical objectives

### Relevance to VCL

For alloy discovery, LILO-style feedback could incorporate expert metallurgical knowledge:
- "Compositions with >15% Si tend to form brittle intermetallics"
- "Powder morphology should be spherical for good flowability in LPBF"
- "Laser power above 300W with thin layers causes keyhole porosity"

## 2. LLAMBO — LLM-Augmented Bayesian Optimization (Liu et al. 2024)

### Overview

LLAMBO (Liu, Feng, et al. 2024, ICLR) was the first systematic framework for integrating LLMs into the BO loop. With 166 citations, it is the most influential paper in this space.

# Alloy Databases for AI-Guided Design Campaigns (Topic 3B — Critical Minerals)

Comprehensive survey of databases relevant to the FLAIME Genesis Mission proposal targeting **DOE Topic 3B: "AI-Enabled Materials Discovery and Engineering" (AMMTO)** under "Securing America's Critical Minerals Supply." Emphasis on aluminum and magnesium alloys and materials criticality data sources for supply-risk-aware alloy optimization.

**Partnership context:** Letters of collaboration from Valimet (gas atomization), AMAZEMET (ultrasonic atomization — atomizer installed at BYU), and Thermo-Calc (CALPHAD/AM Module — simulations already running on BYU HPC). Letters of support from Ames National Lab, Fehrmann Alloys, Taylor Sparks (University of Utah), Ashley Speer, Adam Clare, Chris Stiles, Jae Hattrick-Simpers, and Keith Brown.

**Preliminary results available:** AMAZEMET atomizer installed, AlSi10Mg tensile specimens (University of Utah + 3D Powder Tech), tensile data, SEM/EDS of precursor powders and atomized mixture, high-temperature tensile data, Thermo-Calc AM Module simulations (provided by TC), BYU HPC CALPHAD runs, full pKGFN pipeline implementation, and automated powder dispensing demonstration.

Informed by Edison Scientific (PaperQA3 LITERATURE_HIGH) research — full outputs in [edison-trajectories/alloy_databases_overview.md](edison-trajectories/alloy_databases_overview.md), [edison-trajectories/al_mg_databases.md](edison-trajectories/al_mg_databases.md), and [edison-trajectories/materials_criticality_databases.md](edison-trajectories/materials_criticality_databases.md).

## 1. Aluminum Alloy Databases (Priority)

### 1.1 Knovel (Elsevier)

- **Coverage**: Digitized handbooks covering wrought (1xxx–8xxx) and cast aluminum alloys
- **Properties**: Mechanical (YS, UTS, elongation, hardness), thermal (conductivity, expansion), corrosion data — varies by source handbook
- **Data type**: Experimental
- **Access**: Proprietary subscription; **University of Utah has access**
- **Format**: Interactive tables, Excel export for individual datasets; no bulk API
- **ML suitability**: Low–Moderate — document-oriented format requires manual extraction for large-scale ML use (green2017fulfillingthepromise pages 17-18)

708. composition-weighted supply-risk index
709. $\mathrm{MBS}(\mathbf{x})=\sum_i w_i\,x_i$ (weights from USGS

741. \textbf{Two-Level Hierarchical Search.}
742. The search proceeds in two levels.
743. \emph{Level~1 (Element Combination Selection):}
744. \bofn{} explores all $\sum_{k=2}^{8}\binom{\elementcount}{k}=\subsystemcount{}$
745. sub-systems---from ternary (e.g., Al--Fe--Si) through 9-component
746. alloys---spanning ${\sim}$\num{119000000} unique compositions at
747. 1\,at.\% resolution (Al\,$\geq$\,85\,at.\%), via an asynchronous
748. multi-fidelity evaluation, a novel NChooseK element-selection problem
749. solved via Bayesian optimization~\cite{mamun_2025_ada47d,daulton_2022_22101019}.
750. All three CALPHAD fidelity levels run concurrently at maximum HPC
751. parallelism; since the binding constraint is fairshare rate (not cost),
752. asynchronous BO treats pending HPC jobs as fantasy samples, updating the
753. surrogate as each completes---no synchronous batch waits.

  abstract = {AbstractWe present a benchmark test suite and an automated machine learning procedure for evaluating supervised machine learning (ML) models for predicting properties of inorganic bulk materials. abstract = {In the evolving landscape of scientific research, the complexity of global challenges demands innovative approaches to experimental planning and execution. Self-Driving Laboratories (SDLs) automate experimental tasks in chemical and materials sciences and the design and selection of experiments to optimize research processes and reduce material usage. This perspective explores improving access to SDLs via centralized facilities and distributed networks. We discuss the technical and collaborative challenges in realizing SDLs' potential to enhance human-machine and human-human collaboration, ultimately fostering a more inclusive research community and facilitating previously untenable research projects.},
  title = {Benchmarking materials property prediction methods: the Matbench test set and Automatminer reference algorithm},

  abstract = {QUANTUM ESPRESSO is an integrated suite of computer codes for electronic-structure calculations and materials modeling, based on density-functional theory, plane waves, and pseudopotentials (norm-conserving, ultrasoft, and projector-augmented wave). The acronym ESPRESSO stands for opEn Source Package for Research in Electronic Structure, Simulation, and Optimization. It is freely available to researchers around the world under the terms of the GNU General Public License. QUANTUM ESPRESSO builds upon newly-restructured electronic-structure codes that have been developed and tested by some of the original authors of novel electronic-structure algorithms and applied in the last twenty years by some of the leading materials modeling groups worldwide. Innovation and efficiency are still its main focus, with special attention paid to massively parallel architectures, and a great effort being devoted to user friendliness. QUANTUM ESPRESSO is evolving towards a distribution of independent and interoperable codes in the spirit of an open-source project, where researchers active in the field of electronic-structure calculations are encouraged to participate in the project by contributing their own codes or by implementing their own ideas into existing codes.},
  title = {A Review of Materials Data Infrastructure Projects},
  abstract = {Access to digital data and the ability to use it in an integrated computational materials engineering framework are critical needs for materials and manufacturing innovation. Since the start of the Materials Genome Initiative in 2011, several efforts have been launched to develop the resources and protocols necessary for a robust materials data infrastructure. These projects have yielded promising results, while helping to uncover and clarify the challenges that remain. ASM International's Computational Materials Data Network is active in several of these initiatives, and closely tracks others with similar goals. This presentation reports on the status of CMD Network projects and gives a brief update on many others. It also suggests ways to consolidate efforts and accelerate the development of an infrastructure for ICME.},
  abstract = {Abstract To close the gap between the rates of computational screening and experimental realization of novel materials 1,2 , we introduce the A-Lab, an autonomous laboratory for the solid-state synthesis of inorganic powders. This platform uses computations, historical data from the literature, machine learning (ML) and active learning to plan and interpret the outcomes of experiments performed using robotics. Over 17 days of continuous operation, the A-Lab realized 36 compounds from a set of 57 targets including a variety of oxides and phosphates that were identified using large-scale ab initio phase-stability data from the Materials Project and Google DeepMind. Synthesis recipes were proposed by natural-language models trained on the literature and optimized using an active-learning approach grounded in thermodynamics. Analysis of the failed syntheses provides direct and actionable suggestions to improve current techniques for materials screening and synthesis design. The high success rate demonstrates the effectiveness of artificial-intelligence-driven platforms for autonomous materials synthesis and motivates further integration of computations, historical knowledge and robotics.},
  abstract = {Abstract Despite the wide availability of density functional theory (DFT) codes, their adoption by the broader materials science community remains limited due to challenges such as software installation, input preparation, high-performance computing setup, and output analysis. To overcome these barriers, we introduce the Quantum ESPRESSO app, an intuitive, web-based platform built on AiiDAlab that integrates user-friendly graphical interfaces with automated DFT workflows. The app employs a modular Input-Process-Output model and a plugin-based architecture, providing predefined computational protocols, automated error handling, and interactive results visualization. We demonstrate the app’s capabilities through plugins for electronic band structures, projected density of states, phonon, infrared/Raman, X-ray and muon spectroscopies, Hubbard parameters (DFT+ U + V ), Wannier functions, and post-processing tools. By extending the FAIR principles to simulations, workflows, and analyses, the app enhances the accessibility and reproducibility of advanced DFT calculations and provides a general template to interface with other first-principles calculation codes.},

abstract = {Circular economy, sustainability and design for environment are some of the keywords that identify new formidable challenges to be faced in the next years. Raw materials have a dominant role in reaching that goal. Green energy, electric vehicles, communication, etc. depends on raw materials labeled as critical because of their economic importance coupled with high supply risk. For this reason, mitigating actions need to be used in materials selection and design such as material substitution, materials efficiency improvement and recycling. In this work, a method to implement raw materials criticality issues in materials selection for mechanical design is described according to the recent literature. The strategy is based on Ashby’s approach and the definition of the alloy criticality index quantifying the criticality per unit of mass of the material.},
  abstract = {A comprehensive methodology has been created to quantify the degree of criticality of the metals of the periodic table. In this paper, we present and discuss the methodology, which is comprised of three dimensions: supply risk, environmental implications, and vulnerability to supply restriction. Supply risk differs with the time scale (medium or long), and at its more complex involves several components, themselves composed of a number of distinct indicators drawn from readily available peer-reviewed indexes and public information. Vulnerability to supply restriction differs with the organizational level (i.e., global, national, and corporate). The criticality methodology, an enhancement of a United States National Research Council template, is designed to help corporate, national, and global stakeholders conduct risk evaluation and to inform resource utilization and strategic decision-making. Although we believe our methodological choices lead to the most robust results, the framework has been constructed to permit flexibility by the user. Specific indicators can be deleted or added as desired and weighted as the user deems appropriate. The value of each indicator will evolve over time, and our future research will focus on this evolution. The methodology has proven to be sufficiently robust as to make it applicable across the entire spectrum of metals and organizational levels and provides a structural approach that reflects the multifaceted factors influencing the availability of metals in the 21st century.},
  abstract = {High entropy alloys and amorphous metallic alloys represent two distinct classes of advanced alloy materials, each with unique structural characteristics. Their emergence has garnered considerable interest across the materials science and engineering communities, driven by their promising properties, including exceptional strength. However, their extensive compositional diversity poses substantial challenges for systematic exploration, as traditional experimental approaches and high-throughput calculations struggle to efficiently navigate this vast space. While the recent development in data-driven materials discovery could potentially help, such efforts are hindered by the scarcity of comprehensive data and the lack of robust predictive tools that can effectively link alloy composition with specific properties. To address these challenges, we have deployed a machine-learning-based workflow for feature selection and statistical analysis to afford predictive models that accelerate the data-driven discovery and optimization of these advanced materials. Our methodology is validated through two case studies: (i) a regression analysis of the bulk modulus, and (ii) a classification analysis based on glass-forming ability. The Bayesian-optimized regression model trained for the prediction of bulk modulus achieved an <i>R</i><sup>2</sup> of 0.969, an mean absolute error (MAE) of 3.958 GPa, and an root mean square error (RMSE) of 5.411 GPa, while our classification model for predicting glass-forming ability achieved an F1-score of 0.91, an area-under-the-curve of the receiver-operating-characteristic curve of 0.98, and an accuracy of 0.91. Furthermore, by leveraging a wide array of chemical data from diverse literature sources, we have successfully predicted a broad range of properties. This success underscores the efficacy of our modeling approach and emphasizes the importance of a comprehensive feature analysis and judicious feature selection strategy over a mere reliance on complex modeling techniques.},
  abstract = {With the growing emphasis on sustainability, criticality, and availability in materials research, providing actionable information about mineral commodities is crucial for informed decision-making and strategic planning by researchers, policy makers, and industry stakeholders. While the United States Geological Survey (USGS) offers valuable information on mineral-commodity summaries, their unstructured nature makes analysis challenging. To address this, we present a comprehensive data-analytics application () that processes the past 10 years of USGS mineral-commodity summaries into actionable insights. The application offers country-specific insights into global elemental production and reserves, along with quantitative metrics such as the Herfindahl-Hirschman index (HHI) to evaluate market concentration, identifying risks and opportunities in resource availability. It also features an artificial-intelligence assistant powered by a large language model (LLM) and a retrieval–augmented generation (RAG) system, enabling users to query various aspects of raw materials, including reserves, production, market share, usage, price, substitutes, recycling, and more. We evaluated multiple open-source LLMs for the RAG task and selected the best-performing model, , to implement in the system. This application provides valuable support for material scientists in assessing sustainability, criticality, and market risks, thereby aiding in the development of new materials. We demonstrate its application in energy materials, and by describing the application architecture and providing open access to the code, we aim to enable data-driven advancements in materials research.},
  title = {Methodology and technical input for the 2025 U.S. List of Critical Minerals—Assessing the potential effects of mineral commodity supply chain disruptions on the U.S. economy},
  abstract = {The global effort to curb carbon emissions is accelerating demand for clean energy technologies and the materials they rely on. Demand for these materials will only continue to grow, especially as some nations aim to achieve net zero emissions by 2050. While some major materials like steel, copper, and aluminum are already powering the fossil fuel economy, others are more minor materials with potential supply risks. These risks could jeopardize the ability to reduce greenhouse gas emissions within the desirable timeframe to avoid significant climate change. In some cases, it may be necessary to take action to improve the resilience of material supply chains and mitigate supply risks. Understanding the importance of individual materials to clean energy and the supply risks associated with them is necessary to identify which materials may serve as potential roadblocks to a clean energy future. The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) issued a series of 13 supply chain deep dive assessment reports on various energy technologies in 2022 in response to President Biden’s Executive Order on America’s Supply Chains (E.O. 14017). These reports emphasized that supply chain bottlenecks can occur at any stage of the value chain from mining and refining to component and even sub-system manufacturing. The bottlenecks are a combination of factors such as material availability, equipment availability, work force availability and quality, logistics, regulatory framework, and market conditions. These bottlenecks were worsened during the global Covid-19 pandemic. Its lingering impacts have hindered capacity expansion for material supply chains and prevented product lead-time recovery. One approach to reduce supply chain risks for the United States is to have a strong domestic manufacturing sector with a diverse set of producers. Boosting responsible domestic production would require leveraging the latest science not only in material extraction but also in developing substitutes, recycling, reuse, and remanufacturing. This report is an updated analysis of previous Critical Materials Strategy (CMS) reports published by the DOE in 2010, 2011, and 2019 based on national and global priorities, technology advancement, and technology adoption trends. Like the CMS reports, this analysis presents the results of a formal material criticality assessment to identify which materials are critical to the continued deployment of clean energy technologies globally. The analysis in this report leveraged the DOE supply chain deep dive assessments to develop the initial list of materials to evaluate. This DOE Critical Materials Assessment (CMA) is conducted independently of criticality assessments performed by other U.S. government agencies, such as that conducted by the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS). This analysis complements the USGS critical minerals determination in three aspects. First, the DOE assessment is performed from a global perspective, while the USGS analysis focusses on the importance of minerals to the U.S. economy. Second, this report focuses on the importance of materials to clean energy technologies, rather than to the economy in general. Lastly, this study is forward looking to 2035 based on clean energy deployment scenarios, whereas the USGS assessment is retrospective. Materials evaluated in this report that do not appear in the USGS Critical Minerals List include copper, uranium, electrical steel, and SiC. A draft version of this report received ~80 public comments related to supporting data and methodological improvement. Those comments have been incorporated as much as possible where appropriate. Highlights of findings from this 2023 CMA include: Rare earth materials (neodymium, praseodymium, dysprosium, and terbium) used in magnets in electric vehicle (EV) motors and wind turbine generators continue to be critical. While dysprosium (Dy) and terbium (Tb) are both heavy rare earth elements that serve the same function in magnets, the criticality of Tb is slightly lower than that for Dy in the short term due to the widespread use of Dy in high-grade magnets and Tb’s present role as a substitute. Similarly, praseodymium (Pr) is critical in the medium term but only near critical in the short term because it is more substitutable in magnets than neodymium (Nd); Materials used in batteries for EVs and stationary storage are now considered to be critical. While cobalt (Co) was found to be critical in this and previous reports, lithium (Li) becomes critical in the medium term due to its broader use in various battery chemistries and the rampant growth of the EV industry. Natural graphite is a new addition in this assessment and is also found to be critical; Platinum group metals used in hydrogen electrolyzers, such as platinum (Pr) and iridium (Ir), are critical due to an increased focus on hydrogen technologies to achieve net zero carbon emissions, while those used in catalytic converters, such as rhodium (Rh) and palladium (Pd), were screened out due to the decreased importance of catalytic converters in the medium term; Gallium (Ga) continues to be critical due to its use in light-emitting diodes (LEDs). In addition, the use of Ga has increased in magnet manufacturing and in semiconductor in forms such as gallium arsenide (GaAs) or gallium nitride (GaN); Major materials like Aluminum (Al), copper (Cu), nickel (Ni), and silicon (Si) move from noncritical in the short term to near critical in the medium term due to their importance in electrification; Electrical steel is near critical due to its use in transformers for the grid and electric motors in EVs.},
@techreport{usgs_mcs_2024,
  title = {Mineral Commodity Summaries 2024},
  url = {https://pubs.usgs.gov/publication/mcs2024},
  hiddenNote = {Net import reliance as \% of apparent consumption (2023): manganese 100\%, zirconium 100\%, chromium 74\%},
<exited with exit code 0>

Natural graphite is a new addition in this assessment and is also found to be critical; Platinum group metals used in hydrogen electrolyzers, such as platinum (Pr) and iridium (Ir), are critical due to an increased focus on hydrogen technologies to achieve net zero carbon emissions, while those used in catalytic converters, such as rhodium (Rh) and palladium (Pd), were screened out due to the decreased importance of catalytic converters in the medium term; Gallium (Ga) continues to be critical due to its use in light-emitting diodes (LEDs). In addition, the use of Ga has increased in magnet manufacturing and in semiconductor in forms such as gallium arsenide (GaAs) or gallium nitride (GaN); Major materials like Aluminum (Al), copper (Cu), nickel (Ni), and silicon (Si) move from noncritical in the short term to near critical in the medium term due to their importance in electrification; Electrical steel is near critical due to its use in transformers for the grid and electric motors in EVs.},
